articles.title: British police say no explosives found in vehicles near U.S.-run base
articles.summary: A surprise decision by the U.K.'s counterterrorism police to release five suspects on bail during an investigation into a suspected bomb plot at a U.S.-operated air force base in England has prompted…

image.caption: Police officers guard an area as roadblocks remain in place near RAF Fairford airbase. Police said no explosives were found in the suspicious vehicles after five men arrested were freed on bail. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A surprise decision by the U.K.'s counterterrorism police to release five suspects on bail during an investigation into a suspected bomb plot at a U.S.-operated air force base in England has prompted questions and uncertainty about the incident.
5 British men were arrested Sunday under terrorism-related suspicion, but freed on bail

A surprise decision by the U.K.'s counterterrorism police to release five suspects on bail during an investigation into a suspected bomb plot at a U.S.-operated airbase in England has prompted questions and uncertainty about the incident.
Police confirmed Tuesday that no explosives were found in three vans linked to the suspects, and said the decision to grant bail was grounded in "experience and strategy."

U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he was surprised the five young British men who were arrested Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences near the RAF Fairford airbase were freed a day later.
"I wouldn't have done that," Trump said.
U.K. police arrest 5 near airbase on suspicion of terrorist plot
'Multiple lines of inquiry'

The base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran. Counterterror detectives have said they were investigating "multiple lines of inquiry," including whether the suspects had a link to Iran. Iran has denied involvement.
The head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, stressed that the suspects — all British nationals in their 20s — face stringent conditions and "absolutely remain under investigation."
"Now, I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and strategy," he said.

items: British police release 5 London-based men after arrests near airbase used by U.S.

blocks.text: Taylor said people's concerns about the incident were being "heightened by the international commentary that we are seeing."
In an interview with Fox News, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the case "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor," but did not name a specific country or give more details.
"I know a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have been released on bail, as some of the people are being investigated," he said.
Officials hint at possible Iran role
A police cordon remained in place around three vans found close to the Fairford base on Tuesday, as armed police and counterterrorism officers continued to examine the scene.

A local farmer said she called police after seeing the vans blocking a road near the airbase as she drove home in the early hours of Sunday. She said she came across a group of men, some with their faces covered, nearby, and that the men ran away when they saw her vehicle.
Earlier, army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine the vans. Taylor said "a quantity of petrol was recovered" from the vans, but no explosives.

Taylor, the counterterror police chief, said lines of inquiry include whether the suspected offences were committed by "proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."

Investigators haven't concluded whether the incident was state-backed or what the motive was, but authorities have strongly hinted that Iran is possibly involved. They are also investigating a possible link to Russia or non-state militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners.

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the U.K. "shouldn't be cowed by sabre-rattling from Iran." He said the Iranian regime "is one that wishes harm to our country, our allies and the freedom and democracy that we enjoy."
The Iranian embassy denied the country's involvement in the suspected plot.

Iran and allied militant groups have been accused of plotting or carrying out attacks on U.S. , British and Jewish targets in the past, allegedly acting through local proxies while denying responsibility.

The airbase houses the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing and is a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. Fairford was used during the 1990 Gulf War, the 2003 Iraq war and the U.S.-Israeli bombardment of Iran this year.
British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50 per cent in the six months to December 2025.
Trump rejects Iran ceasefire proposal, Tehran says talks could resume
Possible security or intelligence failures

It was unclear whether the arrested men had been on the security services' radars. Local residents described seeing heightened security around RAF Fairford in recent days, with heavy vehicles parked across entrance gates.

Trump said the suspects were detained following cooperation between the U.S. and Britain, and had been "under view" for some time. Police, however, said the arrests were triggered by a late-night call about the suspicious vehicles near the base.

The farmer who called the police, who didn't want to be named, alleged that her call to police may have foiled the suspected plot. She added that several hours passed between her call and when police "suddenly decided to evacuate people" in the area.
"But meanwhile, those vans were right in the middle of the village next to everyone's houses and no one did anything," she said.
Streeting, the defence secretary, said Monday that the farmer only had a "partial picture" of the operation.
Local lawmaker Roz Savage said there was "anger and anxiety" from residents, especially those who were evacuated from their homes and still haven't been able to return.
"I have so many questions right now, more questions than answers," she said in a video message on X. "This should not have been allowed to happen."

articles.title: Give BrewDog second chance, says new owner as it invests £50m
articles.summary:
US cannabis and drinks firm Tilray, which took over in March, will improve beers, pubs and working conditions

BrewDog’s new owner has urged drinkers to give the ailing brand “a second…

blocks.text: BrewDog’s new owner has urged drinkers to give the ailing brand “a second chance” as it invests more than £50m in improving the company’s beers, pubs and working conditions.

The US cannabis and drinks company Tilray bought BrewDog for £33m in March this year, after the company collapsed into administration after five years of losses and a series of controversies relating to the treatment of workers under the founder James Watt.
Some staff accused Watt in 2021 of fostering a “toxic work culture”. He apologised for some of his conduct and left the company in 2024.
Tilray’s chief executive, Irwin Simon, said it was listening to BrewDog’s customers and staff and had increased pay this year.

He said Tilray was working on the launch of new beers while investing in the company’s brewery in Aberdeenshire to improve the quality and reliability of existing lines, adding that more than £1m of beer that did not meet quality standards had been thrown away.

Simon said Tilray was a long-term investor that aimed to grow the company and was also considering buying additional British craft beers for its portfolio. He said Tilray may also consider reviving BrewDog’s closed distillery business if it felt there was a sufficient market in the UK.

Administrators said earlier this month that creditors owed about £190m by the collapsed “punk” brewer would not be paid back in full. However, it is understood that Tilray has picked up the bill on some key suppliers in order to ensure continuity on items such as ingredients.
Its deal in March to buy BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars rendered the shares of more than 200,000 crowdfunding investors worthless.
However, these “equity punks” continue to receive benefits, including discounted beer, and some were invited along to ask questions at a relaunch of the brand on Tuesday.
One asked why BrewDog beers could not be as cheap as a £2 Bud Light in Wetherspoons. Simon said its craft beers would never be that cheap but added: “We deserve a second chance.”

Speaking from BrewDog’s giant bar in Waterloo, central London, with music blaring in the background, the American said: “We are different. We are not a big company like [Budweiser maker] Anheuser-Busch. We are entrepreneurial, nimble and want to connect to consumers.”

March’s deal only included 11 of BrewDog’s chain of bars, with 38 closing and 440 staff losing their jobs. Tilray has since reopened five of those bars and Simon said it was hoping to open more but he said he would only do so in “A locations” and not the “BCD locations” that BrewDog’s owners had previously considered.

He said BrewDog could bounce back from the negative publicity it suffered under Watt’s leadership and return to the annual sales of £350m a year, up from about £225m at present, and become profitable again with the right support. He believes it could be worth as much as £2bn in the future.
after newsletter promotion
“The name of the brand is BrewDog; it is not anyone’s name,” he said. “It is not about one person; it is about a team.”

Before a new ad campaign launching next week based around the slogan “choose craft”, Simon said: “What we have to do is perform. What we have to do is what we’re doing here today. Bringing people together and launching campaigns and doing what we say we’re going to do.”

Last week the new owners launched an ad campaign that appeared to take a shot at Watt, with lines including: “No More Cunning Stunts. Just Great Beer” alongside an image of its Punk IPA and “A Little Less Allegation” alongside its Elvis Juice.

Tilray also published a letter outlining its commitment to BrewDog’s future, saying that under its ownership BrewDog would have “sensible working practices, community initiatives and a people-first approach”.
It said: “We’re going to take good care of this beloved Scottish craft beer business.”
The company has also introduced 24 Tilray-owned American craft beers into BrewDog bars and is planning to produce some of those at BrewDog’s brewery in Scotland.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy returns to court as lawyer asks judge to find her not guilty
articles.summary:
In new posture, Kevin Reddington argues there was insufficient evidence that she murdered her children

Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Tuesday in her lawyers’ fight against a possible…

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Tuesday in her lawyers’ fight against a possible retrial after a jury earlier in September failed to reach a verdict on charges that she murdered her children – a proceeding that ended without definitive action.

Clancy’s team asked William F Sullivan, the superior court judge in Plymouth, Massachusetts, to deem Clancy, 36, not guilty of murder for killing her ⁠three young children in 2023, which she maintains she did while suffering postpartum psychosis and is therefore not legally responsible for. Sullivan on Tuesday only heard arguments on that request.
Meanwhile, the office of the Plymouth country district attorney, Timothy Cruz, again chose to not disclose whether it plans to try Clancy again.

Sullivan concluded the hour-long proceeding on Tuesday by setting another hearing on 2 November, when, he said, he wanted to discuss potential upcoming trial dates. A gag order requested by prosecutors against Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, is also expected to be considered at that hearing.

Sullivan held Tuesday’s hearing after declaring a mistrial on 4 September due to the deadlocked jury. A lone juror prevented the 12-member jury from agreeing to a unanimous verdict on whether to find Clancy guilty or not guilty by reason ⁠of insanity.
Several members of the jury have said 11 members of the panel wanted to find her not guilty by reason of insanity.
A first-degree murder charge carries a life sentence.

Clancy did not dispute at trial that she fatally strangled her children with ⁠exercise bands on 24 January 2023 in the family’s suburban Boston home. The former nurse then cut her neck and wrists with a knife and threw herself from her second-story bedroom window in an attempted suicide.

Reddington argued at trial that Clancy did not understand the wrongfulness of her actions and that she was experiencing postpartum ‌psychosis when she killed Cora, five; Dawson, three; and eight-month-old Callan.
On Tuesday, in a new posture, Reddington argued there was insufficient evidence to support beyond a reasonable doubt that she actually murdered her children or admitted doing so.
Investigators, he said, “just immediately assumed that this woman is guilty”, according to CBS News. “There’s no evidence that she admitted she did this … Why would she kill those three children?”
Redding also contended: “This entire case is based on speculation.”

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told Sullivan that this was the first time Reddington had questioned in court the sufficiency of the evidence linking Clancy to her children’s killings. Buckingham said the evidence of Clancy killing her children was “voluminous” and dismissed claims to the contrary as “laughable”.

Reddington said non-lawyers had difficulty understanding the notion that someone could admit culpability while also not being criminally responsible. He said that difficulty had prompted many public observers and high-profile figures to describe Clancy as a “demon” and demand her execution.
“This is coming from politicians,” said Reddington, who singled out Donald Trump.

When previously asked for his reaction to the verdict, the president said: “Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something.”

If found not guilty by reason of insanity, Clancy would be committed to a Massachusetts state psychiatric hospital. The court would regularly re-evaluate whether to keep Clancy committed to that hospital.

Prosecutors don’t have to retry Clancy on first-degree murder charges. They could try brokering a plea deal or retrying her on second-degree murder charges, which would allow Clancy to waive a jury trial and be tried by a judge.

In arguing against a retrial, Clancy’s legal team has argued that jury notes clearly said the holdout juror had been ​refusing to apply Sullivan’s instructions on how to decide whether prosecutors proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt. Clancy’s attorneys contend that the holdout juror should have been dismissed rather ‌than allowing the case to ​be retried.
Her attorneys have also requested to review confidential records about the jury and question the holdout about his truthfulness during the jury selection process.
The holdout’s attorney, Edward Paltzik, has told Fox News that his client, Michael Desronvil, “had zero doubt” and “rigidly applied the reasonable doubt standard”.

In a video shared on Fox on Monday, Desronvil argued that focus on him should instead be channeled to “the ones that can’t defend themselves, and the ones that can’t fight the battles – and those are Cora, Dawson and Callan”.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Burnham stakes his future on care, electoral reform and Europe in emotional Labour conference speech
articles.summary: PM says his plan, which includes ending pensions triple lock to fund national care service, will ‘allow us to rise again’

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has staked his future on a gamble that the public will back radical progressive policies on social care, electoral reform and Europe, telling voters that his agenda will break the mould of the last 40 years and “allow us to rise again”.

In a deeply personal speech at Labour’s conference, Burnham began building his next general election manifesto, acknowledging that he may end up paying the price for creating sharp new dividing lines in politics.
“I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,” he said. “I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.”

However, while the prime minister said he would try to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living, he admitted his ambitious policy prospectus would have to wait until after the next election because of the state of the public finances.

“These things are not everything, but I hope you will see it as a sign – a strong one – of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come,” he told Labour activists.

“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down. The approach I am outlining today is the responsible one.”

With global economic storm clouds gathering and Labour dropping behind Reform UK in one poll this week, Burnham was determined to leave his audience in the conference hall in Liverpool, and at home, some hope.

During his hour-long speech, in which he paused several times after being overcome with emotion at mentioning the death of his father, he said he wanted to show the UK was “something worth saving, worth fighting for”.
He said: “I believe the plan I have outlined today will not just hold us together, it will allow us to rise again.”

Burnham promised to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong, saying it was time to admit “Brexit hasn’t given us control” and that it was a handbrake on growth.
In his strongest hint yet that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he said he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship with the bloc at the reset summit this autumn.
Options could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, the customs union or single market, or even reversing Brexit in its entirety.

“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” he said. “I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. We need to restore a high level of growth and prosperity for Britain.”

While public attitudes towards leaving the EU have shifted over time, Burnham’s shift away from Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines will still be a big political gamble in seats such as his own, Makerfield, which voted for Brexit.
Burnham confirmed he would end the pensions triple lock should Labour win the next election and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.

He plans to break the link between wage growth and pensions and promised instead a rise based on inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, which he claimed would still leave millions of pensioners better off.

He said pensioners would benefit from the new care system – which would be expected to follow the Scottish system in covering care costs but not accommodation – and a promise to exempt them from income tax.

Burnham suggested that care workers were “invisible to the political class” but he told them: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.”
As well as a promise to fix the broken system, the prime minister’s words will be interpreted as a sign he is preparing to carve out migrant care workers from Shabana Mahmood’s immigration measures.

blocks.caption: Members of the cabinet watch Burnham’s speech. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

blocks.text: In another commitment to a long-held belief, Burnham also confirmed he would put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto, announcing a cross-party national commission to consider options to replace first past the post with a form of proportional representation.

“We can’t succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times,” he said. “It is always in my mind that I’m the seventh prime minister in 10 years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.
“We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on 30% of the vote or less.”
Burnham said it was the drive of his government for every person to feel greater control over the basics of life and renew faith that systems could work for them.

He said the common wealth of Britain, its homes, energy, water and care, had been stripped out and sold for profit. “The wealth we had created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few,” he said.
“The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said in remarks that drew a standing ovation.
Burnham promised two new pieces of legislation later this year, including a leasehold reform bill that would put curbs on charges for homes.

“The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” he said. “This is the break we are making with the flawed thinking of the last 40 years. Not seeing housing only as a market with winners and losers, but as an essential everyone needs for a good life.”

blocks.caption: Burnham addresses his audience in Liverpool. Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He said a water bill would repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on state-owned water companies, which was a “symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain”. There will be new curbs on bosses and pay and new powers for mayors over water systems.

He also confirmed the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid, while ministers will speed up the breaking of the link between energy prices and the international gas market.

The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “Burnham wants to take Britain back to the 1970s – a time of more government control, more trade union control and no economic growth. There is a reason our country took a different course after that decade.

“Nothing Burnham announced today will do anything to fix Britain’s long-term problems. He had no plan to fix our stagnant economy. No plan to fund defence. No plan to sort out the spiralling welfare bill beyond more government schemes.”

Reform UK’s Nigel Farage said: “By potentially scrapping the triple lock, Andy Burnham will abdicate his responsibility to British pensioners. Instead of cutting our bloated benefits bill, stopping migrants from accessing benefits, or slashing foreign aid, he’s considering launching an offensive against our elderly.”

Labour MPs responded with relief and enthusiasm to Burnham’s conference address, which the prime minister wrote almost entirely alone, with more than one describing it as the speech of their political lifetimes.
However, there were words of caution from some ministers and Downing Street insiders, who will be more interested in how the speech goes down with the wider public at home than in the room.

“I don’t want to be negative, but we’ve got to be realistic,” one cabinet minister said. “We just don’t know what’s going to happen with the economic headwinds. But if anybody can get us through it, Andy can.”

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on defense company
articles.summary: The Estonian government accused Moscow of an "act of sabotage" that is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe. The Baltic state has received support from EU and NATO leaders.

image.caption: Milrem Robotics makes autonomous unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine [FILE: December 2022]Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: NATO and EU leaders rallied behind Estonia on Tuesday, after the Baltic country accused Russia of being behind an arson attack in its capital Tallinn.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Moscow was found responsible for the August 15 arson attack against defense company Milrem Robotics, after the government conducted an investigation into the incident.
Milrem Robotics develops ground drones that are used in Ukraine.

"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," Tsahkna said on X, adding that the perpetrators had been arrested, and Russia's ambassador had been summoned.
"This act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine," Tsahkna said.
NATO chief Mark Rutte backed Estonia, accusing Russia of furthering "its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies."

"It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine," Rutte said, adding that Russia is "failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine."
Kremlin says links to arson are "baseless"
Estonia has a population of 1.2 million and it borders Russia to the east.

The incident took place on the night of August 15, when a fire broke out in a building used by Milrem Robotics in Tallinn. According to a statement from the Estonian government, authorities were on the scene right away and no injuries were reported.
Three suspects were later detained in Latvia in connection with the arson attack and were handed over to Estonia this month.
The Kremlin responded to the arson investigation findings by dismissing them as "baseless" and with "absolutely no relation to reality."
"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow.
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare
EU and NATO leaders rally behind Estonia

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged Germany's "full solidarity" with Estonia. "Russia's reckless hostilities will not divide us. They only strengthen our resolve to bolster NATO deterrence and support Ukraine," Wadephul wrote on X.
The EU said it stood by Estonia, saying the arson attack was "reckless" and would not deter the bloc in its support for Ukraine.
"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand said.
French President Emmanuel Macron labeled the attack a "dangerous escalation" by Russia. He said it represented another in a "multiplication of these hostile acts."
"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron wrote on X.
Lithuanian foreign minister Kestutis Budrys said "Russia's fingerprints are all over" the arson attack, adding that it was proof that Moscow's "hostile activities do not stop at Ukraine's borders."
Neighboring Latvia's President Edgars Rinkevics said in response to the incident that "more support for Ukraine ... will be needed and must be provided."
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also commented ont he matter, saying attribution of the arson attack was "extremely serious" and "directed against Europe as a whole."
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats

articles.title: Key data missing for half of US child labor deaths, official report finds
articles.summary:
Over half of 260 workplace child fatalities between 2013 and 2023 lacked data on cause of death or the industry worked

Information is missing on over half of deaths at work of people under…

blocks.text: Information is missing on over half of deaths at work of people under the age of 18 in the US because of significant gaps in child labor data, according to a government accountability office (GAO) report released on Tuesday.

The report found that between 2013 and 2023, an average of 24 children under the age of 18 died each year due to work-related incidents. Over half of the 260 child fatality cases did not contain detailed data on the cause of death or the industry the child worked in.

Among the 109 fatalities with a reported industry, 75% worked in agriculture. Among the 111 fatalities with a reported cause of death, two-thirds of fatalities were caused by transportation incidents.

The report cited a lack of coordination between agencies as a source of data-collection issues. Since January 2025, the US Department of Labor’s collaboration with other federal agencies to address child labor law violations has “largely diminished”, the GAO found.

Data gaps cited in the report include missing information regarding industry worked and cause of death on the agency’s workplace fatality data. Data collection on working children’s injuries and illnesses changed in 2021, so data cannot be compared with earlier years. A labor department survey and two other federal datasets that included child labor injury data have also ended.

The report found that between fiscal years 2015 and 2025, 59% of child labor law violations involved employers scheduling 14- or 15-year-old children to work longer or later than permitted by federal child labor laws. Sixty-two per cent of child labor violations during this period occurred in the accommodation and food services industry.

It also found that the labor department’s wage and hour division “has not fully addressed” challenges the agency faces in enforcing child labor laws and that since January 2025: “DOL’s collaboration with federal agencies on activities to prevent and detect child labor violations has largely diminished.”

The report was issued in response to a July 2023 request led by the House education and workforce committee ranking member, Bobby Scott of Virginia, for the Government Accountability Office to assess the scope of the issue of child labor in the US, the capacity of government agencies to monitor, research, and enforce child labor laws, and the effectiveness of current efforts to address illegal child labor.
“The GAO report shows that the Trump administration’s upheaval of federal agencies has harmed children,” said Scott.

“As a result of the administration’s chaos, the federal government’s response to child labor lacks coordination, and its enforcement of child labor laws is less effective. Additionally, the cost of slashing budgets at critical research agencies such as the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has led to real harms. The federal government cannot effectively prevent child labor if it does not have the information it needs to know where children are working, if they are being injured, and where the greatest risks exist,” said Scott.
Scott has introduced a bill, the Protecting Children Act, which would improve data collection and usage to inform child labor enforcement.

The report comes as child labor violations in the US have surged over the past decade, 19 states have moved to relax child labor laws since 2021. The number of minors employed in violation of child labor laws in the US increased from 1,012 children in fiscal year 2015 to 5,272 in fiscal year 2025.

articles.title: Smart ring maker Oura puts off initial public offering due to market ‘uncertainty’
articles.summary:
Researchers say the IPO market was off to a solid start but tailed off in the third quarter

Smart ring maker

blocks.text: Smart ring maker Oura Inc says it is postponing a planned initial public offering due to market “uncertainty”.
In a Tuesday press release, Oura said it is delaying the stock market float “despite strong demand”.

The IPO market had a solid start to the year but tailed off in the third quarter, according to research firm Renaissance Capital. Concerns about a possible slowdown in spending on artificial intelligence, the Federal Reserve’s resumption of rate hikes and a surge in bond yields – making borrowing more expensive – all played a factor, Renaissance said.
Oura customers use the ring to monitor their health, including sleep patterns and fitness activity. The company gets the bulk of its revenue from ring sales, with the rest coming from subscriptions.

The company approached the IPO with momentum: the introduction of the Oura Ring 5 helped boost the number of paid members to 5.7 million and the company expects revenue for the fiscal year ending on Wednesday to have grown by 90%.
after newsletter promotion

Oura had planned to sell 50m shares in the IPO between $40 and $44, with nearly three-quarters of them being sold by current shareholders. At the midpoint of the price range, Oura’s IPO would have given it a market value of $13.5bn.

articles.title: No explosives found in three vans searched near RAF Fairford, say police
articles.summary:
Head of counter-terrorism policing defends decision to bail five British men arrested in connection with incident

No explosive devices were found in three vans searched near RAF Fairford as…

blocks.text: No explosive devices were found in three vans searched near RAF Fairford as part of a terrorism investigation but a quantity of petrol was recovered, police have said.
Five British nationals were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after a resident living near the Gloucestershire airbase reported suspicious activity involving three vans.

Defending the decision to bail the men, Laurence Taylor, the head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “Yesterday we released the five men on police bail. They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision making, and this was certainly the case yesterday.

“I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”

Taylor said of the van: “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.”

The vans were marked by the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles, which prompted speculation online and in the local community that the men could have been fuel thieves.
Residents were returning home on Tuesday after spending days evacuated from their village.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, claimed the events were the work of a “foreign actor” but did not provide further details. He said “a lot of people are disturbed” after the release of the suspects from custody. Donald Trump had earlier said he was “surprised” the group had been freed.

Speculation has been growing about a connection between the weekend’s incident and Iran. The potential link was a key reason behind Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, attended by senior police and security officials among others.
The same day Taylor said he knew there was “significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident”.

He added: “But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”
In March the British government gave the US permission to use the base for “specific defensive operations into Iran”.
The country’s London embassy has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.

Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on the village of Whelford, where five British nationals were arrested for terror and explosives-related offences.

Mark Richings, a butcher in Fairford, told the Press Association: “There’s no change in here and we just got on with it as normal. We are a bit quieter today, but everybody seems to be OK, and we are having a bit of a chat about it.
“We just carried on as normal. We have enough to do to occupy our minds. If anything did happen, there isn’t a lot we could have done about it.”

Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.

Father Michael Robertson, the priest at the nearby St Thomas Catholic church, told PA: “A lot of parishioners didn’t think they could get to church. Those that came were worried but perfectly happy with the situation.

“In fact, quite a lot of Americans who have deployed here actually come to mass and some of the permanently deployed Americans are full members of the parish. We’re quite contented with the situation generally. Obviously, the disruption upsets people.”
Additional reporting by Jamie Grierson

articles.title: Police investigating after 10K litres of diesel stolen from 3 Calgary gas stations
articles.summary: BG Fuels says it's had 10,000 litres of diesel stolen from three Mobil gas stations in Calgary, with surveillance footage suggesting the fuel was pulled directly out of underground tanks.

image.caption: BG Fuels says it's had 10,000 litres of diesel stolen from three Mobil gas stations in Calgary, with surveillance footage suggesting the fuel was pulled directly out of underground tanks. (Nate Luit/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
BG Fuels says it's had 10,000 litres of diesel stolen from three Mobil gas stations in Calgary, with surveillance footage suggesting the fuel was pulled directly out of underground tanks.
Footage suggests fuel was pulled directly from underground tanks
Sam Babcock didn’t think much of it when he got a call that his company’s fuel inventory was missing a massive amount.

Typically, the BG Fuels territory manager in southern Alberta would chalk up the dip to a simple input error. Babcock didn’t realize the loss was the first in a string of thefts equalling a loss of roughly 10,000 litres of diesel fuel, costing the company approximately $20,000.
“We’ve never seen this. Never across the country as well. At least in my time here, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” said Babcock.

BG Fuels is a Canadian wholesaler operating under the Mobil, Esso and Waypoint Convenience brands around the country. It's raising alarm after three Mobil gas stations in Calgary were hit with thefts in the last few weeks, with diesel fuel pulled directly out of underground tanks.
Most of the total was sucked up in an initial incident where the company lost about 8,000 litres of fuel, Babcock said.

After reviewing surveillance footage of the first theft, Babcock said it showed a truck arrive at around 4 a.m. while the station was closed and remain for roughly 25 minutes while removing diesel from the site, before driving away.
Given that a large commercial truck was used to store the fuel, Babcock pointed out anyone driving by at that hour wouldn't have thought anything suspicious was amiss.
But the thefts are creating a lot of stress for station agents, he said.
“A lot of them have come at nighttime to check in on their sites. They can’t sleep,” said Babcock, who oversees 28 gas stations in southern Alberta.

Surveillance footage shows something went wrong for the perpetrators during the second theft, resulting in only about 50 litres taken. About 2,000 litres was stolen during the final theft, Babcock said. The company said it believes the same perpetrators were involved in all three thefts, judging from the footage.
The thefts present a large safety concern, Babcock said, as the amount of diesel stolen is a lot of flammable material that needs to be handled correctly.
Police investigating thefts
The Calgary Police Service confirmed on Tuesday that it is investigating the incidents.
Nick Wilsher, a sergeant with the service’s crime prevention team, said that while smaller thefts involving siphoning fuel are more common, thefts like what BG reported are unusual.
Wilsher compared the market for fuel to other online marketplaces where a consumer may see a cheap product, know its low price may be because it’s stolen, and “pretend ‘well, maybe it’s not.’”
“It’s not a victimless crime ... Those costs are passed on to you as the consumer," said Wilsher.

“You might think you're getting a deal, but you’re actually making it more expensive for everybody else, including yourself when you can’t buy this cheap diesel anymore. You’re going to have to get it at the pump.”

items: Poilievre urges tax cuts to make diesel fuel more affordable
If Trump bans U.S. diesel exports, global prices will go even higher, experts say

blocks.text: Wilsher said retailers could look to increase security, improve locks and introduce tamper-proof alarm systems and more video surveillance to protect against thefts.

He added that the surveillance footage recovered by BG is helpful to show police the kind of vehicle used in the thefts, where they came from and drove to, and to potentially give them a closer look at the people involved.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Andrew Jeffrey is a multimedia journalist with CBC Calgary. He previously worked for CBC News in his hometown of Edmonton, reported for the StarMetro Calgary, and worked as an editor for Toronto-based magazines Strategy and Realscreen. You can reach him at andrew.jeffrey@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Everything you need to know about the 10 questions in Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum
articles.summary: CBC News breaks down each of the referendum questions to help voters prepare to mark the 10 ballots.

image.caption: Canada and Alberta flags flap in the breeze with Wedge Mountain in the background in Kananaskis, Alta. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
CBC News breaks down each of the referendum questions to help voters prepare to mark the 10 ballots.
CBC News breaks down every ballot question to help you prepare ahead of voting day
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 1:46 PM EDT | Last Updated: 14 minutes ago
The clock is ticking down to Alberta's province-wide referendum on 10 questions, with polls set to open at 9 a.m. on Monday, Oct. 19.
Five of those questions are related to immigration, while four propose constitutional changes — each of these are "yes" or "no" questions.

The final question has to do with the future of Alberta independence. Voters will be asked to choose only one of two options: for the province to stay in Canada, or to hold a second binding referendum on separating from the country.
CBC News has reported extensively on the questions to help voters prepare before marking the 10 ballots.
Scroll through the referendum questions below and click on the links for in-depth analyses of each of the questions.
Question 1

"Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?"

items: The first immigration question suggests Alberta take more control over immigration

blocks.text: At the heart of this question is a tug of war between federal and provincial control over immigration. In our analysis, we break down the wording of the question step-by-step and explore the complex history that has led to this particular question.
Question 2

"Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?"

items: Temporary residents who are not 'Alberta-approved' lose eligibility to public health and education

blocks.text: This question suggests denying certain non-permanent residents public health care, education and other social services altogether — that is, unless the province approves their immigration status. Our story explores how this question, and questions 3 and 4, are interconnected and could re-shape how the province approaches temporary residents' access to services.
Question 3

"Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?"

items: Non-permanent residents wait at least 12 months to access social services

blocks.text: This question asks whether people who hold temporary permits should have to wait at least one complete year after arriving in Alberta before becoming eligible for social services, but not including public services like health care and education.
Question 4

"Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family's use of the health care and education systems?"

items: Alberta charges temporary residents for public health care and education

blocks.text: The Alberta government suggests charging non-permanent residents a fee or premium for access to public health care and education. The amount of the premium or fee would be decided after the vote, the province said. Premier Danielle Smith recently floated a $1,900 fee for temporary residents' access to health care, similar to a premium charged by the United Kingdom.
Question 5

"Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?"

items: Alberta referendum pitches proof of citizenship at the polls

blocks.text: The province suggests if this question is adopted it will develop "clearer voting rules" that require individuals to show proof of citizenship to vote in a provincial election. Our examination explores the underlying motivation behind this question, whether voter fraud is a widespread problem and which groups may be impacted most in the case of a "yes" vote.
LISTEN | Calgarians read and react to the 10 referendum questions:
Calgary Eyeopener5:00Calgarians read and react to the 10 referendum questions
Question 6

"Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King's Bench and Appeal courts?"

items: Province pitches gaining power to elect its own judges for certain courts

blocks.text: With this question, Alberta is proposing a constitutional change that would rewrite an arrangement that dates back to Confederation in 1867. Our story explores the role Alberta has in appointing judges today and the province's push to secure control over judicial appointments, which predates the referendum.
Question 7
"Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?"

items: Amending the Constitution to abolish the federal senate

blocks.text: Alberta governments have long expressed disillusionment with the federal Senate, and this ballot question proposes doing away with the whole thing entirely. Our story traces the history of Alberta's grievances and explores why abolishment is highly unlikely even in the event of a "yes" vote.
Question 8

"Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?"

items: Albertans to vote on opting out of federal programs — while keeping cash

blocks.text: Here, Alberta is pitching an attempt to limit what constitutional experts refer to as constitutional spending power — essentially, Ottawa's ability to transfer money to provinces while attaching conditions to it. This story explores the varied constitutional perspectives tied to a push like this, and what it could mean for existing federal programs.
Question 9

"Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province's laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province's laws and federal laws conflict?"

items: Prioritize provincial laws over federal laws in some areas where they conflict

blocks.text: This question is tied to the concept of federal paramountcy in Canadian constitutional law, which essentially means that when federal and provincial laws are at odds, federal law wins out. Our story explores why Alberta wants to flip the script and what it means for the concept of Canada as a federation.
Question 10

"Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"
This isn't a "yes" or "no" question. Voters will be asked to choose one of the following two options:
Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada.

Option 2: The government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

items: Referendum on whether to have binding referendum on separating from Canada

blocks.text: This question has often been at the centre of referendum-related discourse across Alberta. CBC News has covered the Albertan independence movement and responses to it, including federalist sentiment. Here are some of the stories we've recently reported:

items: With time running out, new poll suggests Alberta separatism support is slipping
Establishing independent Alberta could cost up to $170B over 5 years: report

articles.title: 'Keep demanding space:' Marcos highlights ASEAN women's role in economy, innovation
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. underscored on Tuesday the significance of women"s leadership and representation in driving ASEAN's economy and innovation, urging them to keep asserting their place in…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 1:31am

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. underscored on Tuesday the significance of women’s leadership and representation in driving ASEAN's economy and innovation, urging them to keep asserting their place in leadership.
In his speech at the 4th ASEAN Women Leaders’ Summit, Marcos pointed out that women remain underrepresented in the Cabinets and parliaments of ASEAN member states.
“For decades, women across Southeast Asia have sustained our families, strengthened our communities, driven our economies, and yet their contributions have too often been undervalued,” Marcos said.

“That must change. Women are not simply beneficiaries of our progress. They are leaders and innovators, shaping ASEAN’s future, and our policies, institutions, and investments must reflect this,” he added.

Marcos said the underrepresentation of women in national and regional dialogues reflects not only a gap in representation, but a gap in the perspectives that shape key policy decisions across the region.

“Our work is far from complete. Women remain underrepresented in the Cabinets and Parliaments of ASEAN member states. This is not simply a gap in representation; it is a gap in leadership in whose voices shape the decisions that affect our region,” the President said.
He urged women leaders to never stop leading and pushing forward their sector’s regional agenda and calls.
“To our women leaders in governance, civil society, business, and technology: Keep leading, keep demanding space, keep pushing our region forward,” Marcos said.
“Together, let us shape an ASEAN where equality is not just a policy target, but a lived daily reality for every woman and child,” he added.
Marcos also mentioned the ASEAN Women, Peace, and Security Agenda, emphasizing that having women at the decision-making table makes peace agreements “more durable and rebuilding is more inclusive.”
To further expand women's economic inclusion, Marcos pointed out that the care economy should no longer be overlooked, noting its vital function in sustaining overall economic growth.

“Unpaid care work falls disproportionately on women, restricting their time and opportunity to lead in the formal workforce, especially in the so-called non-traditional fields,” the President said. —LDF, GMA News
“By investing in care infrastructure and redistributing care obligations, we do not just support women, we unlock billions of dollars in economic potential across our region,” he added.
The Philippines holds this year's ASEAN Chairmanship. Last May, it hosted the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu, and is set to host the 49th Summit in November. (END)

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy appears in court as her lawyer pushes for murder case to be dismissed
articles.summary: Clancy's defence lawyer wants her to be cleared of murdering her three children in 2023 but prosecutors say the state proved guilt.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide
Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, has appeared in court for the first time since her murder trial fell apart earlier this month.
Her defence team on Tuesday argued the judge should dismiss her case but prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt.

Clancy, 36, does not deny killing her three children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
It is still not clear if she will face a retrial. The request to dismiss the case is among those that will be discussed at a hearing on 2 November, Judge William Sullivan said.

One of the motions addressed on Tuesday was from Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, who asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts motion that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not argue their case effectively.
Reddington also brought a new defence forward arguing there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children.
"This entire case is based on speculation," he said.
It was a change of argument from the defence lawyer, who during the trial focused on Clancy's mental health - urging the jury to find her not criminally responsible because of it.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called Reddington's argument "laughable".
She said state prosecutors had presented numerous pieces of evidence showing Clancy was in a healthy mental state at the time of the murders during the trial.
"The Commonwealth met its burden," Buckingham said.
She argued Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months, in their Massachusetts home.

articles.title: First female prime minister named in Morocco after winning elections
articles.summary: Her appointment by the king makes her only the second woman to lead a government in the Arab world.

blocks.text: At a victory press conference, prior to her announcement as prime minister, El Mansouri was asked whether the state would need to make changes to accommodate her in Muslim religious ceremonies attended by the king, including Friday and Eid prayers, where men and women pray in separate sections.
She did not directly answer the question, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country.
"His Majesty is the holder of wisdom… If I am entrusted with the responsibility of head of government, it will be a great honour," she said.
El Mansouri is one of Morocco's most prominent female politicians.
A lawyer by training, she studied at Mohammed V University in the capital, Rabat, before continuing her education in France and the US, specialising in business and corporate law.
She entered politics after Pam was founded in 2008 and became the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh in 2009. She returned to the post after the 2021 elections.
In the past five years, she served as a minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under former Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
In February 2024, she became the co-ordinator of Pam's leadership coalition.
El Mansouri has rejected her portrayal as an "iron woman", telling Pam's magazine in 2021: "I am neither a woman of steel nor iron... I am a free activist."

During her political career, El Mansouri has rarely spoken publicly about women's rights or gender inequality, despite ongoing debates in Morocco over issues such as whether polygamy should be banned and whether men and women should have equal inheritance rights.
Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives.
Pam has been led by a collective leadership since February 2024, rather than a single secretary general.
After the results were announced last week, El Mansouri said the decision was ultimately up to the king to choose between her and Lekjaa.
In the past, the appointment was largely a formality, as most Moroccan parties were led by a single secretary general, making it clear who would be nominated to head the government.
With 97 seats, Pam does not have a majority and will need to form a coalition to reach the 198 seats required for an absolute majority in the 395-member parliament.
It is not clear which party it will work with as it has fallen out with the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which led the outgoing government in which Pam was a junior partner.
The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) ⁠rebounded with 54 seats, from only 13 in the previous election - buoyed by the return of party leader Abdelilah Benkirane, a former prime minister.
After the vote, Benkirane said the party would stay in opposition, refusing a partnership with Pam.

articles.title: Burnham’s emotional solo act had Labour in raptures but his promises will take time to come good
articles.summary: PM’s speech, written almost entirely alone, was full of radicalism but his biggest plans will have to wait until after the next election

blocks.text: Hope Again is the conference slogan. But what felt even more apt was Try Again.

Just forget about the last two years, after the party won a historic majority but where the mood never matched the achievement. Now, as conference delegates and MPs filed out of the hall after Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister, it was close to euphoria. Where the hell have you been all our lives? What have we been doing – when you were right there all along?

That feeling rarely lasts: Burnham himself warned he would make choices that would be a harsh comedown from this Labour high. But the “people pleaser” prime minister said he was prepared to weather the worst political pain to change the country.
In his sights are some of the most untouchable topics in British politics – social care, the triple lock, Brexit, public control of water and council homes and changing the voting system.

Burnham wrote the speech almost entirely alone, working on it until the very last minute. Cabinet ministers have been full of tales of how often meetings overrun with the new prime minister, clearing their diaries for the extra half an hour, because of his desire to chew the fat, to understand, to argue, to persuade.

Close friends saw the speech just the night before, as Burnham reworked it. But strategists in Number 10 were very clear that the new prime minister did need to introduce himself, his story, to the country who barely know him.

Each judicious choice of an anecdote from his past drew on his personal history to explain his desire to make fundamental change. The home in Old Roan in Merseyside bought by his grandmother Kitty, which gave his family security that the younger generation cannot now experience: sold, he explained, to pay for Kitty’s care, which he will promise future generations will never happen under a new national care service. The care of his dad, Roy, who died two weeks ago, and his promise to his care workers that he would elevate their profession.

Burnham was overcome with emotion at the moment he spoke about his father, pausing for so long it caused one member of the audience to cry out: “You can do it Andy.” They want to back him, they want to believe.

Unusually for a conference speech, Burnham did not use the speech to attack his opponents. There were no reference to either Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage. But one of the loudest cheers came from the crowd as Burnham drew the dividing line with the right in the starkest terms on public ownership.
“The British right talk about ‘taking back control’. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said, the reddest of red meat to a jubilant Labour crowd.

So, was it Burnham – and Labour – unleashed? No, because the prime minister is still constrained by his own party manifesto and the state of the public finances. “I would love to go quicker,” he said. “But I have to be honest about what the country can afford.”

His most radical promises are promises deferred. The party will overhaul the triple lock by 2030, the national care service can only be paid for if the party ditches its tax pledges, it can only explore a customs union, the single market, even rejoining, outside the manifesto’s “red lines”.

Even at this most united Labour conference the party has seen in two decades, there remains a proud Labour tradition – pessimism. And there are causes for concern, which creep in when cabinet minsters are at their most candid. The first is the impatience of the country for change – and that being told to wait will not be enough.
People, they say, are suffering now. The budget will need to show that any sparse funds that remain must be delivered to giving people relief from everyday costs.
“People need to start feeling actual benefits next year. We have got less time than we might think,” one cabinet minister said.

The second is a fear that Labour is not speaking to a broad enough base, no matter the elevation in Liverpool. Though there has been a discernible “Burnham bounce”, the polls are volatile. A YouGov poll on the eve of Burnham’s speech put Reform UK back in first place by a tiny margin.

Labour is reuniting a progressive coalition with a divided right, which is an advantage but which is unlikely to put them in majority territory. There are few cabinet ministers who are so frustrated with the constraints of their own legacy manifesto who want to swap that for the constraints of a Lib Dem manifesto. There is no sign of revival yet in Wales or Scotland, so crucial to a Labour majority government.
When the dust clears and Labour strategists pick over the bodies of the sacred cows that Burnham promised to slay in his speech, many will probably wonder why he didn’t choose an easier life.
But perhaps now Burnham has waited this long to be prime minister – and watched so many others squander the office – he knows he has no choice but to tool up for the fight.

articles.title: Philippine Coast Guard challenges China's claim over Batanes waters
articles.summary: China is expanding its claim over more of the Philippines" maritime territory, including waters around Batanes, according to the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 1:01am
China is expanding its claim over more of the Philippines’ maritime territory, including waters around Batanes, according to the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).
A "24 Oras" report from Chino Gaston on Tuesday said the BRP Sierra Madre warded off a Chinese Coast Guard vessel 25 nautical miles away from Cabra Island in Mindoro.

The BRP Sierra Madre then headed to Batanes, where the Chinese Research Vessel Jia Hai Ke 7 is operating 38 nautical miles away from Itbayat Island. The Chinese Embassy said that this area was under the jurisdiction of Beijing.

"The relevant Chinese vessel is operating within waters under China’s jurisdiction. China and the Philippines have overlapping maritime claims in the relevant waters. In accordance with the provisions of Articles 74 and 83 of UNCLOS, as well as the consensus reached between China and the Philippines, such issues should be properly resolved through negotiations," said a statement from the Chinese embassy.

In response, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said in a mix of English and Filipino, “This is the first time that they are confirming and claiming that they have legal jurisdiction in the seas of Batanes. They responded to my post saying that this is in adherence with UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea) and falls within their own sovereign rights.”
The PCG viewed the waters of Itbayat as critical because this is where the undersea cables from mainland Asia connect into the Philippines’ communications infrastructure.
In another part of the country, the PCG also had to ward off Chinese vessels in the waters of Kota Island, which is part of the Kalayaan Island Group.
PCG personnel had to chase away Chinese fishing vessels after a few of them approached the island within 30 yards. Despite the PCG’s radio challenges, the Chinese fishing boat would not leave.
When the PCG approached them one by one, the Chinese vessels retreated into their mother ship.
The PCG suspected that this was not a mere fishing trip.

“It could also be a possibility to survey what are the activities in Kota Island, to document the personnel staying sa Kota Island these…Hindi sila naglay ng net, hindi naman sila nagbaksak ng mga fishing gear, it was just intentionally designed na paikutan ang kabuuan ng Kota Island,” Tarriela said.

(It could also be a possibility to survey what the activities are in Kota Island, to document the personnel staying in Kota Island these… they did not lay down nets, they did not drop fishing gear, it was just intentionally designed to rotate around the entirety of Kota Island.)

Under UNCLOS, Kota Island is treated as a rock that created its own 12 nautical mile territorial sea. While foreigners are allowed to pass through territorial waters, they are not allowed to fish or do scientific research without permission. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: CDC reports second measles death in US while excluding Pennsylvania deaths
articles.summary:
Pennsylvania has reported over 900 measles cases and four deaths as governor and health chief RFK Jr spar over data

A second measles death in the
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: A second measles death in the US has been announced on Tuesday by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as the country grapples with an outbreak affecting 47 states.

As of 24 September, a total of 3,659 measles cases have been confirmed by the CDC, with the two deaths having been confirmed on Tuesday. The confirmation did not specify in which states the deaths had occurred.
Although Pennsylvania is the hardest-hit state, having reported more than 900 cases and four deaths from measles, the CDC is not including the deaths there in its national data.

Differences in the federal measles death figures compared with those from Pennsylvania’s department of health is part of an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.
The CDC, which used to collect data from states, has now shifted to using mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for its national measles death count.

Pennsylvania also reported 114 new cases of measles in the last seven days, with a third of these being children aged under 18. The state has also reported 176 hospitalizations, and less than 1% of the total number of measles cases involve people who have been fully vaccinated against the disease.

Pennsylvania’s health department said: “While daily numbers fluctuate, tracking these trends provides Pennsylvanians and health care providers with visibility into community transmission across the [state] and helps inform the department’s ongoing response.”
The US has now recorded more measles cases this year than any other since 1991. The disease was declared to be eliminated by the US government in 2000.
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious health complications. And although rare, deaths from measles occur in approximately one to three patients per 1,000 cases
The announcement also comes as the CDC has faced a dramatic reduction in its work force, with the Trump administration laying off 18% of its staff in 2025.

According to the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), the largest federal employee union representing 82,000 workers, there are 3,810 fewer civil service employees within the CDC in the past year, a total reduction of a third.

Measles symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after infection, according to the CDC. These symptoms can include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash that spreads down the body.
The CDC advises that two doses of the MMR vaccine “provide the best protection against measles”.

articles.title: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
articles.summary: The company that runs the Eiffel Tower said the removal of female staff during the visit earlier this month was "unacceptable".

blocks.text: The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group.
Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, will leave his job at the end of the year, the company SETE said in a statement.
It said an internal investigation found that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of female staff.
They were replaced by male colleagues as a delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the Eiffel Tower earlier this month.
BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.
At the time, SETE said the Hindu delegation had requested that the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted".
A staff union representative said "women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated".
Staff at the monument said female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".
The visit led to the closure of the tower as staff went on strike to show their outrage and politicians condemned the incident.
Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said after the visit: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."
The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, called it an "absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision" and ordered two separate investigations.
SETE chair Ariel Weil said on Tuesday that he had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented.
"The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions," he said.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen
articles.summary:
Relations between the two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudi Arabia in Yemen

Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back.

Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which it had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently effectively quit Yemen.

But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthi drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.

The future role of the UAE in Yemen was discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, UAE president Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat the Houthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen.
A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice president.
It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy.
Following the Houthi push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, its forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz.

“The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city. The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence think tank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz.

“Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.”
The STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled into exile following the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force.

But the former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provide some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance.
The Giant Brigades, however, have been urged by the STC to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause.
“We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said.

“The UN recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.”

The White House has also been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done sometimes to brutal effect in the past in Yemen.

Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has also always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations.

Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis.
The World Health Organization stated that 838 people were killed and 3,643 others were injured due to the recent escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year.

The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait, but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday it published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal.
The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power, and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country.

April Longley Alley, senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war is existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis are not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”
