articles.title: U.S. forces set to leave Iraq after first arriving in 2003
articles.summary: U.S. forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans…

image.caption: In this March 27, 2020 file photo, U.S. soldiers stand guard during the hand over ceremony of Qayyarah Airfield, Iraqi Security Forces, in the south of Mosul, Iraq. The U.S. withdrawal from Iraq was put into motion by president Joe Biden in 2024. (Ali Abdul Hassan/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war.
U.S. troops originally left in 2011 but drawn back in after emergence of Islamic State

U.S. forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies, who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war.

Iraqi security experts say ‌the withdrawal — agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump's administration even as it wages war against Iran — could give Tehran and its powerful allies free rein, while also allowing other U.S. enemies to stage a comeback, including Islamic State.

Abu Mojtaba ​al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the U.S. withdrawal as "a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honourable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project."

"On Sept. 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq's history and the failure of the occupation to impose ​its will on our country," he told Reuters. "Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people."

items: Iraq scrambles to address fallout from alleged militia attack on Saudi oil pipeline

blocks.text: While the eventual departure of U.S. forces is ⁠broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature.

"We believe ‌Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time," Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, once a bastion of anti-American resistance, told Reuters.
"All Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the [U.S.-led coalition] leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear."
Deadlier than U.S. deployment in Afghanistan

American forces invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Sunni Muslim dictator Saddam Hussein, going on to occupy the country, install a Shia-led government and fight a years-long counterinsurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011.
They returned less ⁠than three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Sunni militant group Islamic State, also known as ISIS at the time, in a major war from 2014 to 2017.
Around twice as many Americans died in "Operation Iraqi Freedom" as in the parallel war in Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt U.S. withdrawal in 2021.
In recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the United States and Iran, which sometimes used Iraqi territory as a proxy battlefield.
The United States killed ‌a top Iranian commander, Qasem Soleimani, with a strike on Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran's allies repeatedly fired on U.S. bases, sometimes drawing reprisals.

In this year's war against Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
Fears of imminent attacks

Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave the entire Middle East, casts the U.S. withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.

"Lasting ​security will prevail in Iraq" once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security Commission of Iran's parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said on Monday.
LISTEN | 3 reporters from Iraq war on similarities with Epic Fury (March 2026):
Front Burner37:17In Iran, echoes of the Iraq war

Iran "welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it," he told Iran's parliamentary news service. "Resistance groups are currently taking ⁠action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops."

Washington has accused Iran-backed militia groups in Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighbouring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting ⁠a major Saudi oil pipeline this month. The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence.

Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish ⁠region, say the U.S. ⁠pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the ​defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
At their height, the fighters occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former U.S. ​military base.

items: Iraq, 20 years after U.S. forces arrived (2023)

The plot highlighted concerns that the militant group remains capable of exploiting security gaps despite years of military setbacks, said four Iraqi security and army officials.

Islamic State "is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks," said Col. ⁠Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town ‌of Kirkuk.

articles.title: Dennis Haskins, Saved by the Bell's principal Belding, dead at 75
articles.summary: Dennis Haskins, best known for playing principal Richard Belding on the hit sitcom Saved by the Bell, has died. His agent Jay Schachter confirmed the news to CBC News in a statement, though no cause…

image.caption: Actor Dennis Haskins, who played Mr. Belding on Saved by the Bell, poses for a portrait at the Saved by the Max Los Angeles opening night pop-up on May 1, 2018, in West Hollywood, Calif. Haskins has died at age 75, his agent confirmed. (Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Updated

Dennis Haskins, best known for playing principal Richard Belding on the hit sitcom Saved by the Bell, has died. His agent Jay Schachter confirmed the news to CBC News in a statement, though no cause of death was given. He was 75.
'He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely loved his fans,' his agent wrote in a statement
Dennis Haskins, best known for playing principal Richard Belding on the hit sitcom Saved by the Bell, has died.
His agent Jay Schachter confirmed the news to CBC News in a statement. He was 75.
"It’s a tragic loss. Everyone loved Mr. Belding, and those of us who got to know Dennis loved him even more," Schachter told CBC News in an email.
"He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely loved his fans. He always had time for them, no matter what. He was my client and dear friend for over 20 years, and I will miss him terribly."
Bayside's principal, Mr. Belding

Haskins became a recognizable face on screen playing Bayside High's loveable, fair, father-figure of a principal, known for his signature trouble catching hallway phrase: "Hey, hey, hey, what is going on here?"

The Chattanooga, Tenn.-born actor first played Mr. Belding on Disney Channel's Good Morning, Miss Bliss — a show that would go on to be picked up and revamped by NBC as Saved by the Bell, running from 1989 to 1993.

He'd go on to reprise his role on Saved by the Bell: The New Class and eventually in a sketch alongside former co-stars Mark-Paul Gosselaar, Elizabeth Berkley, Mario Lopez and Tiffani Thiessen on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in 2015.
His fellow co-stars are sharing their love on social media.

"Dennis Haskins was a steady presence in my teenage years, the kind of figure who kept us in line while making sure we knew he was in our corner," Thiessen, who played cheerleader Kelly Kapowski on the show, wrote on Instagram.
"I will always remember his kindness and be grateful for the memories we as a cast got to share with him," she added.
Lopez, who played wrestling team captain A.C. Slater on the show, also shared a tribute on Instagram.
"Heartbroken to hear about my old friend," he wrote.

"If you knew him, you loved him—and if there was karaoke, you knew Dennis was getting on that mic! I’m grateful for the laughs, the memories, and the friendship we shared all these years. Rest easy, my friend. You’ll always be part of our Bayside family," he continued.
Lark Voorhies, who starred alongside Haskins as Lisa Turtle, described knowing him for nearly 40 years as "one of the truest blessings" of her life.

"We shared so much history together from our earliest days, and through it all, he remained a fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart," she wrote on Instagram, adding that she is heartbroken.
Haskins made his onscreen debut in a 1979 episode of The Dukes of Hazzard, kicking off a decades-long television and film career.
Over the years, he appeared in hit shows like Mad Men, Hot in Cleveland, New Girl and in Seth MacFarlane's film A Million Ways to Die in the West.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Digger review: Tom Cruise is fantastic, but you might hate the film
articles.summary: This climate morality tale suggests that director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and his audience are engaging in the same self-satisfied ritual that got us into this real-life mess in the first place. Of…

image.caption: Tom Cruise, left, and Riz Ahmed appear in a scene from Digger. The topsy-turvy dark comedy follows Cruise's Digger as he attempts to save the world from a catastrophe he caused. (Warner Bros. Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

This climate morality tale suggests that director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and his audience are engaging in the same self-satisfied ritual that got us into this real-life mess in the first place. Of using high-minded entertainment to point out, and joke about, our impending doom, as if that alone is admirable. As if that could change anything at all.
Alejandro G. Iñárritu's dark comedy tells the story of an evil oil tycoon and the end of the world
Rise early. Work hard. Strike oil.

Those words are etched into the wood on a mantel, in all caps, below a reverently displayed 10-cent shovel — a shovel that oil baron Digger Rockwell's grandfather purchased around the turn of the century and used to start the empire Digger himself now steers to global domination.

As the film opens, Digger (Tom Cruise) stands next to it while screaming down a trio of his walleyed climate-expert subordinates about their general lack of resolve. He is delivering a diatribe for the ages about his grandfather's legendary work ethic, about toiling in the dust and the dirt and nearly dying under the blistering sun and — wait a second. Why aren't they listening to his story?

Well, there are a few good reasons. The first being that the purpose of his tirade was to keep those experts from shutting down his oil rig in Greenland due to a widening crack in the ice shelf upon which it sits. But as of a few minutes ago, Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) explains, the crack itself ceased to be a problem. It is now a crater.

The result is a smouldering methane explosion directly caused by Digger's willful negligence that is sure to, at least, raise a few eyebrows from the families of all those dead oil workers. As well as from a few world governments.

The second reason no one feels like listening to Digger's personal history: U.S. President Compson (John Goodman) has just arrived, and will probably want to know why this accident now implicates him in a cascading climate catastrophe that could drown Norway — and that's just to start.

That's not to mention the ambitious, destabilizing narrative twist that elevates Alejandro G. Iñárritu's newest beyond-farcical fable into what it is — a surprise second strand to the story that, without giving away the game, has us questioning why we're watching this at all. It suggests that Iñárritu and his audience are engaging in the same self-satisfied ritual that got us into this real-life mess in the first place. Of using high-minded entertainment to point out, and joke about, our impending doom, as if that alone is admirable. As if that could change anything at all.

At least, that's what you could get from it. The winding, tongue-in-cheek story is typical Iñárritu in a way that makes its basic worldview feel self-evident: like the ego-destroying reckoning with our own insignificance in Biutiful; the fascinating futility of perseverance in The Revenant; or the vulnerable self-criticism against egotistical legacy-building in Birdman.

It’s all there as Digger freewheels between a madcap Cruise caring for his dying, 30-year-old corpse of a cat and screaming down pussy-footed eco-activists still blindly dependent on fossil fuels. Or as he delivers self-aggrandizing, Shakespearean monologues about his own virility in a lecture hall inexplicably populated by mannequins in wigs.

The story about a self-obsessed, self-mythologizing opportunist pillaging a dying planet for his own profits unravels into something stranger, more confusing, more barbed and angry and ultimately defeatist. Digger is a comedy in the way one could find their own funeral funny.

Explaining exactly why would probably be a mistake (though we can confirm this is unequivocally not a musical) Without quite getting close to M. Night Shyamalan territory, going in blind to Digger’s actual format is probably for the best. (For example, revealing how Jesse Plemons’s red-haired Svengali fits into all this would probably spoil the fun.) Because the befuddling delight in discovering exactly how Iñárritu has chosen to make his demoralizing point about where we’re all headed is one of the movie’s few uplifting spots.

Suffice it to say, this and Birdman — Iñárritu's Oscar-winning 2014 examination of a man at war with his pathetic and inescapable impulse to matter — share serious DNA. And without the reprieve offered by the surprise reveal, the rotating cast of idiot oligarchs, preening politicians and sad-eyed scientists steering the Earth straight off a cliff in search of endless profits would be a bit too on-the-nose.

Which is not to mention the stilted, infinitely self-aware style — anyone who felt Wes Anderson fell a little too in love with his own schtick in the relentlessly obscure Asteroid City should probably steer clear of this one.

Digger is built for smug unpacking and film-critic scene analyses — "inaccessible," "artifice" and "up-its-own" are the three descriptors you could most readily use to describe it. Alienatingly ambitious, as is often seen in works by esteemed directors late in their careers, Iñárritu's latest does perform like a riddle he expects you to solve. A uniformly colour-graded cartoon for pretentious, beige-loving children, the film's deliberate mix of vomit humour and metaphor-laden philosophizing seems to scream all three descriptions at you the whole time. Imagine Megalopolis if it was, somehow, actually good.

items: Megalopolis is one of the worst big-budget movies ever made
Asteroid City is a masterful puzzle — and likely to be Wes Anderson fans' most hated movie

blocks.text: Which raises the question of why Tom Cruise would want to take this project on. The 64-year-old actor's last movie that wasn’t a franchise-focused blockbuster came nearly a decade ago: 2017’s American Made. The last time he made such an obviously transgressive and politically relevant movie was — being generous — 2007's Lions for Lambs or 1989’s Born on the Fourth of July. Realistically, the actual answer is "probably never."

Cruise is fascinating here, delivering searing, complex, southern-inflected line after line, reminding you that he was once one of the most talented and interesting leading men in Hollywood. But why re-enter the critical limelight with this, a movie that seems to intentionally attack the current U.S. administration? Especially when he chose to avoid criticizing that same government when it proposed instituting tariffs designed to limit American productions' abilities to film abroad — a move that could easily have tanked his globetrotting Mission: Impossible series?

Maybe Digger allows Cruise to have his cake and eat it, too. Maybe the meta turn later on allows him to do something that equally doomeristic films like Don’t Look Up, Silent Night, Greenland or even the upcoming Musk documentary can’t.

Because even while partaking in the indulgent wave of multimillion-dollar films openly claiming capitalism has killed us all, Digger does something decidedly more Iñárritu. It turns inward, and then out at the audience. It acknowledges the situation, pointing to a likely future when stepping outside means stepping into a roiling cloud of poison and autonomous police bots with guns.

But it also asks: If we’re not going to do anything about it, what are we accomplishing here? Are we doing anything but stroking our own egos, distracting ourselves, by showing we understand a reality we’re powerless to fix? As it directly asks, are we so enthralled by our own opinions that we’ll happily keep arguing about them as the world crumbles around us?
Maybe. Maybe not. Either way, they’re maybe less politically dangerous questions for Cruise to ask. And newer ones for us to answer.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: American taps small Sask. business to solve international photo mystery
articles.summary: For more than four years, American Bill Delzell has been trying to figure out the identity of the photographer who captured San Francisco history in the 1960s. Now he's hoping a Sask. company will be…

image.caption: An unknown photographer snapped this image of San Francisco in the 1960s, along with countless others that show a turbulent time of protest against war and racial injustice. An American man has been trying to uncover the identity of the photographer for more than four years. (Submitted by Speaklocal

blocks.text: Saskatchewan

For more than four years, American Bill Delzell has been trying to figure out the identity of the photographer who captured San Francisco history in the 1960s. Now he's hoping a Sask. company will be able to develop 75 rolls of unprocessed film to crack the mystery.
Film Rescue developing photos that may help reveal unknown photographer's identity
American photographer Bill Delzell has spent more than four years consumed by a mystery. Now, he can feel himself inching toward a conclusion.

Sometime in the 1960s, an unknown man or woman wandered through San Francisco, capturing vivid moments of that turbulent decade. Muhammad Ali on stage burning a draft card. A young Carlos Santana bent over his guitar. Countless pictures of the counterculture moment, with flower-painted vans, and long-haired men and women frozen in time, holding signs for peace, love and freedom.

"When I saw the work, I only turned a few pages of these albums and I felt like I'd seen enough. I had this sort of powerful emotional feeling about it," said Delzell, who himself lives in San Francisco.
A collector first showed him the photos, with the explanation that they were discovered abandoned in a Bay Area storage locker in the 1980s.
"I just felt like, what a tragic loss, this notion that someone could have devoted that much time and then walked away. There had to be a story behind that."

Delzell has spent years trying to track down the identity of the photographer. How did this man or woman get so close to so many critical moments in San Francisco history, like Forrest Gump with a camera?
"We have since found footage from other news outlets that shows a mysterious figure wandering through the crowd. And we think that's our person," he said.
There's another tool in his sleuthing efforts. Delzell has purchased the collection, and has also acquired 75 rolls of unprocessed film that might give clues to the photographer's identity.
"As a photographer, I knew that film sort of expires over time," he said.
In his mind, the precious unprocessed film could have been exposed to hostile temperatures or light. It needed to be developed with care.
"So I knew I needed to find an expert."
Sask. lab's expertise sought worldwide
He found his expert in Sask-based Film Rescue International. Rather than fly and risk exposing the film to X-rays, he drove 25 hours to its location in the town of Indian Head, Sask.

Here at this old bank building, film archivist Gerald Freyer has gotten used to uncovering old family mysteries, cracking out old cameras and rolls of film, and revealing never-before seen parts of the past. People from all over the world seek out the company's expertise in developing old film.

items: Sask. company uses new technology to preserve memories caught on film

blocks.text: "I need a bell for each amazing picture, and I should ring that bell nearly three, four times a day when I'm digitizing," Freyer said, shaking his head with wonder. "It's like watching The History Channel all day long, you know, because we have these amazing jobs."

It will cost tens of thousands of dollars to do this work, but it's not the biggest job the lab has undertaken. It has also processed and digitized thousands of photos from the late American photographer Charles Daniels, showing rock stars like Rod Stewart and Mick Jagger in intimate moments, on planes and in hotel rooms.
Film Rescue International's work astounds Delzell.
"The devotion that it takes to do this kind of work — it's far beyond the imagination, really," he said.
Moments of synchronicity
Delzell has combed through internet tips and shared the work with friends and strangers alike, fundraising along the way to support the work.

In his quest to uncover the photographer's identity, Delzell sent five photographs out of thousands to a friend, who had an unbelievable reaction of seeing her younger self at five or six years old on a march. Fellow photographer Michael Zagaris can also be seen in a picture with Ali, who asked him for his draft card and then proceeded to burn it on stage, according to Delzell.
"Some might call [these] coincidence, some might call it synchronicity," Delzell said. "I am not looking for an explanation. I'm just continuing the search."

Having lived through the 1960s himself, Delzell thinks that people have a tendency to overromanticize that era. He recalls the turbulence of the decade, including anger over the Vietnam War and racial injustice. He was only 10 when he attended his first anti-war protest with his father in 1967.
"I distinctly remember him saying, 'I'm going to send you to Canada if you're ever drafted. And here we are!'" Delzell said, chuckling.

Now, he's pinning his hopes on this small Sask. company to help uncover the secret he's chased for four years. The staff's passion for film and photography, along with their expertise, makes the company one-of-a-kind when it comes to excavating history, he said.
"It's a Canadian treasure."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Janani Whitfield is a community engagement producer who also edits feature storytelling and First Person columns for CBC Saskatchewan. Contact her at janani.whitfield@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ethiopia: No regard for civilians as fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region continues
articles.summary: Fighting has returned to northern Ethiopia, shattering a fragile peace in the region. DW spoke to civilians caught in the crossfire amid communication blackouts, as rebel and federal forces keep…

image.caption: Prices in Tigrayan towns like Mekelle have surged since the onset of the fightingImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: As fighting keeps spreading across northern Ethiopia, civilians find themselves caught in the crossfire between opposing forces. Little information is emerging from the affected area as the internet and other communication services remain largely disrupted.
However, DW managed to speak to eyewitnesses whose accounts point to a growing toll on civilians.
A 22-year-old woman from the small town of Selenwuha told DW that her relatives were sheltering at home when heavy weaponry shelling struck their residences.
"I have lost six family members," she said. "Those who survived the attack, including the wounded, are currently confined to their homes.
"They have no access to medical facilities or vehicles, and the nearest treatment center is far away."
Strategic town of Alamata reported taken by ENDF

According to local residents, several violent incidents took place in recent days, especially in the border region between the Tigray and Amhara regions, with multiple further reports of civilians being killed by artillery fire.
The overall strategic situation on the ground meanwhile remains difficult to assess, with both rebel and federal forces reportedly making advances in different areas.
DW heard from a source in Tigray that the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) keeps advancing towards the regional capital Mekelle. The ENDDF is the country's official military force.
Tigrayan forces are reportedly fighting to defend other towns, including Mekoni and Maychew in southern Tigray, the source told DW on the strict condition of anonymity.

blocks.caption: TPLF fighters are patroling Mekelle — far from the frontline of the present conflictImage: AFP

blocks.text: Pro-government militia and affiliated media outlets in the country had reported earlier that the ENDF had made significant progress by seizing control of Alamata in southern Tigray on September 27.
The purported takeover was also recorded by the US-based conflict-monitoring organization ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data).
Located about 120 kilometers south of the regional capital Mekelle, the strategically important town is situated on a major highway.
During the 2020-2022 war, Alamata changed hands several times between the two warring parties.
Residents accuse federal forces of deliberate attacks
A 40-year-old resident of Alamata told DW that civilians had deliberately been targeted, citing the account shared by militia members in the region.
"The attacks… were acts of retaliation against the people of Alamata," the local said. "The militias told us that government forces had fired the artillery at us."

Another resident, aged 45, said he believed the attack had deliberately been timed to maximize civilian casualties during the opening hours of a market, "when large numbers of people would be gathered there."
"At the Saturday market in Alamata, 11 people were killed and 15 others were wounded", he told DW.

blocks.caption: Alamata has changed hands several times during the 2020-22 civil war (archive picture from January 2021)Image: Alemnew Mekonnen/DW

blocks.text: It's important to note that these claims could not be independently verified.
An ENDF spokesperson was also contacted by DW for comment; by the time of the publishing of this article, the spokesperson had not responded to the request.
Shifting alliances and mutual blame
Large-scale fighting erupted on September 23, when Tigrayan forces seized the airports of the regional capital Mekele as well as the regional hubs of Aksum and Shire.
Three days earlier, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups had announced a new alliance aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

Unexpectedly, the alliance was joined by the Amhara Fano National Movement, which had supported federal forces against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, but has since then switched side and turned to fighting the federal government.
The federal government and Tigrayan forces meanwhile have accused each other of starting the latest escalation, both sides portraying their military actions as defensive in nature.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
The unraveling of Ethiopia's fragile peace accord
Depending on the source, between 162,000 and 600,000 people were killed in the brutal 2020-2022 war, which was fought over the political status of the northern province of Tigray.

The war ended in November 2022 with the Pretoria Agreement, under which the TPLF agreed to the disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of its combatants, and to respect the federal government's constitutional authority.

However, key provisions remained unimplemented and major disputes unresolved, including the status of contested territories, the return of displaced people and the full demobilization of Tigrayan forces.
Meanwhile, a power struggle within the TPLF ended with the more hardline faction around Debretsion Gebremichael reasserting control in Tigray, further straining relations with Addis Ababa.
The TPLF also reinstated Tigray's pre-war regional council, a move the federal government viewed as a violation of the Pretoria framework.
Concerns mounted even further when the TPLF lost its legal party legislation, thus excluding the party from participating in national elections in June this year.
Tensions steadily increased, culminating in renewed clashes between Tigrayan and federal forces beginning in August 2026.

blocks.caption: The headquarter of Tigray's state broadcaster was reportedly hit in a drone strike earlier in SeptemberImage: AFP

blocks.text: Fears grow over civilian toll and rights violations

Local residents meanwhile are bracing for further fighting, as organizations like the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have managed to evacuate only few people caught up in the conflict.
According to the ICRC, the global NGO got to evacuate only around 160 individuals from Tigray, including Ethiopian Federal Police personnel, Ethiopian Airlines staff and African Union monitors.

With reports of damage to civilian infrastructure, disruptions to essential services and interrupted communication and transport routes, observers are worried about the situation of residents not only in Tigray but all across northern Ethiopia.

Amdegebreal Admassu, an Ethiopian lawyer focused on political and legal affairs, told DW he had received reports of fighters impacting public facilities including hospitals, schools and religious institutions.
"We observe instances where these facilities — which also serve as shelters for residents — are either accidentally hit or deliberately targeted.
"Under both international law and our country's penal code, such actions are classified as war crimes," Amdegebreal further explained.
Nearly everyone in Tigray impacted by fighting
Mebrihi Birhane, vice director for the NGO Human Rights First Ethiopia, told DW that many of those civilian facilities had already been impacted during the 2020-22 war.
"The population must have access to essential services even in times of war. Ensuring this is an obligation for all armed forces involved in the conflict," he said.

Meanwhile, the prices of goods are reported to be increasing dramatically, as supply routes are disrupted, affecting residents of Tigray whose communities had so far been spared from the direct fighting.

blocks.caption: According to local journalists, residents of Tigray have rushed to buy flour and other productsImage: AFP

blocks.text: The latest reports indicate that Tigrayan forces have advanced into the Afar region and were said to be controling the area around Erebti.
Analysts say this advance could be aimed at threatening Ethiopia's main trade corridor — a vital route used for imports and exports and a lifeline for the country's economy.

The renewed conflict meanwhile could spread beyond the confines of Ethiopia to the Horn of Africa and beyond, as Prime Minister Abiy has already accused neighboring countries of picking sides and supporting rebel forces.
Several DW journalists contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.summary: The US president continues to push back on calls to establish guardrails around artificial intelligence, arguing it will stifle growth.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.

During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US is "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and does not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.

"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remains steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.

"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder AI governance.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.

The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

articles.title: Marcos hails Metrobank's outstanding Filipinos
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. honored on Tuesday the 10 recipients of the 2026 Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos Award, urging them to keep on inspiring and setting a good example in their…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 12:01am

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. honored on Tuesday the 10 recipients of the 2026 Metrobank Foundation Outstanding Filipinos Award, urging them to keep on inspiring and setting a good example in their respective fields.

“To our 10 awardees, know that your fellow Filipinos see you and are grateful to you for all that you have done and continue to do,” Marcos said during the awarding of the Medallion of Excellence in Malacañang Palace.

“You remind us that nation-building is not confined to high office. It is carried out in classrooms, in institutions, [and] in communities all over the country. May this award inspire you to keep going, and may it inspire many more Filipinos to follow your shining example,” he added.
The recipients of the award span the education, military, and police sectors—individuals who Marcos said share the same story of both service and sacrifice.
Marcos pointed out that government policies and programs only go as far as the people who implement them in communities.

In his speech, the President mentioned the progress of Filipino learners in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), which showed an improvement in reading, mathematics, and science scores compared to 2022.

“These remind us that improving education requires sustained work from teachers and innovators who strengthen literacy, to make difficult concepts easier to understand, and to bring new technologies and opportunities closer to our learners,” Marcos said.

For the military awardees, Marcos recognized their contributions to national defense, specifically their roles in inter-agency coordination, improving digital platforms, and enhancing maritime awareness and operational preparedness in the West Philippine Sea.

Meanwhile, recipients from the police sector were honored for their role in public safety, guiding young people away from crime, and strengthening the role of women in anti-drug efforts by using digital systems and timely data to improve road safety.
The President reminded the awardees to appreciate the stature and prestige that accompany the award, as it recognizes exemplary professionals in their respective fields of service.

This year’s Ten Outstanding Filipinos who received the Medallion of Excellence are Dr. Emmanuel Guarde, Master Teacher Sheila Marie M. Amigo, Dr. Cecilia Bucayong, Dr. Jefferson Hora, SSgt. Joebelle Cerdinio, SSgt. John Daren Noche, Lt.Col. Rommel Geli, PMSgt. Dwight Alexis Supsupin, PMaj. Baby Rose P. Cajulao, and PLtCl.Robert R. Mansueto. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ICC rejects Duterte camp’s request on digital evidence
articles.summary: Trial judges of the International Criminal Court have rejected the request of the defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte to adopt a stricter protocol in verifying digital materials.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — Trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have rejected the request of the defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte to adopt a stricter protocol in verifying digital materials.

In a seven-page decision dated Sept. 26, the ICC Trial Chamber III denied the defense’s request for an additional “expert verification” field to accompany all forms of open source and user-generated evidence.

It said such an amendment to the ICC’s protocol would not align with the framework set by the Trial Chamber, which states that it is the defense’s primary responsibility to identify and raise issues for individual evidence presented by the prosecution.

“To the contrary, the requested amendment, if implemented, requires the prosecution to prepare additional materials that contain information regarding the relevance and admissibility of open-source and user-generated evidence, before the defense analyses evidence and raises any abovementioned issues,” read the decision.
Defense lawyer Peter Haynes earlier recommended the amendment to E-Court Protocol, citing the need for extra caution to ensure that evidence is properly verified before it is submitted to the court.

“The current case operates in a uniquely challenging information ecosystem, in which a large volume of misinformation, or ‘fake news’ has circulated and will continue to circulate, online,” Haynes said.
“The defense is concerned that the evidentiary record in the present case risks being overwhelmed by material of dubious relevance, authenticity and reliability,” he added.
The ICC prosecutor, however, described the request is “unreasonable, unnecessary and against the interests of judicial efficiency.”
“Open source and user-generated evidence are extremely broad categories of documents that capture numerous types of evidence,” wrote ICC acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.

“As such, whether open source or user-generated evidence requires an accompanying expert report should be determined on a case-by-case basis by the submitting party that has the burden of establishing its relevance, probative value and assessing its potential prejudicial effect,” Niang added.
The Trial Chamber III instead granted the prosecution’s request to add a URL (uniform resource locator) metadata field for each of the open source or user-generated evidence submitted in the case.
The prosecution said the additional field will allow parties to easily identify the URL or link “associated with the open source evidence at the time it was captured.”

articles.title: ‘VP can’t be compelled to admit bank accounts’
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court yesterday denied the prosecution’s request for admission to compel Vice President Sara Duterte to admit to some pieces of evidence, including the ownership of bank…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court yesterday denied the prosecution’s request for admission to compel Vice President Sara Duterte to admit to some pieces of evidence, including the ownership of bank accounts, as it will be equivalent to self-incrimination.

In his ruling read in open court on Day 31 of the trial, presiding officer Francis Escudero denied the prosecution’s request for the Vice President to admit to “104 matters concerning respondent’s personal circumstances and former public offices, her spouse Manases Carpio’s business interests and various Bureau of Internal Revenue and bank records.”

The court agreed with the defense panel’s opposition to the prosecution’s request for “admission by adverse party” under Rule 26 of the Revised Rules of Civil Procedure, with Escudero saying it cannot prevail over Section 17, Article III or the Bill of Rights of the 1987 Constitution, which reads: “No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.”
Escudero cited the Bill of Rights, which protects even impeached officials’ “right against self-incrimination.”
He added that if the request is allowed, the respondent’s failure to answer a request for admission “will be ‘deemed as an admission of the fact requested to be admitted.’”

“That Rule 26 requires the answer be under oath exposes the party requested to ‘the additional peril of being held liable for perjury’ and thus, constitutes compulsion that is not allowed under the Constitution,” Escudero said

Escudero said while the court welcomes the prosecution’s bid to narrow the issues for trial, “any such measure to expedite the proceedings must always yield to the protection of the substantial rights of the respondent under the Constitution.”

While the court sided with the defense camp’s objections, Escudero said it is denying the Vice President’s move to “expunge” the request for admission, saying it will remain in the court’s records but with “no evidentiary or prejudicial
effect against Respondent.” Escudero also assured the Vice President that “her failure to answer (the Request for Admission) shall not be deemed an admission.”
The court also no longer tackled the Vice President’s camp’s “objection based on marital and filial privileges.”
Sought for comment, the prosecution panel said it does not consider the ruling a setback and would still present its case through witnesses and documents.

“Even if the ruling was adverse to the prosecution, I think we will still continue with the strategy, the plan of the prosecution. This is not a setback,” House prosecutor and San Juan Rep. Ysabel Zamora said.
Trillanes ready to testify
Even without a subpoena, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said he is ready to take the witness stand before the impeachment court.
In a chance interview as he attended yesterday’s hearing, Trillanes said the prosecution has tapped him as an alternative witness in case Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte will not appear.
Duterte did appear yesterday and took the witness stand as prosecutors drilled down on the alleged ill-gotten wealth of his sister, the Vice President.
Trillanes said it was a coincidence that he and Mayor Duterte were both present before the Senate impeachment court yesterday.
“I hope to be presented as a witness after Mayor Baste, that’s all,” Trillanes added.
“The subpoena is issued if you need to be summoned, but I am willing and ready even if they don’t issue a subpoena. I am ready to be presented,” he added.
He was, however, mum on the testimonies of Mayor Duterte.
“Even if I want to answer that, I can’t…,” he said.
Trillanes is expected to reveal before the court details of the alleged sources of the reported P6.7-billion wealth of the Duterte couple.
Investigate own turf

Meanwhile, Sen. Erwin Tulfo advised Mayor Duterte to investigate his inner circle for failing to flag local government contracts awarded to a company linked to his sister, warning that the local chief executive could face legal liability for his staff’s oversight.
Tulfo pointed out that the mayor signs documents based on the approval of his subordinates, leaving him highly vulnerable to irregularities.
However, when asked if he would initiate the probe on his own accord, the mayor deflected to the justice system.
“As long as my sister’s name, the Vice President’s name was not on the contract, then there’s nothing,” he stated.

The exchange stemmed from Duterte’s admission that he signs between 50 to 300 documents daily, including payrolls, ordinances and contracts, relying entirely on the countersignatures of his city administrator and legal team. — Bella Cariaso, Neil Jayson Servallos, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: DENR: Clean energy vital to national security, sovereignty
articles.summary: Transitioning to renewable power is essential to protecting the Philippines against international supply shocks and geopolitical instability, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources said.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Photo taken on March 7, 2025, shows the facade of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources central office on Visayas Avenue, Quezon City.
Philstar.com / Dominique Nicole Flores

MANILA, Philippines — Transitioning to renewable power is essential to protecting the Philippines against international supply shocks and geopolitical instability, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources said.
DENR Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said decades of heavy reliance on imported fossil fuels have left the Philippine economy exposed to global market disruptions.

Under the Philippine Energy Plan, the government is driving toward a target of exceeding a 50 percent renewable energy share in its power generation mix by 2050, alongside a near-term goal of reaching 35 percent by 2030.
To accelerate this shift, Manila recently opened the renewable energy sector to 100 percent foreign ownership and established priority “green lanes” to fast-track key infrastructure approvals.

Speaking at a reception hosted by Danish green fund manager Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, Cuna pointed to the government’s growing partnership with CIP, which is developing three offshore wind projects in Northern Samar, Pangasinan, La Union, Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte, with a total potential capacity of around 2,000 megawatts.

The cornerstone of this collaboration is CIP’s $3-billion, one-gigawatt San Miguel Bay Offshore Wind Project in Camarines Sur, which became the first offshore wind initiative in the Philippines to earn a pre-development environmental compliance certificate (ECC) from the DENR.
Calling the issuance of the pre-development ECC a “watershed moment,” Cuna emphasized the DENR is committed to accelerating clean energy development while upholding strict environmental safeguards.
“The oceans that will power our offshore wind turbines also feed millions of our people and sustain coastal economies,” Cuna said, addressing senior decision makers at the New York Climate Week.

articles.title: Senators to DOT: Keep ‘Love the Philippines’
articles.summary: Senators have asked the Department of Tourism to stand by its present “Love the Philippines” campaign so it can catch up with the gains of the previous and successful “Wow…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Former tourism secretary Christina Frasco fields questions from the media during a press conference in this file photo from June 2023.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Senators have asked the Department of Tourism to stand by its present “Love the Philippines” campaign so it can catch up with the gains of the previous and successful “Wow Philippines” and “It’s More Fun in the Philippines” slogans.
During the DOT budget hearing on Monday, Senate finance subcommittee chairman Erwin Tulfo asked newly appointed DOT Secretary Dita Angara-Mathay about her plans in promoting the current slogan.
Tulfo asked the agency about the need of each administrationto change tourism slogan, which affects continuity and success in inviting tourists to the country.

“It’s like we’re the only country that changes its tourism slogan with each administration. There’s ‘Love,’ ‘More Love.’ There’s ‘Love-Love.’ There’s ‘It’s More Fun.’ There’s ‘Wow Philippines.’ I ask why?” Tulfo said.
Tulfo compared it to Malaysia’s catchy and long-running tourism slogan “Malaysia, Truly Asia,” which has been the neighboring Southeast Asian country’s campaign for years now.
Tulfo said he would no longer be surprised if the DOT in the next administration would try to change “Love the Philippines.”
“Why do we change? I don’t see anything wrong with ‘Wow Philippines.’ Then we changed it,’” Tulfo said.
“What is going on here?” he asked.
Senate finance committee chair JV Ejercito agreed with Tulfo’s stance against changing tourism slogans every administration.
“I agree to stick with one branding,” Ejercito said.

He also pointed out the challenges faced by the Philippines as an archipelago, where foreign visitors travel around by air and sea, unlike in neighboring countries like Vietnam and Thailand which can be toured around by land.
The DOT and its attached agencies have a proposed P4.029-billion budget next year, according to the National Expenditure Program.

articles.title: Gatchalian vows to block Sandigan budget cut
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian has vowed to block a proposed P551-million budget cut for the Sandiganbayan, arguing that the anti-graft court needs more funding to handle a surge of high-profile…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian at the Senate in Pasay City on July 29, 2026.
Ryan Baldemor / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian has vowed to block a proposed P551-million budget cut for the Sandiganbayan, arguing that the anti-graft court needs more funding to handle a surge of high-profile cases involving lawmakers.
During the recent Senate deliberations on the judiciary’s proposed 2027 budget, Gatchalian firmly rejected the Department of Budget and Management’s recommendation to slash the tribunal’s funding.
“I don’t subscribe to the recommendation to reduce its budget by P551 million. We should actually add more budget to speed up the trials,” he emphasized.

The push for greater financial support comes as the Sandiganbayan faces a mounting caseload. Presiding Justice Geraldine Faith Econg reported to the chamber that the number of cases has steadily increased since the Office of the Ombudsman filed its first complaint in November 2025.
Econg revealed that 26 cases have already been filed before the anti-graft court against various senators and congressmen in connection with the widespread flood control anomaly.

articles.title: Authorities closing in on youth ‘groomers’
articles.summary: Authorities are closing in on people allegedly grooming minors into criminal activities, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Monday.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Long queues are observed at the entrances of several schools across Tacloban City on June 24, 2026 as enhanced security measures are implemented following the school shooting.
Tacloban City Information Office via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Authorities are closing in on people allegedly grooming minors into criminal activities, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Monday.

According to Remulla, President Marcos has ordered intensified efforts against emerging groups targeting young people, including an alleged community-based syndicate known as True Brown Style (TBS), which he said recruits teenagers into criminal activities.
“We are almost there,” Remulla told reporters at Camp Crame.
The group allegedly targets children as young as 14 or 15, with members in their late teens or early 20s grooming them to commit crimes such as robbing convenience stores.
Remulla said authorities are studying the group’s command structure and will take steps to prevent it from expanding in communities.

He also distinguished the alleged TBS recruitment from online grooming linked to a recent shooting incident, explaining that the latter involves a different group whose influence includes Satanism, Nazism and nihilism, which authorities believe can encourage young people to view life as meaningless.
The government is preparing a nationwide communications program for parents on how to talk to children about these online influences and respond to warning signs, Remulla said.
Part of the President’s directive, the campaign aims to help parents understand emerging threats facing young people as internet use changes the way criminal and extremist influences reach them.
Remulla revealed that the government would also look into officials and other people who may be linked to such activities, stressing that there would be no exemptions.

articles.title: DOH: Leptospirosis cases up, dengue down
articles.summary: The number of leptospirosis cases in the country is increasing, with nearly 12,000 infections recorded this year, while dengue numbers have dropped, according to the Department of Health.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
A gym at the National Kidney and Transplant Institute in Quezon City became a leptospirosis ward as cases ballooned due to flooding from Typhoon Carina in this file photo from August 2024.
Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The number of leptospirosis cases in the country is increasing, with nearly 12,000 infections recorded this year, while dengue numbers have dropped, according to the Department of Health.
As of Sept. 23, DOH data showed 11,965 leptospirosis cases have been reported, which is 46 percent higher than 8,189 cases in the same period last year.
From Aug. 27 to Sept. 9, however, the DOH monitored a decline in the number of cases after 3,284 infections were recorded, compared to 3,330 cases from Aug. 6 to 19.
Despite possible reporting delays, the one percent decrease may signal that the current surge is easing, the DOH said.
The cumulative case fatality rate stands at 5.08 percent, lower than last year’s 10.53-percent CFR.
People should seek medical advice upon exposure to floods, with or without symptoms, the DOH stressed.
Cumulative dengue cases this year remains lower at 168,060 cases, a 30 percent drop compared to 239,001 cases during the same period last year.
The DOH recorded an eight percent increase in the recent three to four weeks with 21,122 cases, compared to the previous five to six weeks with 19,572 cases.
Up to 656 deaths were reported, which is 28 percent lower than last year’s 910.
Forty-eight percent, or 312, of fatalities were clinically classified as severe dengue.
Students were identified as the most affected population.
Zero-balance billing
Close to 50 public hospitals benefited from the P1 billion released for the implementation of the zero-balance billing program, the DOH said.
The budget will be spread out in 48 hospitals in Aklan, Batangas, Benguet, Laguna, Quezon and Sarangani.
Fifteen Laguna hospitals were allocated P294.1 million, while 12 hospitals in Batangas were provided P141.1 million.
In Quezon, 11 hospitals were allotted P152.85 million.
Four hospitals in Benguet were allocated P114.99 million, four in Sarangani will receive P84.2 million and two in Aklan will have P212.69 million.
Under the program, no payment is required from patients for hospital services, including medical procedures, doctor’s professional fees and medications.

articles.title: BI, NBI confirm Velasco, wife out of Philippines
articles.summary: Former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco boarded a flight to Japan on Aug. 30 and did not fly back to Manila on Sept. 14, his expected date of return, the Bureau of Immigration confirmed yesterday.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Allegations that Velasco ordered cash deliveries to members of the Duterte family are being verified by the National Bureau of Investigation.
Lord Allan Jay Velasco / Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco boarded a flight to Japan on Aug. 30 and did not fly back to Manila on Sept. 14, his expected date of return, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed yesterday.
Velasco’s wife Rowena followed him to Japan a day after, an airport insider said. Other reports, however, said she took a flight to Hong Kong.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., a former member of Velasco’s security team, had passed a polygraph test on his identity and links with the people he implicated, but the test did not establish the truth of his claims.
Photos, videos and other documents that Gracioso submitted are being authenticated by the NBI. Corroborating testimonies are being sought.
People named in Gracioso’s affidavit, including the Vice President, Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte, Velasco, his wife Rowena and others, will be invited by the NBI to state their case.
Gracioso claimed he delivered suitcases filled with cash to the Vice President and other members of her family on Velasco’s instructions.
Perjury charges could be filed against Gracioso if his claims are proven false, the NBI said.
No existing hold-departure order or derogatory alert would have prevented Velasco’s departure, the BI maintained.
Meanwhile, the Bureau of Customs is waiting for the completion of the NBI’s probe into Gracioso’s claim that BOC personnel also delivered money to Velasco.
Gracioso alleged that personnel of the BOC, Department of Public Works and Highways and Bureau of Internal Revenue had delivered money to Velasco’s house in Valle Verde 2 in Pasig.
If these allegations are true, Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said they happened before he took leadership of the BOC.

“I will have to wait first. This is a hot issue and I don’t want to interfere in the process. This is happening in the context of the impeachment (trial of the Vice President),” Nepomuceno said. — Evelyn Macairan

articles.title: Comelec prepared to comply with SC ruling on BSKE
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections is operationally and financially prepared to abide by any Supreme Court order pertaining to the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections, following a legal challenge…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am
Comelec Chairman George Garcia on February 4, 2026.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) is operationally and financially prepared to abide by any Supreme Court order pertaining to the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE), following a legal challenge mounted at the SC over the weekend.

During the poll body’s budget hearing before the Senate on Monday, Comelec Chairman George Garcia projected the number of registered voters to reach 74 million by the 2028 national and local elections, an increase of about three million from the current count.
He noted that another one million voters could be added by November 2028 for the BSKE.

The Comelec is preparing for the 2028 polls after President Marcos signed Republic Act 12326, which postponed the BSKE from Nov. 2, 2026 to November 2028 and extended the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years.
Following the signing of the law, the Comelec halted preparations for the 2026 BSKE, including the filing of certificates of candidacy originally scheduled from Sept. 28 to Oct. 5.
On Sunday, election lawyer Romulo Macalintal challenged the BSKE postponement with a petition for certiorari and prohibition before the SC.

“Whatever the Supreme Court may issue, the Comelec is prepared. However, we have already stopped all activities related to the 2026 barangay and SK elections in recognition of the new law,” Garcia said.

Macalintal has asked the SC to issue a temporary restraining order or status quo ante order against the implementation of RA 12326, and to declare the law invalid or unconstitutional insofar as it postpones the BSKE.
Garcia said the Comelec would need additional time to resume preparations if the SC orders the 2026 BSKE to proceed.

The poll body has spent about P8 billion on preparations for the postponed BSKE. Garcia said procured election materials and equipment could still be used for the rescheduled elections if properly stored.
The Comelec is also drafting the terms of reference for the voting machines to be used in the 2028 national and local elections as it prepares to procure new units. — Rainier Allan Ronda

articles.summary: With over 60 million micro, small and medium enterprises in Southeast Asia owned or managed by women, President Marcos is pushing for measures designed to address women’s limited access to…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 12:00am

President Marcos attends the 4th Asean Women Leaders’ Summit in Mandaluyong City yesterday, bringing together regional leaders and stakeholders to advance women’s leadership, gender equality and inclusive growth across the region. With Marcos is Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.
Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — With over 60 million micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Southeast Asia owned or managed by women, President Marcos is pushing for measures designed to address women’s limited access to capital and digital financial services,.

At the 4th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Women Leaders’ Summit in Mandaluyong City, Marcos said removing barriers to women’s participation in the economy would help expand opportunities for women entrepreneurs and strengthen inclusive growth across the region.
“If we are serious about inclusive prosperity, we must transform the economic landscape for women,” the President said.
He noted that MSMEs are an important part of the region’s domestic economies.

“Under the Philippines’ chairship, we are accelerating digital financial inclusion and ensuring market integration explicitly benefiting women-led enterprises,” Marcos said. The President also called for greater investment in care infrastructure.

“We must also acknowledge a long overlooked truth – no economy functions without the care economy. Unpaid care work falls disproportionately on women, restricting their time and opportunity to lead in the formal workforce, especially in the so called non-traditional fields,” he said.
“By investing in care infrastructure and redistributing care obligations, we do not just support women, we unlock billions of dollars in economic potential across our region,” Marcos pointed out.

articles.title: N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears
articles.summary: Douglas Smith, 75, was sentenced Tuesday for killing his wife in their home four years ago after she had asked for help taking her own life, according to court documents.

image.caption: Douglas Smith, 75, has been senteced to six years in prison for the death of his wife Iris Dodd in their home in Kingsport, N.S. on April 30, 2022. (Jeorge Sadi/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New
Douglas Smith, 75, was sentenced Tuesday for killing his wife in their home four years ago after she had asked for help taking her own life, according to court documents.
Douglas Smith, 75, sentenced Tuesday to 6 years for manslaughter
WARNING: This story includes references to suicide and details a killing.
A 75-year-old man smothered his ailing wife in their Kingsport, N.S., home more than four years ago after she made him promise to help her take her own life, a court was told Tuesday.

Douglas Smith was sentenced in Nova Scotia Supreme Court in Kentville, N.S., to six years in prison for the death of Iris Dodd, 72, on April 30, 2022. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter in April days before he was set to stand trial for second-degree murder.
Smith and Dodd, who had serious health issues, had been married for 33 years but faced eviction and had nowhere to go, according to an agreed statement of facts.
Court documents illustrate a harrowing situation the couple, who had a "long, supportive and happy life together," found themselves in that night.
Dodd’s health had been deteriorating since she suffered a stroke in 2018 and they were going to be kicked out of their home the next day, the documents say.
She used a wheelchair, was losing her eyesight and lived with chronic pain from arthritis and fibromyalgia — a long-term condition that causes muscle pain, extreme fatigue and sleep difficulty.
She had just had a long stay in hospital due to bouts of pneumonia.
On the night she died, court documents say Dodd told her husband she didn’t want to spend her final years in a health-care or long-term care facility.
She told Smith she planned to take all of her medication at once in an attempt to overdose and Smith should leave the house so he wouldn't be culpable.
The only thing she needed from her husband was for him to arrange the pills because she couldn’t see them very well.
Initially, the documents say, Smith didn’t support his wife’s plan when she raised the topic abruptly.
However, “The victim was very upset and made Mr. Smith promise to help her with her plan and he promised he would,” said the agreed statement of facts.
They couple agreed they’d go ahead with the plan the following day, which helped Dodd calm down and go to sleep.
Smith couldn’t sleep, though, worrying about his wife dying alone. He became increasingly concerned her plan might fail and leave her with permanent brain damage.
“Mr. Smith resolved all these thoughts and fears in his head by getting up and holding a pillow over the victim’s face,” the agreed statement of facts said.
‘She was in distress and I eased her distress’
The day after Smith killed Dodd, he drove to the local RCMP detachment to turn himself in.
After discovering the office was closed, he called 911 from the parking lot and admitted to taking her life.
A recording of Smith's 911 call was released by the court.
The call began with a dispatcher asking Smith what emergency he was reporting. The senior replied that he wanted to report a death.
The dispatcher asked if the death had been sudden or unexpected and Smith said that his wife had died and he was responsible.
Smith said he didn’t want to provide any details but the dispatcher said she required some information before an officer could be sent to meet him.
“She was in distress and I eased her distress,” Smith replied.
An officer came out of the detachment, arrested Smith and took him to a cell inside the building where Smith confirmed it was his voice on the 911 call, according to court documents.
Emotional day in court
Smith was emotional in court Tuesday, holding his head in his hands while the agreed statement of facts was read.
He wept when Crown prosecutor Daniel Rideout reached the part detailing how Smith had smothered his wife.
Smith was asked if he wanted a break but replied: "Let's get this over with."

items: More stories from the Annapolis Valley

blocks.text: During submissions, Rideout noted the case differed from the spate of domestic homicides in Nova Scotia in recent years.
Smith was driven by compassion when he took his wife's life, but he still broke the law and had other options available, Rideout said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 31: Baste Duterte defends P33M GenCorp contracts
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte on Tuesday defended P33 million worth of government contracts awarded to GenCorp Industries Inc. as he testified at the impeachment trial of his sister,…

blocks.text: Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte on Tuesday defended P33 million worth of government contracts awarded to GenCorp Industries Inc. as he testified at the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.
The prosecution panel called Baste to testify after the Vice President listed GenCorp as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 SALNs.

Although he assured the public that the P33 million government contracts awarded by the Davao City government to GenCorp are all above board, the mayor said he would not have allowed such contracts to push through had he known about his sister’s ties to the firm.
“I would not have allowed it,” he said.
Mayor Duterte concluded after he testified that he is aware that the President and Vice President are not allowed to have business interests under Article 7, Section 13 of the Constitution.

The provision states that, “The President, Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants shall not, during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries."
Likewise, the mayor said he would know of any irregularity in these contracts, if there are any.

Later in the hearing, the mayor said that he has no independent knowledge of GenCorp and that its 19 contracts with the Davao City government worth over P33 million in the last five years “are not too much.”
Former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV, who was present during the proceedings, raised doubts on the mayor’s assertion that he is unaware of his sister’s GenCorp links.

"Kung pwede ‘yung sinasabi niya, lahat ng mayor sa Pilipinas, pwede makipag-kontrata sa kapatid sa kanila. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. Ayun ang implication dito," the former senator told reporters.
(If what he's saying is allowed, then all mayors in the Philippines could enter into contracts with their siblings. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. That's the implication here.)

In a separate news conference, the House prosecution panel said Baste’s claim that he was unaware of his sister’s links to GenCorp raised questions about why the Vice President did not disclose those links to him.

“The contracts were granted repeatedly and reached P33 million. Was the Vice President remiss in allowing these contracts to happen, considering that she declared financial interest in GenCorp and given the Constitutional prohibition on President and Vice President engaging in businesses? I’m sure it will be considered by the senator-judges in determining whether she violated the prohibition in this case,” private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. said.
Meanwhile, defense lawyer Michael Poa denied that he shared the sentiments of Vice President Duterte’s spokesperson Paolo Panelo that the new threshold needed for conviction was a foolish act.
Adverse ruling

Ahead of the mayor’s testimony, the Senate impeachment court denied the prosecution’s request for admission seeking to make the Vice President admit ownership of bank accounts, saying this will violate her right against self-incrimination, among other rights.

It wasn’t the only unfavorable ruling for the prosecution for Day 31 since the Senate impeachment court also admonished Tolosa over his previous statements on the impeachment case against the Vice President, which came close to violating the sub judice rule.

The sub judice rule is provided under Article 18 of the Rules on Impeachment. It states that the presiding officer and members of the Senate “shall refrain from making any comments and disclosures in public pertaining to the merits of a pending impeachment trial.”
The rule also states that “the same [prohibition] shall likewise apply to the prosecutors, the person impeached, and their respective counsel and witnesses.”

“With all due respect, I respectfully disagree with respect to that admonition because, as I’ve stated, there is no finding that I violated the rule. While I respectfully disagree, of course, I respect the authority of the impeachment court as an institution,” Tolosa said.

“Nonetheless, even if there’s no express statement that I violated the rule, there’s at the end an admonition to exercise greater restraint in giving public statements that may affect the merits of the case,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Dutch police arrest suspected member of group that claimed FBI hack
articles.summary: The suspect, 24, was arrested before the alleged cyber attack took place.

blocks.text: Dutch police have arrested a suspected member of the ShinyHunters cyber-crime group that claimed to have stolen sensitive information on all FBI bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After the alleged attack last week, the group claimed to have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address and phone numbers.
In a statement, Dutch police said it had arrested a 24-year-old man from Amsterdam on suspicion of being part of the group, which has also claimed other hacks.
The suspect was arrested on 15 September, before the alleged FBI attack. He is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders, police said.

Police said they seized his devices and found a "large amount of information" on his laptop, including "details about two murders that were to be committed abroad" that they suspect he may have ordered.
The suspect has been held since his arrest. Dutch officials have not ruled out further arrests.
Stan Duijf, who leads Dutch investigations into cybercrime, said in a statement: "The ShinyHunters group is responsible for a large number of national and international victims.
"It is good that we have been able to arrest a suspect in the investigation into this group."

Taking to X, FBI director Kash Patel thanked Dutch partners and said: "As we speak, FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest."
Following the arrest, Brett Leatherman, assistant director of FBI Cyber, urged members of the group to hand themselves in "while the choice is still yours".
He added: "Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them... but arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk.
"The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you, you know how to find us, we know how to find you."
ShinyHunters claimed to have breached the FBI's servers on 21 September and began contacting reporters the next day sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data.
The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine.

ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May.

The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records, and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information.
In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money.
Instead, the cyber-criminals asked the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation.

The public service announcement, external, which is still up on the FBI's website, described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims".
"They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said.
