articles.title: Spanish government approves measures to ease housing crisis after outcry over eviction
articles.summary:
Decrees include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable people after 87-year-old was forced out of her home

Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of…

blocks.text: Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, after a public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week.

Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible.

Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028.
A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements.

blocks.caption: Maricarmen Abascal attends an event organised by housing activists the day before her scheduled eviction from her home in Madrid.  Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, is transported on a stretcher to an ambulance after she was evicted from her Madrid home on Wednesday. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters

blocks.text: Hundreds of people remained camped out in ⁠one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest against Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the ⁠automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.

It is believed that the first decree has the approval of the conservative Catalan and Basque parties, which previously opposed the government’s housing overhauls, but they are likely to vote down the second decree.
Mónica García, the health minister, celebrated the decision, saying: “We’ve achieved something that even a month ago was unthinkable.”
She added: “It’s time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to restore the balance between citizens and vulture funds.”

The Tenants’ Union, which has been the driving force behind the demand for changes to the housing law, as well as the occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol by protesters in recent days, said it needed to read the small print but opposed the policy of dividing the issue into separate decrees.

“It’s a tactic of tearing something into shreds so that all that’s left are scraps,” said Alicia Del Río, a union spokesperson in Madrid. “The union demands the implementation of the Maricarmen decree in its entirety,” she said, referring to a set of changes drawn up by the union. “They have to accept what people are demanding.”

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with police near the Puerta del Sol encampment in Madrid.  Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing to ‌it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.
after newsletter promotion
“Owning two properties isn’t the same as owning entire buildings,” said Míriam Nogueras, Junts’ spokesperson in congress. “But here they’re not making any distinction between the two.”

blocks.caption: Housing rights protesters remain camped at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Photograph: Mario Mor ³N/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, dismissed the proposals. “The government has created a problem that didn’t exist when it took office,” he said. “A problem that was created over eight years can’t be solved in five minutes.”

Urbagestión, the company whose eviction of Abascal last Wednesday forced the housing crisis to the top of the political agenda, has said Abascal can return to her apartment at a rent that will not exceed 30% of her income. On Tuesday, she accepted the offer and will pay €533 (£457) a month – less than a third of the original demand of €1,650 that had led to her eviction.

blocks.caption: A protester in the encampment at Puerta del Sol. The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Underlining the lack of affordable housing, Ada Colau, a housing activist and a former Barcelona mayor, recently revealed that she has had to move out of her rented apartment after 15 years because it became impossible to pay the rent with a single income since she separated from her husband.

Colau, who renounced most of her mayoral salary during her eight years in office, said the market was geared towards dual incomes, whether couples or people sharing, adding that she had gone to live with a relative.

articles.title: COA flags over P700-M undisbursed fuel subsidy in 2025 audit
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged over P700 million worth of fuel subsidies that were not distributed to beneficiaries in its 2025 annual audit report for the Department of Transportation (DOTr)…

blocks.text: The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged over P700 million worth of fuel subsidies that were not distributed to beneficiaries in its 2025 annual audit report for the Department of Transportation (DOTr) but 70% or P1.9 billion were already distributed.

In a "24 Oras" report by Mariz Umali on Tuesday, of the P709.88 million undisbursed amount, P179.96 million was processed but not credited to the bank accounts of beneficiaries, the majority of whom are tricycle drivers, accounting for P120 million.
COA also flagged P1.589 million in fuel subsidies that were disbursed but rejected due to bank transaction issues, such as incorrect account numbers or mismatched beneficiary names in bank records.
Aside from fuel subsidies, other funds were also reportedly undisbursed, such as those allocated for drivers or operators in Cebu, which was under a state of calamity at the time.
According to the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB), the amount does not represent a single year's funds but rather the combined remaining funds from 2022, 2023, and 2024.

“Bale po, nagkulang po ang benepisyaryo na ibinigay ng DILG. ‘Yung ibang benepisyaryo naman po ng LTFRB, hindi na po mahanap, hindi na po mabigay, kaya po may natira,” LTFRB Acting Chairman Atty. Greg Pua explained.
(The list of beneficiaries provided by the DILG was insufficient. Meanwhile, some of the LTFRB’s beneficiaries could no longer be located or reached, which is why a balance remained.)

“‘Yung 120 million po na sumobra naman po sa sa tricycle, undistributed naman po sa tricycle, dahil naman po ito sa problema sa kanilang account number, sa pangalan. So, hindi po ma-transfer ng LandBank noong panahon na yun,” he added.

(Regarding the excess P120 million intended for tricycle drivers that remained undistributed, this was due to issues with their account numbers or names. Thus, LandBank was unable to process the transfers at the time.)

While COA acknowledged that 70% (P1.9 billion) of the total subsidy allotment was distributed as of November 30, 2025, it stressed that the remaining balance must be promptly delivered to qualified beneficiaries.
The LTFRB stated that legally, the remaining subsidies can no longer be distributed as the funds expire every two years.

“Legally, technically, hindi pwede. Kasi ‘yung pondo ay nag-expire na siya every two years. Kung pwede, palitan na lang namin ‘yung benepisyaryo para maitulong din namin sa mga nangangailangan po ngayon,” Pua said.

(Legally and technically, it is no longer allowed because the funds expire every two years. If permissible, we would prefer to replace the listed beneficiaries so we can assist those currently in need instead.)
Overpayment, Love Bus
The government auditors also flagged P2.853 million in overpayments due to duplicate submissions of the “authority to debit account,” which have yet to be refunded according to the audit report.
The undisbursed funds are not lost but have been returned to the national treasury.

Meanwhile, for the P380 million budget for the Love Bus “Libreng Sakay” (Free Ride) Program, the commission questioned why the Department contracted only one company to operate the route, noting that the program intends to support various bus drivers and operators.
According to the LTFRB, the funds were donated to them by the Office of the President and provided specific requirements.
“Dapat ay electric at dapat po ay PWD (person with disability) friendly. So wala pong ibang nakita except this one,” Pua said.
(The buses had to be electric and PWD-friendly (persons with disabilities). No other provider met these specifications except for this one.) — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about…

image.caption: Andy Burnham evoked surely Labour's most universally popular past government, the post-war adminstration under Clement Atlee, in his speechImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, only in the role for a few months after replacing Keir Starmer, has told the Labour Party conference in his native Liverpool that his government wants to restore hope and end "politics as usual."

But the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade is trying to balance a series of evidently conflicting fiscal goals: bolstering economic growth, reducing cost-of-living pressures, safeguarding pensions and making care costs more affordable, upgrading creaking infrastructure and significantly boosting military spending.

That's all while battling a populist challenge from Reform UK and Restore Britain on the right and the Green Party on the left. This led Labour to severe local and regional election defeats in May and ultimately spelt his predecessor Starmer's demise.

blocks.caption: Housing Secretary and party members' favorite Angela Rayner was among the speakers warming up the audience on Tuesday ahead of BurnhamImage: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Burnham say in his conference speech?

Burnham, a Liverpool lad who was mayor of Manchester prior to moving to take up Britain's top political job, repeated his most common mantra since coming to power, namely that "more of the same" will not solve the various issues facing the UK.
"We can't carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards," Burnham said. "More of the same isn't good enough and isn't going to get us where we need to be."
The conference's banner headline "hope again" was not incompatible with a more honest conversation, Burnham said.
"Hope comes from honesty ... and saying the things politicians usually avoid," he said.

He cited Labour's post-war government under Clement Atlee, famed for achievements like setting up Britain's National Health Service, as an example of his party past credentials, having "built the peace" in the public interest. He said that since the 1980s and the Conservative-dominated Margaret Thatcher era of his youth, this direction was lost.

"I will say it straight, Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialization, deregulation, privatization, austerity, Brexit, and what has it given us? A country run for vested interests, not in the public interest — with power held in too few hands, and too many places left to drift," Burnham said.

Burnham told the audience he would take on "the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long," including social care, high levels of youth unemployment, and greater public control of once-nationalized core interests like energy, water and housing.
"The British right talk about 'taking back control," Burnham said, evoking the slogan of the 2016 Brexit campaign. "Never forget that they are the ones who gave it away in the first place!"

blocks.caption: Major UK broadcasters are also on site in Liverpool for Labour's conference week, hoping for face time with the prime minsiter and other leadersImage: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why is Burnham, and Britain, in such a tricky bind?
Burnham said on coming to power that he wanted his premiership to be a "circuit-breaker for Britain" after years of rising prices and anemic growth.

He hit the ground with a handful of new policies like a cap on bus fares, temporarily removing value added tax from electricity bills amid the Iran war, and announcing a bid to stamp out rough sleeping.
But critics say his more grand stated strategy lacks detail and could prove economically unfeasible.

Burnham is constrained by a series of factors, including Labour's 2024 election campaign pledges under Starmer's leadership, Britain's strained public finances, and the suddenly risk-averse debt markets that have started heaping pressure on most developed economies of late.
Borrowing costs for his UK government, as it eyes a series of new banner spending plans, hit a 10-year-high on the morning of Burnham's speech.
In a sign of this lacking spending wiggle room, Burnham has already pushed back his stated aim to formulate reform plans for Britain's social care system.

He said on Tuesday that a "National Care System" would be put forward in time for the next election, currently scheduled for 2029. He said it would be a change "as significant" to the UK as the foundation of the state-funded National Health Service, and also essential to ensure the wider NHS' survival.
He said the plan would be "fully funded, and not by borrowing."

Burnham said that he did not expect such reforms to be easy, and acknowledged "I may pay a political price," but he said they were necessary steps and the kind of leadership he'd promised the party when seeking to replace Starmer this summer.

blocks.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood addressed the conference on Monday, with the anti-migration Reform UK probably the biggest electoral threat to Labour — if not necessarily the party Labour voters are migratingImage: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: These challenging economic realities coincide with Labour facing multi-pronged political threats. They hail from right-wing populist parties like the anti-immigration Reform UK, from left-wing populists claiming to hold an economic magic wand like the Green Party, and from nationalist parties in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland advocating independence from the UK.

articles.title: North Korea has recently completed two road bridges easing transport to strategic allies Russia and China
articles.summary: Two recently opened bridges are expected to ease trade and transport between North Korea and its powerful neighbors. The new connections come as Pyongyang builds strategic ties with China and Russia.

image.caption: Stretching 3 kilometers, the New Yalu River bridge can carry more traffic and ease trade Image: Kyodo News/IMAGO

blocks.text: A long-delayed bridge linking North Korea and China could finally open in early October, more than a decade after its completion, as Pyongyang simultaneously expands transport links with Russia.

South Korean news outlets have reported that the New Yalu River Bridge, connecting China's northeastern city of Dandong with the trade hub of Sinuiju in northwestern North Korea, could formally open by October 6, which marks the 77th anniversary of North Korea-China diplomatic relations.

Analysis published by the 38 North think tank showed significant progress on customs, immigration and warehouse facilities on the North Korean side, where construction had remained largely unfinished for years.
The cable-stayed New Yalu River Bridge is located about 15 kilometers (9 miles) downstream toward the Yellow Sea from the older crossings connecting central Dandong and Sinuiju.
The four-lane road bridge stretches over 3,000 meters across the river, with a network of approach roads connecting it to the surrounding areas.

It was intended to ease pressure on the aging Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which carries both road and rail traffic and remains one of the most important routes between North Korea and China, Pyongyang's top trading partner.
Improving links to both Russia and China

The expected opening of the improved link with China comes after a road bridge crossing the Tumen River located across the peninsula was opened on September 7 connecting North Korea's Rason region with Khasan in Russia's Primorsky region.
Until then, the two countries' narrow land border had been connected by rail but not by road.

"North Korea allowed the Chinese bridge to sit unused for more than a decade, but North Korea hurried more than Russia did," Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW.

That difference, he argues, provides clues to Pyongyang's strategy, which appears to be deliberately managing the pace of its improving relations with Russia and China to avoid returning to excessive dependence on Beijing.

"If it depends too much on China as it did in the past, North Korea's autonomy could be undermined," Han said, adding that Pyongyang is seeking to take advantage of good ties with both China and Russia while preserving its independence.

The former Unification Ministry official added that Russia has an interest in expanding transport routes through North Korea toward the Pacific, including through the port of Rajin, while Pyongyang could benefit from increased trade, tourism and opportunities to send workers to Russia.
He added that Russia needs North Korean labor, arguing that North Korean workers are more diligent than their Russian counterparts.
China, meanwhile, has its own reasons to ensure that North Korea does not become excessively reliant on Russia, the former official said.
"From China's perspective, it needs to keep North Korea from leaning too far toward Russia," Han said.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have grown since 2023, when North Korea began providing weapons and troops for the Ukraine war. As the Russia-North Korea strategic relationship has deepened, China has been taking steps to reassert itself as the North's primary partner.
Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said the bridges have added geopolitical implications.

"Pyongyang could now use its deepening ties with China and Russia, along with Trump's interest in engaging Kim, to strengthen its diplomatic leverage and take a more assertive approach toward South Korea," Ahn told DW.
North Korea slowly reopens
Pyongyang virtually sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, sharply reducing trade and restricting even the entry of foreign diplomats.

Cross-border freight trains between Dandong and Sinuiju resumed in 2022. Passenger trains followed on March 12 this year, restoring rail travel between North Korea and China for the first time in six years.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
Ahn described the prospective bridge opening as historically significant.
"The New Yalu River Bridge is effectively the first modern bridge between North Korea and China," Ahn said.
Plans for a new bridge date to 2009, when then-Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and North Korean officialsagreed on the project to relieve the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, built in 1943.

Construction on the new bridge began in 2011, largely financed by Beijing, and the bridge itself was essentially completed in 2014. The opening was complicated by delays on building a customs center on the North Korean side.
Ahn added the opening could be interpreted as a signal that Pyongyang intends to move toward greater economic openness, even if that process proceeds slowly.
Yalu River Bridge to bolster China trade
A former senior South Korean Unification Ministry official, who requested anonymity, told DW that renewed trade could also benefit China's northeastern provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang.
Before sanctions and the pandemic disrupted commerce, businesses in the region imported North Korean goods, including seafood, while Chinese products flowed in the opposite direction.
"Both sides need this," the former official said.
North Korea needs Chinese goods and opportunities to earn foreign currency, while parts of northeastern China can benefit from renewed cross-border commerce, he added.
The official said the long delay also reflected Pyongyang's previous reluctance to build customs, logistics and other infrastructure required on its side.

blocks.caption: The bridge itself was completed several years ago, but its opening has been delayedImage: Yomiuri Shimbun/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The fact that it is opening now means North Korea has built customs, clearance facilities and logistics warehouses," he said. "From that perspective, North Korea needs it more. It now needs goods coming in from China."
Former South Korean intelligence official Han expects the new crossing to accelerate trade recovery toward pre-pandemic trade levels.
"The opening of the Yalu River bridge will further stimulate trade between North Korea and China," Han told DW.
North Korea particularly needs imports for construction and industrial production, including factory components, he said.
But Han cautioned against expecting an uncontrolled trade boom.

He pointed to Pyongyang's increasingly centralized trade system, under which the state has tightened control over imports instead of allowing individual factories and enterprises to conduct commerce more independently.
A shortage of foreign currency could provide another constraint, Han said, pointing to the sharp rise in the unofficial exchange rate for the US dollar inside North Korea.

articles.title: Women and children displaced by Nepal's floods say safe housing, privacy and stability remain out of reach
articles.summary: Families living in temporary shelters in northern Nepal say safety and privacy remain out of reach as concerns about trafficking and abuse mount.

image.caption: Uncertainty over permanent housing and livelihoods is putting girls at risk, says Save the ChildrenImage: Prakash Mathema/AFP

blocks.text: One month after deadly flash floods in Nepal swept away Karishma Tamang's community in Rasuwa District, the pregnant 26-year-old is still struggling to find a safe place to call home.

Karishma, who is expecting her second child, has been moving from place to place with her 4-year-old daughter since the devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border at the end of August.
"Initially, we were kept in a covered hall at Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District," she told DW, adding that hundreds of people shared the same shelter for days.

"Now we have shifted to a small makeshift family tent at the nearby Barahachaur area. Still, we can't sleep during rainy nights as it leaks when it rains." Her brother and his two children remain missing after the flood.

blocks.caption: Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environmentImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: There is no proper toilet, although a small makeshift latrine has been set up near the tents, Karishma said.
Children and pregnant women like Karishma need privacy and safety, but such facilities remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas.
"It would be great to have a stable place to stay, where I could cook my own meals, feel safe and have some comfort," she said.
Safety concerns in temporary shelters

The August 26 flood, triggered by a glacier collapse along the Nepal-China border, killed about 1,450 people and left more than 5,500 missing. Reconstruction costs are estimated to be $4.8 billion (€4.2 billion).

At least seven people, including girls, women and local volunteers at temporary shelters and camps, spoke to DW. Although none reported experiencing sexual harassment or abuse, their accounts point to widespread concerns about safety and vulnerability in the aftermath of the floods.

Sabita Tamang, who lost her 5-year-old daughter, nephew and niece in the floods, is also staying in a makeshift tent in Barahachaur. The 24-year-old said she has to travel beyond the nearest tap to bathe and collect water.

blocks.caption: Privacy and safety remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areasImage: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We feel uncomfortable taking a bath in an open space among strangers and unknown locals," she told DW. "Many children have seen their family members, friends and neighbors caught in the floods," she said, raising concerns about the impact on their mental health and education.
Risk of trafficking and abuse

Save the Children Nepal has warned that protection measures for children and their families must be strengthened across flood-affected areas amid concerns about trafficking, violence, exploitation and child marriage.
Many families have moved into rented rooms. Yet hundreds are being housed in temporary shelters and makeshift tents in Nuwakot and Dhading districts.
Save the Children Nepal raised concerns about privacy and safety for girls and women because unfamiliar people have unrestricted access to shared spaces.

Ayush Joshi, director for advocacy, campaigns, communications and media at Save the Children Nepal, told DW that the organization's report was based on qualitative assessments involving affected people, including women and children, as well as volunteers deployed in flood-hit areas.

blocks.caption: The disaster has affected more than 80,000 people. Thousands who lost everything are living in emergency sheltersImage: Pedro Pardo/AFP

blocks.text: "Many temporary shelters are built without planning. Camps on the outskirts of towns have inadequate lighting at night and lack separate washrooms and private spaces," Joshi told DW, noting that there is unrestricted access for unfamiliar people.
"Such situations naturally increase the risk of insecurity, potential harassment and exploitation, especially for young girls and children."

According to Joshi, in the aftermath of the disaster, many people became separated from their families, while some children lost their lives and older siblings had to become caregivers for younger siblings.

"In such circumstances, cases of school dropouts and child marriage could increase," he added, referring to Save the Children's field assessment. "We have seen many children facing mental health issues, like becoming angry, frightened and crying loudly. There is a need for socio-emotional healing."
What does the government say?

The Nepali government has also assessed the risks of trafficking and potential child abuse and has collaborated with organizations such as Save the Children, the police and local authorities to strengthen protection measures at displacement sites.
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes

Chakra Bahadur Budha, spokesperson at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, said the government had increased monitoring and surveillance and was raising awareness about gender-based violence and trafficking.
"We have mobilized and kept all relevant stakeholders on high alert to check at points of entry and exit, so as to protect affected people from being trafficked or abused," he told DW.

Authorities took back at least 78 children from two Buddhist monasteries in Kathmandu and placed them in temporary camps. Budha explained that the monasteries had rescued and supported the children, offering long-term shelter, education and employment, but the government discourages such arrangements outside established procedures.

"We have strictly discouraged religious or charitable organizations from keeping children without following legal procedures," Budha told DW. "Adoption has also been discouraged for now, but children can be placed with close relatives, such as uncles and aunts, for their protection after verification of their relationship."
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said at least 541 children have either lost their parents or become separated from their families.
Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centers in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts.

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia has been accused of launching sabotage attacks across a number of European Nato countries which have been helping Ukraine.

blocks.text: Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details.
Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.

Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine.
The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation".

Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year.

The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month.
Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine".

French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end".
He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes.
"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added.
An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine.
Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine.

"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said.

In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts.

"Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Palloson said, external.
Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said "such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning".
"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Dmitry Peskov said.

articles.title: Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir
articles.summary: The defendant could face jail or a fine after the image sparked a search operation in the city’s largest reservoir.

blocks.text: The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities.
But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police.
The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty.

In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; £5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both.
Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague.
"The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said.
It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague.

articles.title: Marcoleta camp maintains P75M was 'campaign contribution'
articles.summary: Senator Rodante Marcoleta"s defense team maintained that the money he admitted to receiving was part of his campaign contributions, but the prosecution argued that the lawmaker paid a tax that…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 8:57pm

Senator Rodante Marcoleta’s defense team maintained that the money he admitted to receiving was part of his campaign contributions, but the prosecution argued that the lawmaker paid a tax that suggested otherwise.

In a 24 Oras report from Maki Pulido on Tuesday, the Sandiganbayan First Division held its first trial day for the case of Marcoleta, who is accused of violating Presidential Decree 46, which prohibits government officials from receiving monetary gifts.
The prosecution presented Attorney Victoria Besinio of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) Political Finance Affairs Department as a witness.
During the questioning of Marcoleta’s lawyer, the COMELEC determined that the money given to Marcoleta was a campaign contribution.
However, the prosecution argued that Marcoleta’s camp also submitted to the COMELEC proof that they paid donor’s tax.
It could not be treated as a campaign donation because campaign donations are not taxable, the prosecution argued.
Marcoleta had publicly stated on a television program that he received P75 million in campaign donations, which he did not state on his Statement of Contribution and Expenditures.
The prosecution used this statement as evidence during the trial.

While Marcoleta did not state who gave him this money, he would later name former House lawmaker Mike Defensor and Joseph Espiritu as donors in a verified position paper. Both Defensor and Espiritu are his co-accused in the case.

articles.title: Deloitte Canada cuts GDP forecast by 20% as tariffs grip economy amid Trump's trade war
articles.summary: Deloitte Canada has shaved 20 per cent off its growth forecast for Canada's economy in 2027, citing increasingly tough conditions for consumers and businesses. The accounting firm's latest outlook…

image.caption: Workers are pictured at Amazon's 825,000-square-foot fulfilment and distribution centre in Pitt Meadows, B.C, on June 6, 2025. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

Deloitte Canada has shaved 20 per cent off its growth forecast for Canada's economy in 2027, citing increasingly tough conditions for consumers and businesses. The accounting firm's latest outlook comes as a new American ban on select Canadian imports took effect.
Fallout of recent trade escalations likely to cause sharp economic slowdown in Q4 and early 2027, firm says
Deloitte Canada has shaved 20 per cent off its growth forecast for Canada's economy in 2027, citing increasingly tough conditions for consumers and businesses.
The accounting firm's latest outlook comes as a new American ban on select Canadian imports took effect on Tuesday.
Deloitte sees the fallout of recent escalations in the Canada-U.S. trade war causing a sharp economic slowdown in the final quarter of this year and into early 2027.

Chief economist Dawn Desjardins says the weight of billions of dollars in U.S. tariffs and Canada's reciprocal measures will not fall evenly across the Canadian economy, hitting some sectors hard, while others prosper. At the same time, the federal government's fiscal supports, investment initiatives and defence spending are positive signals for targeted growth, she said.

"For some, it's a little bit like the Earth is moving under their feet — and not in a positive way. While in other sectors, I think we can anticipate growth and job creation," Desjardins told CBC News in an interview prior to the report's release on Tuesday.

items: Canada's economy has found its footing. But is it enough to survive the U.S. trade war?

blocks.text: Deloitte's latest economic outlook for Canada calls for GDP to grow 1.6 per cent in 2027. In late June, the firm said it expected two per cent GDP growth next year.
Deloitte currently sees Canada's economy growing by 0.9 per cent in 2026 — a slight improvement from its June estimate of 0.7 per cent.

"It's so uncertain when we think about all the factors the Canadian companies are facing, whether it's the prospect of higher costs, the prospect of more friction with our largest trading partner or perhaps even higher interest rates. All these factors are just creating a very uncertain environment," Desjardins said.
"As a result, we do think that the economy probably is going to be on a slower growth trajectory."
Canada's economic growth flat in July
On Tuesday, Statistics Canada reported that GDP for July was flat from the previous month.

"The goods-producing industries grouping was essentially unchanged in July, as increases in construction and utilities were offset by declines in the other sectors comprising the aggregate," the agency stated.
"The services-producing industries aggregate was essentially flat, as increases across several sectors were offset by declines in retail trade and wholesale trade."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
articles.summary: The US journalist says he realised he was a "a pawn in a greater game" when he was not interrogated or tortured by FSB agents.

blocks.text: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.
In an interview with the BBC, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him.

"I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game".
Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal.

Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false.
On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story.

They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place".
The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service.
"It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned."
What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd.

Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state.

"I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years."
That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap.
"I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right.
Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany.
"They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically."

Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace.
He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space.
"That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine."
Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright.
"I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to."

But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently."

Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed.
Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long".

When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again."
Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions.
He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped.

And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend.
"I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better."

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home
articles.summary: Two homes belonging to the al-Tubasi family were set on fire and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers.

blocks.text: Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablaze
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem

More than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers.

Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence.
"It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC.
"My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us."

Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back.
Image source, Reuters
Mahmoud al-Tubasi said he thought settlers were going to kill him and his family

The family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks. Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons who are married with young daughters.

Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police.

By torchlight, the family inspected one home. A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about. The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste.

A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped.

"As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israel's High Court has ruled that the al-Tubasi family must be allowed to return to their homes

blocks.text: Israel's High Court has ruled that the al-Tubasi family must be allowed to return to their homes

The grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back. Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle.
As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses. Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them.
Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves."
An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces."

The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed."

The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israel's prime minister called on law enforcement authorities to prosecute those he called "rioters"

blocks.text: Israel's prime minister called on law enforcement authorities to prosecute those he called "rioters"
One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud.

The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago.

The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence. He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires."
According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction.

Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank".

Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministers have said they aim to "bury the idea" that an independent Palestinian state could be set up in the territory along with East Jerusalem and Gaza. Settlements and outposts are illegal under international law.

Levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, according to the United Nations, which says that since 2023, more than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks and access restrictions in the occupied West Bank.
In the same time period, the UN's Humanitarian Office (OCHA) has logged 6,199 attacks by Israeli settlers causing casualties or damage, external.

According to OCHA, at least 82 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank this year and four Israelis have been killed - members of the security forces and civilians. At least 23 Palestinians were killed in the context of settler attacks.

articles.title: Tulfo flags alleged favoritism in NHA's housing projects
articles.summary: Senator Raffy Tulfo on Tuesday flagged alleged "palakasan," or patronage in National Housing Authority (NHA) housing projects, particularly for calamity and tragedy victims.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 8:29pm
Senator Raffy Tulfo on Tuesday flagged alleged "palakasan," or patronage in National Housing Authority (NHA) housing projects, particularly for calamity and tragedy victims.

During the Senate deliberations on the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development and its attached agencies’ proposed ₱5.498-billion budget for 2027, Tulfo said that he received complaints that some local officials favor people they knew for housing.

“Talamak daw ang palakasan. Karamihan daw sa nabibigyan ng pabahay eh mga taga-munisipyo o dabarkads ni chairman, etc. Ito mayroon akong feedback galing sa netizens, in fact, may mga nag-email sa tanggapan ko,” he said.

(Favoritism is allegedly rampant. Most of those being given housing are allegedly municipal employees or close friends of the barangay chairman, etc. I have feedback from netizens here; in fact, some have sent emails to my office.)
For its part, the NHA said that the beneficiaries of their housing project comes from the local government unit.
The agency also said that the only validation they conduct is by checking if those in the list have yet to receive a house.

“Mayroon pong resettlement, mayroon pong calamity. So bago kami mag-start, mayroon na po talagang listahan ng beneficiaries. Itong listahan na ito ay galing ng LGU. Vina-validate ng OCD yung biktima ng bagyo o trahedya. Tsaka pinapasa sa amin, so vinavalidate lang namin ito based sa hindi sila naulit, kumbaga hindi pa sila nabigyan ng bahay noon,” said NHA General Manager Joeben Tai.

(There is resettlement, and there is calamity housing. So before we start, there is already a list of beneficiaries. This list comes from the LGU. The OCD validates the victims of the typhoon or tragedy. Then it is passed to us, so we only validate it based on whether they are duplicates—meaning they haven't been given a house before.)
However, Tulfo noted that the NHA should still make sure that those in the list of beneficiaries have no connections to the local officials issuing them.
The senator said that even those who already have a home of their own or have cars are still getting free housing due to connections.

“You have to have a system para masiguro na itong mga LGU na nagbibigay sa inyo ng listahan ay hindi yung listahan nila na pabor sa kanilang mga followers, pabor sa kanilang mga nagka-campaign, pabor sa kanilang mga tauhan,” said Tulfo.
(You have to have a system to ensure that these LGUs giving you lists aren't providing lists that favor their followers, favor their campaign workers, or favor their staff.)
The NHA assured that it will strictly monitor the list of beneficiaries, warning that home ownership rights will be revoked if housing units are sold to non-beneficiaries.

“Ito po yung mga naibebentang unit kung saan binenta ng mga benepisyaryo yung kanilang mga unit sa P200,000, P300,000. Ayan din po chine-check namin, upang masiguro na benepisyaryo lang po ang nakatira,” said Tai.
(These are the sold units where beneficiaries sold them for ₱200,000 or ₱300,000. That is also what we check, to ensure that only beneficiaries are living there.)
“Lugi rin po yung nakabili kasi kina-cancel namin 'yan, at pinapaalis namin yung nakabili,” he added.
(The buyers also lose out because we cancel those rights, and we evict the buyer.) — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Unmatched EJ Obiena shatters Asian Games record to defend throne
articles.summary: EJ Obiena delivers the Philippines' third gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games as he breaks his own record to repeat as men's pole vault champion

blocks.text: CHAMPION. Pole vaulter EJ Obiena in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
EJ Obiena delivers the Philippines' third gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games as he breaks his own record to repeat as men's pole vault champion
MANILA, Philippines – When it comes to Asia, EJ Obiena is in a league of his own.

And he reinforced that notion as Obiena defended his Asian Games crown following a record-breaking performance in men’s pole vault at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Japan on Tuesday, September 29.

Obiena set a new Asian Games mark after clearing 5.91 meters in a single attempt, delivering the Philippines’ third gold medal in this edition after gymnastics star Carlos Yulo won the first two in artistic gymnastics.
He shattered his own record of 5.90m, which Obiena set in 2023 when he won his first Asian Games title in Hangzhou, China.

After two failed attempts at 5.80m, Obiena upped the ante by going for 5.91m, which he surpassed with room to spare on the way to becoming the first back-to-back champion in the event since Kazakhstan’s Igor Potapovich won in 1994 and 1998.
It marked the first time Obiena cleared over 5.90m since he posted 5.97m in ruling the Irena Szewinska Memorial in 2024.
Two Chinese bets completed the podium, with Yao Jie and Li Chenyang bagging silver and bronze, respectively, with 5.70m clearances.

Obiena highlighted the Philippines’ best athletics showing in decades, with the country also bagging a pair of bronze courtesy of John Cabang Tolentino (men’s 110m hurdles) and Victoria Bossong (women’s 800m). – Rappler.com

articles.title: French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism
articles.summary: National Rally President Jordan Bardella says he will sue for libel over comments he is accused of making as a young activist.

blocks.text: The president of France's hard-right National Rally (RN), Jordan Bardella, has said he will sue for libel after a report published antisemitic comments that it alleged he had made as a young activist.
The Mediapart website released what it said was the result of "several months" of investigation into "dozens of written conversations" Bardella allegedly had in 2013.

With seven months to go before France's presidential elections, Bardella condemned "the beginnings of a total war" aimed at destabilising his party, and RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said she had total confidence in him.
The alleged remarks included blatantly antisemitic tropes, and Bardella said they were an attempt to destroy his political career.

Mediapart did not produce screen-grabs of any of the alleged remarks. It said it had "independently authenticated" the conversations, which came from "a bigger documentary base corroborated by witness statements".
But Bardella, 31 – who is a likely prime minister if Le Pen wins the presidential election – said the allegations were a fabrication aimed at derailing the RN's increasingly confident bid for power.

"Everything is going to be done to destabilise the campaign," he told CNews television on Monday night. "Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties.
"Of course I have instructed my lawyer to sue for libel."
Le Pen said the alleged remarks "seem so weird that they can only be a forgery – one of those dirty tricks for which Mediapart appears to hold the secret".

Among the statements that Mediapart alleges Bardella made when he was 17 or 18 are: "All the banks are owned by Jews"; "The Jew has to dominate other people, crush them and rob them"; and "What they want is a new world order dominated by Israel, with of course Jerusalem as its capital."
Mediapart is an avowedly leftwing website which has exposed a number of scandals over the years, though its targets have been politicians of all stripes.

The French hard right is riding higher than ever in pre-election polls, with the latest this week, from Toluna-Harris, showing Le Pen a clear victor over whatever rival she faces in the crucial second round in May.

According to the survey, Le Pen would pick up 35-36% of the vote in the multi-candidate first round. Her likely opponent in the two-way run-off would be Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical left who she would eradicate with 69% of the vote.
But in a stark warning for the political establishment, the poll showed that she would also easily beat the most popular centrist candidate Edouard Philippe, with a score of 57%.

On Sunday the RN received another boost when results of a partial election for the upper house of parliament, the Senate, produced for the first time enough seats for the party to form an official group.
Under Marine Le Pen, daughter of the historic party founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, the RN has made huge efforts to distance itself from the French far-right's antisemitic roots.
Last year Bardella was the first senior figure from the party to be invited to Israel, for a conference on antisemitism.
Today the party regards militant Islam as a pre-eminent threat – a position it shares with many Jews. The RN even styles itself as a "shield for the Jewish community".
The alleged comments from Bardella throw back to a current of far-right thinking that Mediapart says has never been eradicated but only covered up in the new-look party.

Leftwing politicians called on Bardella to resign, and the head of the Jewish umbrella organisation Crif, Yonathan Arfi, said the alleged comments "were an illustration of the limits of the RN's clean-up act".
But RN deputy Jean-Philippe Tanguy said the source of the allegations was disaffected members of the party who had been expelled years ago because of their antisemitic ideas.

"From what I know, it is the antisemitic rabble that were so bravely purged by Marine Le Pen. At the start of the 2010s, they were numerous and well-organised, but they were defeated. These people have always had it in for us."

articles.title: Ontario woman convicted of killing her baby in 2002 acquitted amid new medical research
articles.summary: Jennifer Gaskin was acquitted of manslaughter Tuesday more than two decades after being convicted in the death of her infant son.

image.caption: Jennifer Gaskin was convicted in 2002 in the death of her 2 1/2-month-old son Joeseph after two medical experts testified the child had died as a result of shaken baby syndrome. She was acquitted Tuesday amid new expert testimony. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Toronto
Jennifer Gaskin was acquitted Tuesday more than two decades after being convicted in the death of her infant son.
Experts at the time said Jennifer Gaskin's son died of shaken baby syndrome, but new research disputes that
An Ontario woman sobbed in court Tuesday morning as she was acquitted in the death of her infant son after more than two decades labelled as his killer.
Jennifer Gaskin was convicted in 2002 in the death of her 2 1/2-month-old son Joeseph after two medical experts testified the child had died as a result of shaken baby syndrome.

Significant concerns about that medical evidence emerged years later as the province examined shaken-baby cases from the mid-1980s to the mid-2000s, and Gaskin's legal team eventually retained three more experts to look over the file.

Court heard Tuesday the three experts couldn't rule out the possibility of an inflicted injury, but found Joeseph — a premature baby who spent the first two months of his life in hospital — could also have died from sudden infant death syndrome.
The Crown told the Appeal Court that the new findings should be admitted as fresh evidence and Gaskin should be acquitted.
In its written submissions, the Crown said the original expert evidence supporting her conviction has been "wholly undermined and placed in grave doubt."

articles.title: Spain announces new housing measures after protests over 87-year-old woman's eviction
articles.summary: The measures include a proposed ban on evictions until 2030 and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts.

blocks.text: Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week.
Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a potential ban on evictions until 2030, Health Minister Mónica García said.
She said the measures would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold".
The new housing measures need to be approved in parliament, where the leftist coalition government lacks a majority.

García said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the the purchase of housing by investment firms.
"It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said.
Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible."

But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the pro-Catalan independence party Junts, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped."

"Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.
The minority government, which is made up of the ruling Socialists and the junior partners Sumar, has 30 days from the decree's publication to reach an agreement in parliament.
Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez is set to give further details on the measures at a news conference later on Tuesday.

articles.title: COA finds ‘unverifiable’ beneficiaries in DepEd’s SHS voucher program
articles.summary: The dozens of unverifiable beneficiaries of the senior high school voucher program resulted in an overpayment of P938,000, according to state auditors

blocks.text: DEPED. The Department of Education headquarters in Pasig City.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
The dozens of unverifiable beneficiaries of the senior high school voucher program resulted in an overpayment of P938,000, according to state auditors

items: The Commission on Audit identified 58 unverifiable beneficiaries of the Department of Education's senior high school voucher program, leading to an overpayment of P938,000 for the school year 2025-2026.

The unverifiable beneficiaries included students who dropped out, transferred, were not enrolled, deceased, or absent during validation, highlighting deficiencies in beneficiary validation and monitoring by the DepEd.
In response to the findings, the DepEd has tightened its validation and accountability measures and has begun recovering overpayments.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – There were 58 “unverifiable” beneficiaries of the Department of Education‘s (DepEd) senior high school (SHS) voucher program, which resulted in an overpayment of P938,000 in school year (SY) 2025-2026, the Commission on Audit (COA) found.
According to COA’s compliance audit on the existence and eligibility of voucher beneficiaries, the flagged unvalidated beneficiaries were:

items: 32 students who had officially or unofficially dropped out
12 who transferred to other schools
11 who were not enrolled in the second semester
2 who were reported deceased
1 who was absent during validation with no records available

blocks.text: The overpayment of P938,000, which was for 53 out of the 58 unverified beneficiaries, had already been released to their respective schools, COA said in its 2025 annual audit report on the DepEd released last September 23.
Four beneficiaries were excluded from billing statements prior to payment as of February, while the subsidy for one beneficiary had not yet been released as of March.
Moreover, state auditors found five beneficiaries who were “misclassified under incorrect voucher categories,” resulting in an overpayment of P14,710.

Other deficiencies seen were incomplete or improperly maintained supporting documents and inadequate monitoring by the DepEd and the Private Education Assistance Committee, which helps in implementing the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GATSPE).

“These lapses expose the program to the risk of erroneous billing and overpayment, compromise the reliability of beneficiary validation, and may result in the disbursement of funds to ineligible beneficiaries, contrary to the objective of providing financial assistance exclusively to qualified learners,” COA said.

The SHS voucher program is a government financial subsidy program for qualified Grades 11 and 12 students. It provides assistance in the form of vouchers ranging from P14,000 to P22,500 per year, which are paid directly to the student’s chosen private school.
COA said the program’s participating schools are responsible for encoding and updating student information.
“The status of the concerned [voucher program beneficiaries] should have been duly updated and subjected to DepEd verification to prevent potential overpayments,” the commission added.
On Tuesday, September 29, the DepEd said it had acted on the COA findings.

“As part of its five-layer validation, DepEd, through its co-manager of the senior high school voucher program, Private Education Assistance Committee, has completed its school year 2025-2026 validation. Through this year-end validation, flagged cases are being reviewed and confirmed overpayments will be recovered,” part of the DepEd’s statement read.
The agency said it had “tightened beneficiary validation, billing, refund, and accountability measures” in the revised Expanded GATSPE guidelines released in April.
The DepEd said it will “continue to pursue accountability and the recovery of government funds where warranted.”
The DepEd investigated 12 private schools in February 2025 over the alleged presence of ghost students in the SHS voucher program.
By March 2025, the agency recovered P65 million from the voucher program amid irregularities, with 38 private schools fully refunding the government.

In July 2026, the DepEd said a regional trial court had sentenced an individual to up to 14 years in prison for attempting to defraud the government program by submitting falsified documents. Case details were not provided.
In the same 2025 annual audit report, COA also flagged deficiencies in monitoring the implementation of the SHS voucher program.
As of October 2025, there were 172,909 billed beneficiaries in participating private senior high schools nationwide, excluding the Bangsamoro region and the Negros Island Region, according to COA.

State auditors found the unverifiable beneficiaries from a sample population of 5,507 in SY 2025-2026. Of the number, 995 beneficiaries came from the National Capital Region, while the rest were from other regions, covering 571 senior high schools participating in the voucher program. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Poa denies agreeing with Panelo over 'lokohan' remark
articles.summary: Lawyer Michael Poa, spokesperson for Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team, on Tuesday denied agreeing with Duterte's spokesperson Paolo Panelo, who described as a joke the Senate impeachment…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 29, 2026 8:05pm

Lawyer Michael Wesley Poa, spokesperson for Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team, on Tuesday denied agreeing with Duterte's spokesperson Paolo Panelo, who described as a joke the Senate impeachment court's ruling on the basis for determining the voting threshold for her conviction.
Poa was referring to Panelo's remarks to reporters on September 23, when the latter said the impeachment court's ruling was a "joke" and claimed that Poa shared his sentiments.
"That's not true. Actually, just to set the record straight, I didn't agree with him on anything as to lokohan (a joke) or anything like that," Poa said in a press briefing.
"I always maintained candor with all of you. I always maintained respect to the court," he added.
Poa said any disagreement with the court's decision should be addressed through the proper legal process, not through media interviews or informal discussions.
Senator-judges voted 13-1-6 to set the conviction threshold at two-thirds of those legally allowed to participate in the proceedings.
This means Duterte could be convicted with fewer than 16 votes, as several senators are facing charges, remain in hiding or are on medical leave.
The defense team is considering appealing the Senate impeachment court's ruling before the Supreme Court.
After the impeachment court issued its ruling last week, Panelo said he and Poa believed the decision was a "joke."

Panelo told reporters: "Nung nag-usap naman kami kanina parang agree kami doon sa nangyari na lokohan lang 'to, lokohan na itong nangyayari. Kaya posible silang umakyat sa Korte Suprema. Pero hindi ko narinig actually kung ano sinabi niya sa press briefing."

(When we talked to each other earlier, it seemed like we agreed that what happened was just a farce, that what is happening is a joke. That's why it's possible they'll elevate it to the Supreme Court. But I actually didn't hear what he said at the press briefing.)
For his part, Poa said he had already messaged Panelo about the statement and asked him why he had made such remarks.

“I messaged him personally and basically asked him why he said that. Well, I will just leave it at that. He is the spokesperson of the vice president, but I will not allow my name to be dragged into something that I had nothing to do with,” Poa said.
"He assured me that it won't happen again," he added.— MCG, GMA News

"It's ‌time ​to intervene in the speculative housing market and ​begin to rebalance the scales between ⁠citizens ​and vulture funds," ​Garcia, who belongs ​to the ‌leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, ​wrote ⁠in a post on ⁠X.
Legislation still needs to pass through parliament
The Spanish government, led byPrime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.
But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.
Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.
Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.
A case that triggered mass protests in Spain

Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.
Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.

blocks.caption: Thousands demonstrate against evictions and the housing crisis in Spain Image: Richard Zubelzu/NurPhoto/picture alliance
Demonstrators set up camps at Puerta del Sol squareImage: David Canales/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance
Protesters were angry that Maricarmen was removed from the apartment she lived in since 1956Image: Bruno Thevenin/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.

The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.
Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.
She is a wheelchair user too.
People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.
More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says
Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.

"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.
