articles.title: How often have barangay, SK elections been postponed?
articles.summary: Rappler crunches the numbers and finds that both elections have been moved — either separately or jointly — at least 16 times since 1982

blocks.text: The barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) supposed to be held this year have been officially moved to November 2028 after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed a law fixing these officials’ terms to five years.

This is now the third time Marcos has authorized a BSKE postponement. But the current president is not the only one to have moved the polls — nor is it rare for such a delay to happen multiple times in one administration.

“Barangay and SK elections are already the most frequently postponed democratic exercises in the country’s history,” poll watchdog National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections (Namfrel) said in a September 26 statement criticizing the 2026 BSKE postponement.
So, how often have these postponements actually happened?
Rappler crunched the numbers and found that both elections have been moved — either separately or jointly — at least 16 times since 1982. Here’s a breakdown of the data.
How often terms were extended because of BSKE postponements
This chart shows the start and end of an elected official’s term, starting from the election they won until the successfully held election that chose their successor.

The first-ever barangay polls were held on May 17, 1982, in accordance with the Barangay Election Act of 1982. Before that, elections for barangay officials had been held together with the local elections. (READ MORE: Looking back: The first barangay polls in PH)
The terms of office of these barangay officials were set to six years, which means the next election would have been on the second Monday of May 1988.
But most 1982 barangay election winners were not able to finish their terms, since local elected officials were replaced by appointed officers-in-charge following the EDSA Revolution in 1986.
The May 1988 elections were then postponed twice: first to November 1988 and then to March 1989, which was when the polls finally pushed through.
The succeeding 1994 election proceeded on schedule, but the Local Government Code had limited the terms of office of those elected in these polls to just three years.
The 1997 elections were then promptly conducted after those three years.
The first SK polls in 1992 also got off to a rocky start, with two postponements right off the bat.
The landmark election should have been held 30 days after the May 1992 local elections, but the Commission on Elections (Comelec) passed a resolution setting the polls on September 30, 1992.
In the end, the elections were moved again and finally conducted on December 4, 1992.

The 1991 Local Government Code set the second Monday of May as the date for the 1994 barangay officials, with the SK polls set to happen 120 days after, but only the barangay polls pushed through. An amendment to the law had been passed, resetting the SK elections to May 1996.

The same amendment set the barangay elections for May 1997, which was successfully conducted. Elected SK officials were to serve until the next regular election of barangay officials — which should have been three years later in 2000.
Then-president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo passed a law in 1998 changing the terms of barangay and SK officials from three to five years, starting with those elected in May 1997.

This meant the next barangay and SK polls would be in 2002 instead of 2000. Another amendment to the Local Government Code would later set the exact date of the synchronized BSKE on July 15, 2002, which was successfully held.

The next synchronized polls were then postponed once again from 2005 to 2007, which a 2005 Philippine Star report said was prompted by the Arroyo administration saying there was no money available for the polls.
At the time, P6.4 billion had been allocated for a charter change plan, the same report said. This plan did not come to fruition.
The 2007 and 2010 BSKEs then proceeded as scheduled.

The 2013 polls only pushed through at the barangay level. The SK elections were once again postponed, although there was no holdover for then-incumbent youth officials, who stepped down from office at the end of their terms on November 30, 2013.
The new date for the SK polls was set between October 28, 2014, and February 23, 2015. This did not go as planned, either.

The 2015 SK polls were first set for February 21. But as the election date drew near, another bill seeking the SK polls’ postponement to October 2016 had passed in both houses of Congress, awaiting only the president’s signature.
Because of this, the Commission on Elections initially moved the polls to April 2015.
A month before the April polls, then-president Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III signed the law moving the SK polls to October 2016.
Then-president Rodrigo Duterte signed another law postponing the BSKE schedule by one year, from October 2016 to October 2017.
At that point, barangay officials were set to go beyond their three-year terms, since the new law also allowed a holdover for them to continue serving unless removed or suspended from office.
SK posts, meanwhile, had been vacant since 2013.
Duterte authorized another postponement of the BSKE — just three weeks before the scheduled polls — and set it for May 2018.

The 2018 BSKE finally pushed through on May 14, 2018. It replaced the barangay officials who had been serving for nearly two years beyond their allotted terms, and filled the SK seats that had been vacant for four and a half years.
Duterte again moved the BSKE originally set for May 2020 to the first Monday of December 2022. This gave elected officials a term of five years — beyond the three-year limit required by law.
The 2022 BSKE was again postponed by Duterte’s successor, Marcos. It was moved to October 2023 and successfully conducted.
The succeeding elections were supposed to be conducted on December 1, 2025, but were again postponed after Marcos signed a law increasing the term of barangay officials from three to four years.
The next elections were scheduled for the first Monday of November 2026.
Marcos granted another term lengthening for barangay and SK officials from four to five years, effectively postponing the polls to November 2028.
Barangay and SK election postponements
Number of times elections were postponed during each administration
Postponements have mostly been evenly distributed across presidencies — although each had its own context.

Noynoy Aquino’s postponements were only composed of SK polls, during a time when the Sangguniang Kabataan Reform Act of 2015 was being created in response to criticisms of the barangay youth arm being inefficient and corrupt. (READ: Why the Sangguniang Kabataan needs an overhaul)
In Ramos’ case, two of the three postponements were only months apart.
It is during the last two administrations that postponements became regular for both the barangay and SK polls — and usually spanning one year or more.

Why are these postponements so frequent? Ona Caritos, executive director of election watchdog Legal Network for Truthful Elections, said that the delays are a “carrot” dangled by national and local officials to gain the support of barangay leaders.
“They [can] say, ‘Oh, I’m the one who filed the term-setting bill,’ or ‘I’m the one who filed this postponement of the elections yet again,’” she explained.
And while national and local officials get their incentives, voters get the short end of the stick when underperforming leaders overstay their welcome.

“We can file cases against them, but that’s not an opportunity or an avenue that all of us could explore. So, elections are the most basic accountability measure that every one of us could exact accountability from our elected officials,” Caritos said.
The law to postpone the 2026 BSKE may have been signed by the President, but the onus to set the record straight on these postponements lies with the Supreme Court.

While the Supreme Court had already declared unconstitutional postponing elections without a compelling reason, it has not yet ruled on changing term limits that result in election delays. Now, a petition against the term-setting law has already been filed, with more possibly on the way.

For Caritos, these petitions are the only measures left against the 2026 BSKE postponement. With how frequent BSKEs have been postponed in the last three decades, the impact of the Supreme Court’s decision must go beyond this year’s polls.

“To avoid the possibility, yet again, of postponing the 2028 Barangay and SK elections… then there’s a need for the Supreme Court to really clarify what would be the decision when it comes to a situation like this,” she said. – Rappler.com
Coding for the charts used in this story was done with the assistance of AI.

articles.title: Iraq: US troops withdraw from their Iraqi US-led Operation Inherent Resolve mission against ISIS after 12 years
articles.summary: As the US completes its military withdrawal from Iraq, Baghdad declares a new era of sovereignty. But as US troops leave, questions remain over militias, foreign forces and the country's future…

image.caption: All US troops will are to leave Iraq by September 30Image: Ameer Al Mohammedaw/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Iraq's government in Baghdad, September 30, 2026, marks the end of an era. "October 1 will be a new day in the course of the Iraqi state, with the country free of any foreign military presence and the completion of national sovereignty over its territory," Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said in a statement.
The occasion will be celebrated as "Independence Day" with four official public holidays.

By Wednesday, the United States will have completed the withdrawal of its remaining 2,500 troops from Iraqi territory according to a 2024 agreement. Their departure concludes 12 years of the US-led Operation Inherent Resolve mission against the Islamic State group, or ISIS, which at the time was advancing across the country and in neighboring Syria.

The withdrawal also marks the end of more than two decades of US military involvement in Iraq. Following the US invasion in 2003, US forces withdrew in 2011 and returned in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group. The withdrawal also follows the broader US strategy of reducing its military presence in the Middle East.

However, the US withdrawal does not mean an end to all foreign military deployments in Iraq. Turkey still has troops in Iraq, even though Ankara said earlier this week that it would gradually hand over a military base in northern Iraq to Baghdad.

"In 2024, Baghdad and Washington agreed to what they called a normalized relationship," Renad Mansour, deputy director for the Middle East and North Africa program and director of the Iraq Initiative at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "For Baghdad, the political aim will be now to make clear that Iraq wants to remain an ally of the US," he said.

In his view, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is concerned that Washington could start viewing Iraq and its Iran-backed non-state militias as too close to Iran, given that the US and Israel are at war with Iran.

blocks.caption: The Iraqi non-state militia Kata'ib Hezbollah has rejected Baghdad's plans for disarmament and integration into Iraq's national forcesImage: EPA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Baghdad extends disarmament deadline

Initially, Baghdad had linked the end of the US military mission to the disarmament of Iraq's numerous armed groups and militias. The plan also included bringing these paramilitary groups under state control.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said last week that the new deadline was June 30, 2027. The revised plan includes a 90-day period during which armed groups would refrain from attacks in exchange for assurances that US forces would not target them, followed by a gradual handover of weapons that is due to be completed by June 30, 2027.
Yet not all armed groups are likely to follow this plan as several powerful armed groups have rejected disarmament or demanded conditions that could delay the process.

"The hardest-line armed groups — Kata'ib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada — have so far given no indication that they are prepared to surrender their weapons to the state and integrate into Iraq's armed forces," Alina L. Romanowski, distinguished fellow with the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council's Middle East program, said.

Renad Mansour told DW that he was not surprised by the extension of the deadline. Iraq's political landscape has been highly fragmented since the US invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein in April 2003. There have been more than eight years of war, the rise and fall of ISIS, and the US withdrawal in 2011 and return in 2014. "Many political movements are associated with armed organizations, so it is hard to see a revolution in the security sector happening any time soon," he told DW, predicting that "even next year, many armed groups will continue to remain free of the central government."

blocks.caption: Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous region in northern Iraq has been targeted hundreds of times by Iran and Iran-backed Iraqi militias Image: Gailan Haji/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: What does this mean for Iraq's minorities?

The withdrawal of US troops also includes the departure of military personnel and the removal of US air defense systems in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq. Kurdish Prime Minister Masrour Barzani has already called on Baghdad for protection against missile and drone attacks from Iran. Since the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February, attacks by Iraq's Iran-backed armed groups on US-linked targets in Erbil have been on the rise, while Iranian attacks on infrastructure belonging to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Iraq have also increased.

On Monday, Kurdish officials in Erbil said that three drones targeted a camp affiliated with Iran's Kurdish opposition. Local officials said the drones were Iranian-made, but responsibility for the attack was not independently confirmed.

Yerevan Saeed, a nonresident senior fellow with the Iraq Initiative at the Atlantic Council and the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, is concerned that Iraq's vulnerable ethnic and religious minorities, such as Christians and Yazidis, as well as Kurdish communities, could be left more exposed from October 1, 2026, onward. "The withdrawal signals the end of an era in which foreign boots provided a buffer against central and regional predation," he said.

Chatham House's Mansour, meanwhile, notes that US-Iraqi ties will not end on September 30, but rather shift toward "other arenas, including economic ties rather than having a security-focused relationship."

In July, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said after meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi, that they had discussed how a sovereign, stable and strong Iraq would pave the way for mutually beneficial commercial and defense cooperation.
However, in the statement following the meeting, Hegseth added that "building a normal US-Iraq bilateral defense relationship requires a secure environment free from terrorist coercion."
Iranian Kurds in Iraq face war fears, exile

articles.title: Imams’ council condemns Melbourne Islamic preacher’s call to ‘take up arms’ against enemies
articles.summary:
Independent MP Allegra Spender says the comments reinforce the need for stronger protection against hate speech

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s peak body for imams says it is “deeply concerned” about reports a Melbourne-based Islamic preacher called for followers to “take up arms against his enemies” and not take “Jews and the Christians for friends”.
The Australian National Imams’ Council (ANIC) released a statement on Tuesday after Nine newspapers revealed the preacher who goes by the name Abu Ahmad made the comments during a sermon in July.

Reading from a book chapter, Ahmad said Muslims should not “take the Jews and the Christians for friends” in a video posted to the social media feed of Melbourne-based Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre in July.

“For the sake of Allah, it includes the obligation to declare enmity for his sake, opposition for the sake of Allah. It is to declare opposition, indeed, to take up arms against his enemies, to shun them, and to stay far from them both in word and deed. This proves that simple opposition of the spirit is not enough and that it must be complete by honouring of your commitment,” he said.

“If the aim of the enemies of Islam, whether they are atheists, or Jews, or Christians, or modernists, or Zionists, or communists, is the emasculation of … the Muslims and the erosion of their unique character in order to make them the ass of the chosen people, as it is put in the protocols of the elders of Zion, then the urgency of this issue should become clear to every Muslim,” he said.
In an Instagram post on Monday, the Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre included a statement from the preacher.

“The statements the article is attributing to me were from a passage of a book that I was reading during a lesson on al-Walāʾ wal-Barāʾ. They were not a personal call from me for Muslims to attack Christians, Jews or other non-Muslims,” the post signed off by Ahmad said.

The post attached a video which he said was an “explanation of that very passage from the same lesson” and explained it “does not permit harming, oppressing or being unjust towards peaceful non-Muslims.
“Unfortunately, quoting the book without including the explanation that followed gives a completely different impression of what was being taught,” the post said.

ANIC said it “strongly and unequivocally condemns any call by any religious or non-religious preacher, leader or individual to take up arms against civilians, religious communities or the Australian people”.
ANIC said it would not make findings about the “individual or the precise context of the reported remarks” until it could properly review material.
after newsletter promotion
ANIC reiterated it “categorically rejects incitement to violence, hatred or harm against any person or community”.

“The safety, security and wellbeing of Australia and the Australian people are fundamental responsibilities that Australian Muslims, Imams and religious leaders must uphold. Islamic teachings require Muslims to honour the sanctity of human life, fulfil their responsibilities to society and contribute positively to the communities and country in which they live.”

The peak body called on all religious leaders, regardless of faith, to exercise responsibility in their public statements. It added that the alleged conduct of an individual should not be used to condemn or blame an entire faith or community.

The Albanese government was forced to abandon anti-vilification laws that would have given authorities greater powers to crack down on religious leaders who promote hatred on the basis of religions, race, gender or sexuality after it failed to gain support from the Nationals and the Greens.
On Tuesday, the independent federal MP Allegra Spender told Nine newspapers the comments showed “why we needed stronger and nationally consistent hate speech legislation”.

articles.title: Inside 'Hood 420:' Bishnoi-linked gang tied to threats against B.C. radio station
articles.summary: The main suspect in a brazen shooting and extortion campaign against an outspoken Surrey, B.C. radio station is suspected of playing an organizing role in connection with a series of Ontario…

image.caption: According to Immigration and Refugee Board transcripts, Ravinder Singh has been tied to multiple incidents involving extortion and shooting in Ontario, B.C. and Alberta. He is allegedly part of a group known as Bishnoi-linked gang called Hood 420. (Peel Regional Police; Nav Rahi/CBC)

blocks.text: Documents obtained by CBC News have identified a suspect in a brazen shooting and extortion campaign which took place one year ago against an outspoken Surrey, B.C. radio station.

In addition to the attack on Radio Swift 1200 AM last September, Ravinder Singh is suspected of playing an organizing role related to extortion cases in Ontario that have resulted in more than 100 charges against 17 men earlier this year.
According to Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) records, obtained through an Access to Information request, the 25-year-old belongs to Hood 420.
Hood 420 is a gang authorities claim is either directly linked to Lawrence Bishnoi, or using his name to carry out threats in multiple provinces.

items: 'We will rule in CANADA': Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News
Alleged Bishnoi associate flaunts guns, bullets, cash in video obtained by CBC News

blocks.text: The IRB issued a deportation order for organized criminality against Ravinder Singh in July after he was implicated in shootings across Canada — including one on Sept. 29, 2025, at Radio Swift 1200 AM.

A transcript of the hearing says Ravinder Singh's phone contained a note matching the threat sent to Swift 1200 AM's owner in the names of Bishnoi and gang leader Goldy Dhillon "demanding five (5) million dollars and threatening harm if demands are not met."
Documents raise questions about inmate escape

Ravinder Singh's detention and admissibility hearings provide new insight into major extortion investigations in Ontario, Alberta and B.C. — most notably a mass crackdown by Peel Regional Police last May on a group facing 106 charges connected to 24 incidents.

While police had previously linked those extortions to a group called For Brothers, the IRB documents claim Singh "was part of the Bishnoi Gang or a closely tied subgroup under the name Hood 420 and that he and a number of other individuals were involved in criminal activity."

The documents also raise questions about the November 2025 escape of Ravinder Singh's alleged accomplice in another set of extortions — Jagdeep Singh, a 24-year-old still wanted on a Canada wide-warrant in connection with multiple shootings in Surrey and northern Alberta.
The Canada Border Services Agency previously said only that Jagdeep Singh escaped from Rockyview Hospital in Calgary while undergoing medical assessment.
But the transcripts of Ravinder Singh's hearing suggest Jagdeep Singh complained of drug withdrawal to give the slip to the contracted guards charged with keeping him in custody while at hospital.

The escape was mentioned during Ravinder Singh's admissibility hearing because — despite having previously told the CBSA he had no drug issues — Ravinder Singh also started displaying substance withdrawal symptoms when he was arrested.
He told CBSA officers he "uses black tar heroin or opium daily."

items: One of three men accused of Surrey extortion shootings on the run: RCMP

blocks.text: A lawyer for the Ministry of Public Safety told the IRB Ravinder Singh "was transported to the hospital and it should also be noted that this is the exact same scenario that resulted in the escape of his friend Mr. Jagdeep Singh from CBSA custody."
According to the documents, Ravinder Singh was treated with suboxone and ultimately released back into immigration custody, where he was referred for ongoing medical treatment.
In a statement, the CBSA told CBC News the agency is "conducting a full review" of Jagdeep Singh's escape.

"It is standard practice for the CBSA to use contracted guards to maintain custody and control of detained individuals 24 hours per day, seven days per week. The guards keep individuals safe and secure through regular observation, monitoring, engagement, and intervention," the CBSA statement said.

"Guards are also responsible for transporting individuals, including their luggage and personal effects, to and from various locations as required. All other aspects of detention operations are handled by CBSA officials."
'Get rid of them'

Ravinder Singh has been charged with weapons offences in Alberta and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence of discharging a firearm in connection with the Ontario cases, but has never been charged in the Swift 1200 AM shootings.
The IRB documents claim representatives of the Ministry of Public Safety and the Crown have discussed staying criminal charges against Singh so he can be removed from Canada.
But a spokesperson for the Canada Border Services Agency told CBC News the charges against Singh are still outstanding.
Ravinder Singh represented himself at the immigration proceedings, but declined to respond to the allegations against him.
"My father back home is very sick and I want to go as soon as possible. I want to see him before anything bad happens," he told the tribunal at one point.
"I do want to give a statement, but nobody is going to believe on my statement. So, it's okay. I don't want to make any statement."
Surrey radio station hit by gunfire amid extortion threats targeting South Asian community
Swift 1200 AM host Jinny Sims says she thinks he should be deported — the sooner the better.

"I used to say, 'No, they should pursue the charges.' [But now] I think if there's a quicker way to get rid of them — get rid of them," says Sims, who has served for the provincial and federal NDP as both a member of B.C.'s Legislative Assembly and an MP.

"This extortion business is destroying our community. It has created such big fear that's it's only when you're going to see these deportations — and I'm not saying just pick up anybody and deport them — but where you've got strong evidence then deport them, and they won't be here recruiting people while they're waiting for a trial."
Known by the alias 'Coach'
Ravinder Singh came to Canada in August 2019 on a study permit.
He later obtained a work permit — which expired last January — for employment at a Surrey-based wall and ceiling company.

An Ontario Provincial Police intelligence analyst who testified at Ravinder Singh's admissibility hearing said Singh first came to police attention in fall 2025 after a series of shootings at residences and businesses in Caledon and Brampton, Ont.
"Extortion threats were received by the victim, claiming affiliation to the Bishnoi gang, and there was a demand for finances," the analyst testified.
"Witness statement had provided aliases for involved members. Initially, Mr. Singh was known by the alias 'Coach.' And through investigation, his true identity was determined."

items: Alberta RCMP look for man wanted in connection with extortion scheme, shootings west of Edmonton

blocks.text: According to the IRB transcripts, police began to make those connections after RCMP arrested Ravinder Singh in Red Deer in November — when he met Jagdeep Singh, who was then a suspect in shootings targeting a tire shop owner in Parkland, about 75 km west of Edmonton.
The attackers shot up a home where seven people were present, later sending a video of the incidents and demanding $2 million.
Ravinder Singh allegedly showed up to meet Jagdeep Singh in a Dodge Challenger, where police found a gun linked to seven extortion-related shootings and a phone that tied him to many more.
'Locations and instructions'
Police examined Ravinder Singh's phone, which is how they discovered that his alleged accomplices knew him by the nickname "Coach."
Investigators allegedly found messages sent to Jagdeep Singh with information about the targets of the Alberta shootings.
And they found WhatsApp messages sent to Iqbal Singh Bhagria, the suspect charged in connection with the extortion shootings in Caledon and Brampton.
"This shows Mr. Ravinder sending locations and instructions that align with the shooting events that occurred," a lawyer for the Ministry of Public Safety claimed.
"And it's also noted that these are the same locations and instructions that were found in Iqbal Bhagria's phone when he was also arrested."
Armed with that evidence, authorities in Edmonton arrested Ravinder Singh a second time in February for immigration and traffic safety warrants.

He was driving a grey Toyota Camry when police picked him up — a vehicle allegedly linked, through distinctive damage and CCTV footage, to a series of Surrey extortion cases which took place in the fall of 2025.
The vehicle was also identified as a suspect vehicle in the Swift 1200 AM shooting.
Gang called 'Hood 420'

Ravinder Singh's admissibility hearing included testimony from RCMP Const. Mohamed El Krich, the primary investigator for the Alberta extortion shootings — which also saw Molotov cocktails thrown at a business.

El Krich said the victim in that case received messages citing Bishnoi gang member Goldy Dhillon and threatening, "Pay us or your family is going to find you in a body bag," or, "If we don't find you today, we'll find you tomorrow."

The RCMP officer said Ravinder Singh's phone contained the "extortion script" sent to Swift 1200 AM Radio, as well as evidence of him searching the addresses of extortion victims and directions for shooters "such as where to stand or where to change the vehicle licence plates."
El Krich also drew the connection between Ravinder Singh and the group known as Hood 420.

"There is content in his phone, indicating that he was a member of this group, including photos of ammunition that was laid out to spell Hood 420, as well as photos of an event where bottle service was an option and they had the group name advertised on the bottle service delivery," El Krich said.

Although associated with marijuana in Canada, the number 420 has a particular meaning in Indian criminal subculture — a reference to Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code which concerns "cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property."

A lawyer for the Ministry of Public Safety asked El Krich if Hood 420 is affiliated with Lawrence Bishnoi, the imprisoned gang leader who authorities say has built a global network from an Indian jail cell.
"Considering that the extortion demands claim affiliation to these criminal organisations, I think that it's very likely there is a connection," El Krich replied.
'What's the point?'
Ravinder Singh has been in immigration detention since February.

RCMP in Alberta have since announced charges against Ravinder Singh and Jagdeep Singh in connection with the Parkland shootings, and B.C.'s provincial Extortion Task Force announced charges against Jagdeep Singh and two others for shootings in Surrey.

items: Inside an extortion deportation case: The arsons, auto frauds and shootings linking crime across Canada
'Danger to the public': The story behind the deportation of a 'Ruffian'

blocks.text: And in May, Peel Police's Extortion Task Force included Ravinder Singh and Iqbal Singh Bhagria's names in a roundup of 17 individuals accused of "a [co-ordinated] campaign of intimidation, threats, and escalating violence used to extort local businesses."
A spokesperson for the Peel Police told CBC News the charges remain pending before the courts.
"However, our investigations remain active," Peel Police said in a statement.
"And we anticipate making additional arrests and laying further charges in the near future."
Swift 1200 AM host Sims says that, while recent reports of extortion cases appear to have slowed down, the South Asian community is still very afraid.
She called on police and the CBSA to provide more information.
"You want the victims to keep doing all this stuff, give you everything they do, but then there is silence for weeks and months," she said.
"They need to get updates, and they need to know that you're doing something. Otherwise people are not going to give you names. They're going to say 'What's the point? Nothing happens.'"
Letter from Bishnoi gang to police disclosed to CBC News

articles.title: Why everyone wants a piece of the Lopez group’s Energy Development Corp.
articles.summary: The Lopez group, through First Gen, bought Energy Development Corp. from the government in 2007 and has spent the 19 years since learning how deep the asset actually goes

blocks.text: Three foreign groups have sought different stakes in the same Lopez asset: an Indonesian tycoon has made an unsolicited US$5 billion offer to buy it outright, another Indonesian conglomerate has entered a joint venture to build with its geothermal know-how, and this September, a new investor paid P25.77 billion for nearly a fifth of its parent company, First Gen Corporation, at P36 a share, just P1 above the price First Philippine Holdings (FPH) had recently rejected as inadequate.

What they are circling is Energy Development Corporation or EDC, which turns 50 this 2026 and draws electricity out of hot water and steam trapped beneath the volcanic rock of Leyte, Negros, Bicol and Mindanao, generating power around the clock whether or not the sun shines or the wind blows, without needing fuel deliveries from anywhere. (READ: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target)
The Lopez group, through First Gen, bought EDC from the government in 2007 and has spent the 19 years since learning how deep the asset actually goes.

“We have invested more than P200 billion through the years to build approximately 1,300 megawatts (MW) of reliable baseload capacity,” Francis Giles Puno, president and chief operating officer of First Gen and of its parent First Philippine Holdings (FPH), told shareholders at the group’s annual meeting on Friday, September 25.
But money alone is not the barrier to entry. The knowledge is.

Solar and wind developers can measure much of their resource before construction begins, while geothermal developers have to drill into the earth to prove what is actually there, deciding where to sink an expensive exploration well before knowing exactly what they will find, learning how a reservoir behaves as pressure changes across decades, and figuring out how to keep mineral deposits from damaging the wells and pipes that carry geothermal fluids. Enough wrong decisions can shorten the productive life of a field.

The Lopezes understood early what they had bought. Three years after the acquisition, Federico “Piki” Lopez told First Gen shareholders in the company’s 2010 annual report that the group was “prepared to go global and take this geothermal power development expertise, built on EDC’s ’35-year head start,’ into parts of the world that have only begun to tap their existing reserves.” Puno, writing as president in the same report, described EDC as having “existing steam concessions and a great technical platform supported by its scientists and engineers.”
That 35-year head start is the same clock that reaches 50 this year.

EDC has been doing this since the 1970s, across generations of geologists, reservoir engineers and drillers who learned the craft from the people before them, but not all of that accumulated capability remains housed inside EDC today. Part of it migrated into another branch of the Lopez group through ThermaPrime Drilling Corporation, incorporated in December 2010 and, by its own account, “staffed by many of the same people who comprised the original PNOC (Philippine National Oil Company)-EDC drilling team.” It sits not under EDC or under First Gen but beside them, owned by First Balfour, the group’s construction arm, which FPH owns outright. The drilling knowledge that had accumulated inside EDC was replicated elsewhere in the group and became a business of its own.

Puno highlighted ThermaPrime in his September 25 report to FPH shareholders. “Major infrastructure and renewable energy development demand specialized capabilities built over decades,” he said. “Through First Balfour and ThermaPrime, FPH has developed the engineering, construction and drilling expertise to take on increasingly complex projects.” ThermaPrime, he said, “brings equally specialized capabilities to geothermal development. Its people and equipment helped EDC accelerate its drilling program, completing close to 30 wells over the past 3 years.”

That intensive program has now ended, and the numbers show it. Activity moderated this year, Puno said, with ThermaPrime’s revenues declining 49% to P1.4 billion and net income falling 45% to P276 million.

But the rigs have found work elsewhere. ThermaPrime completed a 4-year program for SM Investments-owned Philippine Geothermal Production Company, drilling 12 production wells and 3 multilateral injection wells. In July, Maibarara Geothermal Inc., the Yuchengco-led venture of PetroGreen Energy, ACEN, and PNOC Renewables, awarded it a 2026-2027 exploratory campaign: 3 firm wells and one contingent well in Batangas and Laguna, to depths of 2,100 to 3,000 meters, with drilling running from October through May 2027.

Puno told shareholders he expects the drilling expertise to be sold beyond the group’s own projects. “The value of these capabilities extends beyond the projects they serve today,” he said, with ThermaPrime “exploring opportunities to bring its geothermal drilling expertise to Japan, Taiwan and Indonesia.”

Puno described a business the company keeps spending on rather than harvesting. “We continue to learn invaluable lessons and reinvest significant resources to maintain, expand, and strengthen our unique leadership position in geothermal,” he said, “including the forthcoming re-envisioning and redevelopment of Leyte.”

The capability built around EDC over half a century is therefore broader than the plants and steam fields sitting on EDC’s books: it includes knowledge about where to drill, how to manage a reservoir and how to keep drawing power from it over decades, while some of the specialized drilling and well-engineering capability that grew out of the old EDC has already become a separate business elsewhere in the Lopez group.
The US$5 billion offer was not the first time an Indonesian group came looking.

More than a year earlier, a different Indonesian house had approached the Lopezes with a different proposition. Sinar Mas, the conglomerate controlled by the Widjaja family with interests running from palm oil to paper mills to telecommunications, did not make an offer for EDC. It signed a joint venture with it, bringing into Indonesia the geothermal capability the company had spent decades building in the Philippines.

The two sides signed an initial agreement in August 2025 and formalized the partnership in Jakarta that October, pairing PT FirstGen Geothermal Indonesia with PT DSSR Daya Mas Sakti, a unit of the Sinar Mas energy company PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa. The 50-50 joint venture targets roughly 440 megawatts across 6 fields in West Java, Flores, Jambi, West Sumatra and Central Sulawesi. By March this year, EDC said the partners were looking at spending about $30 million for the exploration phase alone and hoped to begin drilling at least one well later in 2026.

blocks.caption: JOINT VENTURE.  Officers of PT FirstGen Geothermal Indonesia, a subsidiary of Energy Development, the largest RE producer in the Philippines and part of Lopez-owned First Gen Corporation, sign a joint venture with PT DSSR Daya Mas Sakti, a subsidiary of PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk, part of Sin…

blocks.text: Indonesia holds about 40% of the world’s geothermal reserves, according to EDC, or some 24 gigawatts. Yet only about a tenth of that potential has been developed.
What it does not have in the same measure is 50 years of EDC’s practice.

“We are bringing close to 50 years of geothermal experience and expertise to Indonesia,” Jerome Cainglet, EDC’s president and chief operating officer, said when the partnership was announced. “At the same time, we know that there is also a lot that we can learn there, which we may use in the Philippines.”

His counterpart was equally explicit about what the Indonesian side hoped to gain. “Our goal is to strengthen national capacity in geothermal development and to fully harness the country’s natural potential for clean energy,” said Lokita Prasetya, president-director of PT DSSR Daya Mas Sakti.
Puno described the same partnership to his own shareholders on September 25: the group is “bringing our expertise to Indonesia through opportunities jointly pursued with the Sinar Mas Group.”

blocks.caption: Why everyone wants a piece of the Lopez group’s Energy Development Corp.

blocks.text: Sinar Mas is paying to use what EDC knows, while ThermaPrime sells another part of the geothermal capability developed around EDC to outside customers. Neither requires the Lopez group to sell EDC itself.
Then came July 2026, and a different Indonesian tycoon.

PT Barito Renewables Energy, controlled by Prajogo Pangestu, made an unsolicited, indicative and non-binding proposal to acquire EDC for an equity value of approximately $5 billion, subject to due diligence, transaction documents and regulatory and corporate approvals. First Gen said at the time that there had been no discussions between the parties, no agreements signed and no advisers appointed.

blocks.caption: An Indonesian billionaire wants EDC: The $5-B offer raising the stakes in the Lopez feud

blocks.text: The offer came while the Lopez cousins were in the middle of a public fight over control of its companies, other parts of the corporate structure were confronting their own liquidity needs, and ABS-CBN was trying to raise billions in fresh capital.

There is also a limit to how simply the Lopezes can treat EDC as theirs to sell. First Gen controls EDC with 65% of the votes but has only a 45.8% economic interest, while Philippines Renewable Energy Holdings Corporation or PREHC— the consortium through which Macquarie-managed funds and Singapore’s GIC invested in EDC in 2017—owns 34.9% of its voting stock. The structure gives First Gen control despite holding less than half of EDC’s economic upside, but it leaves another large financial investor with substantial money at stake in any change of ownership.

Then on September 21, First Gen ended the takeover speculation, telling the Philippine Stock Exchange: it “confirms that there are currently no plans to divest itself of EDC, and there are no firms, other than PT Barito Renewables Tbk, looking to potentially acquire EDC.”

First Gen’s own investment plans also show where it intends to put capital next. Puno said the company could spend as much as P160 billion over the next 5 years, including around P70 billion for geothermal exploration and expansion and more than P60 billion for hydropower, with the balance going into solar and other opportunities.
More capital is going into geothermal than into the pumped-storage hydro projects the company recently bought into.

The math behind keeping EDC is visible in First Gen’s own books. In the first half of 2026, EDC generated P29.88 billion of First Gen’s P41.15 billion in consolidated revenue, representing 72.6% of the total. Having sold 60% of its natural gas business to Enrique Razon’s Prime Infrastructure, and with its Wawa and Pakil pumped-storage hydro projects not scheduled to come online until 2030 or 2031, First Gen would be left holding a portfolio whose returns arrive largely at the end of the decade. EDC is what pays the bills today. (READ: The business case of the Lopez-Razon gas and hydro deals)

items: Part 1 | Debt, discipline, and daring: Inside the Lopez Group’s high-risk bets
Part 2 | The Lopezes, presidents, and the cost of dissent
Part 3 | Lopez vs Lopez: The secrecy fight behind the Razon power deals

blocks.text: It is also earning more. EDC’s net income contribution to First Gen rose 73.5% to P3.69 billion in the first 6 months of 2026, up from P2.12 billion a year earlier. First Gen attributed the increase to higher average selling prices, improved generation across its steam fields, and battery energy storage systems that began coming online from September to December 2025.

Put those pieces together and the strategic choice becomes clear: Barito wants to own EDC, Sinar Mas wants to build alongside it, and external developers can hire ThermaPrime for the most specialized parts of the drilling. The Lopez group does not have to sell EDC to monetize what 5 decades of geothermal development built.
The interest in the Lopez geothermal business has also extended one corporate level above EDC.

On September 10, KKR, the American private equity firm that had held a stake in First Gen for 6 years, sold its entire holding of 715.86 million shares (19.99%) to Angsana Finance Limited, a Cayman-incorporated entity owned by Gateway Holdings Limited and managed by Singapore-based Gateway Partners, at P36 a share.

That transaction followed a formal rejection on August 15, when FPH notified the stock exchange it had turned down KKR’s proposal to acquire part of FPH’s holding and launch a voluntary tender offer for First Gen’s public float at P35 a share. “After careful deliberation and consideration,” the filing read, “FPH has determined that KKR’s proposal does not represent FGEN’s true value.” Angsana paid P36 for KKR’s block less than a month later.
Asked by Rappler at the September 25 FPH stockholders’ meeting what governance rights Angsana acquired with those shares, Puno said there was none.

“Because KKR acquired its [common shares equivalent to] 19.9% stake in First Gen directly from the secondary market, no shareholder agreement was established with FPH,” Puno said. “Consequently, Angsana did not obtain any special or contractual governance rights through its purchase of KKR’s holdings, maintaining only the standard statutory rights granted to minority shareholders under the Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines.”

The 19.9% is smaller than it looks. That total accounts only for First Gen’s common shares. Measured against First Gen’s total issued capital, which includes the voting preferred shares that FPH owns outright, Angsana’s stake comes to 14.06%.

Gateway has not publicly explained what it sees in First Gen or what it ultimately expects from its P25.77 billion outlay. The purchase by itself does not establish that Angsana expects any transaction involving EDC. But underneath those shares sits a portfolio that Puno says is now 92% renewable, built around what he called “hard to replicate assets”, with EDC at its center and an unsolicited offer already putting an approximately $5-billion equity value on the geothermal subsidiary.
For most of its corporate life, EDC created value primarily by converting underground heat into megawatts for the Philippine grid.

blocks.caption: Why everyone wants a piece of the Lopez group’s Energy Development Corp.

blocks.text: But 50 years later, that accumulated know-how are creating value in several ways at once: as a cash engine that First Gen wants to keep and expand, as an acquisition target commanding multibillion-dollar benchmarks from foreign suitors, as an exportable development capability in Indonesia with Sinar Mas, and through ThermaPrime, as specialized drilling and well-engineering services that can be sold across the industry.

First Gen has already shown it is willing to sell a major asset when doing so advances its strategy. In 2025, it sold 60% of the natural gas business it had spent decades pioneering to Prime Infrastructure, releasing capital as the company shifted toward a portfolio that is now overwhelmingly renewable. At the same time, it is preparing the comprehensive redevelopment of its flagship Leyte geothermal complex and continuing to pour billions into new wells.
Its public position on EDC, despite Barito’s $5-billion approach, is unequivocal: EDC, for now, is staying.

When the Lopez group bought EDC from the government 19 years ago, the debt burden during the 2008 global financial crisis was so severe that the family famously had to surrender its controlling stake in Meralco to Manuel V. Pangilinan just to protect its balance sheet.

What they preserved was more than power plants and steam fields. They acquired an ecosystem of knowledge that had been developing since the 1970s, then spent the next 19 years adding to it. Part of that capability remains embedded in EDC’s fields, engineers and reservoir expertise, part has migrated into ThermaPrime as an independent drilling arm, and part is now being deployed across Indonesia’s volcanic belts.

In 2010, Piki Lopez wrote that the group was prepared to take EDC’s expertise into parts of the world that had only begun to tap their geothermal reserves. Sixteen years later, Sinar Mas is building with that expertise in Indonesia, Barito has put a US$5-billion equity value on owning EDC, and First Gen is putting billions more into geothermal while saying it has no plans to sell.
The knowledge, its capital allocations suggest, is worth more kept than sold. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Global trade weathers Iran, Ukraine and Trump's tariffs
articles.summary: Over the past six years, COVID, two wars and Donald Trump's tariffs have shaken world trade. With globalization already stalling, is this a temporary shock or the start of a great reversal?

image.caption: Despite severe disruption to global commerce, trade volumes continue to growImage: Noah Berger/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: From COVID to Donald Trump's tariffs — with wars in Ukraine and the Middle East in between — world trade policy is enduring the most unpredictable period of the postwar era.
The pandemic shut factories worldwide and accelerated a shift away from China, the world’s largest manufacturer. The two conflicts then disrupted global supplies of oil and gas, food and fertilizer.
US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, meanwhile, pushed US duties to their highest level in decades, forcing firms to find new suppliers and markets.
Robert Staiger, chief economist at the World Trade Organization (WTO), calls the turmoil "the most serious and sustained disruptions since the [world trading] system was created 80 years ago."

blocks.caption: High-tech exports to help build AI data centers have kept world trade strongImage: Maksim Zabarovskii/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Goods trade buoyed by AI demand
Despite these shocks, global trade has remained surprisingly resilient.

According to the WTO's annual report published last week, goods trade volumes rose 4.6% last year, lifted by strong demand for the advanced technology behind the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. Services trade volumes grew by 5.3%.
China remained the world's largest goods exporter, while the United States was again the largest importer. The European Union came in second in both.
However, Staiger told AFP news agency last week that strong AI exports "may be masking some of the drop in world trade that might otherwise be occurring."
The WTO noted in its March trade outlook that Asian countries dominated the AI goods trade, while Africa, Latin America, the Middle East and much of Europe barely showed up.
AI-related tech accounted for about one-sixth of goods trade but close to half of global trade growth.
Washington sidesteps WTO rules
Since returning to office last year, Trump has continued to pivot from WTO rules on global trade.
The US president has set country-specific duties, breaking the WTO’s equal-treatment rule. He has since negotiated exemptions and "reciprocal" tariffs with individual countries.
Despite this, globally, about 72% of goods are still traded on the Geneva-based agency's core terms, down from roughly 80% in 2022.

On a longer horizon, though, globalization appears to have stalled. WTO data shows that since about 2015, world trade has grown only as fast as the global economy. Despite the recent geopolitical upheavals, globalization has yet to shift into reverse.

Policymakers and economists say it is too soon to know whether the wars, alongside a pivot toward protectionism in the US, China, the EU and post-Brexit Britain, mark the end of an ever-interconnected world.

"The world is certainly not becoming more globalized," Thomas Sampson, an associate professor at the London School of Economics, told DW. "But it's still an open question whether we're actually at deglobalization or just shifting around who we trade with."

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump has questioned the role of the World Trade OrganizationImage: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP

blocks.text: How global trade is changing

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the EU has sharply cut its reliance on Russian pipeline gas from 37% in late 2021 to around 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. EU oil and coal imports from Russia are now negligible.
These moves spurred new energy deals with the US, Norway, Australia and Kazakhstan, with liquefied natural gas (LNG) replacing Russian pipeline gas.
Moscow did find new energy buyers — notably China and India — which took Russian oil at a large discount to global benchmark prices.
How India has become Russia's trade lifeline
Camille Reverdy, an affiliate fellow at the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, doubts whether the EU will rekindle its energy trade with Moscow when the war ends.
"If the alternatives become reliable sources, I don't see it coming back," Reverdy told DW.

When the Iran war began in late February, Tehran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most critical energy transit chokepoints. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates sent some of the missing oil by pipeline to alternative ports.

According to the International Energy Agency, the world also replaced the missing millions of barrels with increased production from the US, Kazakhstan, Brazil and Venezuela. Several nations have also tapped about 300 million barrels from their strategic oil reserves, Reuters reported in August.

Almost seven months into the conflict, energy prices remain elevated, with Brent crude trading above $100 for much of the war. Several analysts are now warning of dangerously tight supply in the fall and winter.
The squeeze from Trump's tariffs is also weighing on trade.

US imports from China, for instance, fell by around 28% last year, according to the Washington-based Peterson Institute for International Economics. At the same time, its imports from the rest of the world climbed by nearly a tenth — much of it from Vietnam, Taiwan and Mexico, as part of rerouting efforts to cut reliance on Chinese suppliers.

blocks.caption: Since the pandemic, many multinationals have been shifting China production to Southeast Asian countriesImage: Nhac Nguyen/AFP

blocks.text: Will Trump's strategy outlast him?
Trump’s attacks on the WTO have raised a sharper question. If the Geneva-based body were shelved, what would replace it? Experts have floated several alternatives.
These include continuing Trump's country-by-country tariffs or a web of free trade deals between economic blocs, including BRICS nations of the Global South.
The third, mooted by think tanks like Chatham House, would see the EU, Japan, Canada, Australia and Mexico keep trading by WTO-style rules at a scale the US and China could not ignore.
Bruegel's Reverdy thinks the EU would prefer a reformed WTO to the alternatives.

"The EU still wants to be seen as the leader of free and multilateral trade," she told DW, noting how Brussels has added new layers of trade policy, including possibly making Canada an associate member.
Canada and Europe: an alliance against Trump?
LSE's Sampson warned that continuing with Trump's "law of the jungle" would disadvantage smaller countries, who he said have a "bigger voice" under the current WTO system.
Noting how "trust in the US as a trading partner has collapsed," Sampson told DW it could take many years for confidence to return, even with a Democratic president.
WTO economists, meanwhile, have modeled different futures, noting how further trade fragmentation along geopolitical lines could cut global GDP by about 5% by 2050.
In a world in which the WTO vanished and only a patchwork of free-trade deals remained, GDP could fall closer to 7%, with the smallest and poorest economies hit hardest.
Reinforcing multilateral rules, however, could raise global GDP by roughly 3%, the agency said.

articles.title: No more VAT on system loss in electricity bills starting October
articles.summary: While the VAT removal is still welcome relief, expect savings to be modest as the much larger underlying system loss charge is unlikely to disappear from electricity bills anytime soon

blocks.text: POWER. Electric company contractors install wires for newly installed electric meters on a utility pole along Jose Abad Santos Avenue in Manila on September 3, 2026.
Rappler
While the VAT removal is still welcome relief, expect savings to be modest as the much larger underlying system loss charge is unlikely to disappear from electricity bills anytime soon

items: Starting this October, customers will see a reduction in their electric bills due to the removal of value-added tax (VAT) on the system loss charge, although the charge itself remains.

The government is planning to phase out recoverable non-technical losses, but immediate removal could financially harm electric cooperatives without support, with an estimated P7.5 billion needed for necessary upgrades.
The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has also standardized 'Other Charges' and capped late payment fees to prevent double charging and ensure transparency in billing.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Your electric bill this October will likely be slightly less now that you no longer have to pay value-added tax (VAT) on the allowable system loss charge starting this billing cycle forward.

Following new rules from the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) that put the tax exemption into effect and change how the charge appears on electricity bills, a Meralco spokesperson confirmed to Rappler that “the VAT removal on system loss will be effective this October billing.”

This means customers should begin seeing the VAT reduction in their October bills, although they will continue paying the underlying system loss charge itself. (READ: Meralco rates dip slightly in September despite higher generation costs)

The change, however, addresses only the tax imposed on system loss, not the system loss charge itself. System loss refers to electricity lost before it reaches paying customers. Some are non-technical, which arise from electricity theft, illegal connections and faulty metering, while technical losses occur as a natural consequence of electricity passing through power lines.

blocks.caption: How much could you save if system loss charges are removed from your Meralco bill?

blocks.text: Removing the underlying system loss charge will take considerably longer. The government has proposed phasing out recoverable non-technical losses, but the National Electrification Administration (NEA) has warned that removing this immediately would push many electric cooperatives into losses without first giving them financial support for equipment updates. The government estimates around P7.5 billion would be needed for a four-stage program to eliminate non-technical system loss. (READ: NEA seeks extra P7 billion to eliminate non-technical system losses)

Technical losses pose an even longer-term problem since they cannot be completely eliminated. The Department of Energy (DOE), ERC, NEA, and electric cooperatives are still in the process of making plans to determine what improvements are needed to lower them, such as upgrades to lines, substations, and other infrastructure. The government has targeted completion of this plan in 2027, meaning the system loss charge itself is unlikely to disappear from consumers’ bills anytime soon even as the VAT on it is removed.

The ERC separately issued another resolution standardizing the “Other Charges” that utilities may collect. These may generally be imposed only for specific customer-requested or account-related services, such as certain connection, disconnection, and reconnection activities.

The rules are intended to prevent double charging. Expenses already recovered through distribution, supply, and metering rates cannot be collected again under Other Charges. Utilities may recover only incremental costs such as direct labor, deployment and fuel, and replacement materials. Administrative and overhead expenses cannot be separately passed on to consumers.

The ERC also capped late payment fees at 2% of the current month’s bill or the unpaid portion, whichever is lower. The fee may be imposed only once per bill and must be separately shown on the next billing statement. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: Malaysia has started repatriating about 1,500 Myanmar nationals, defying warnings from the UN and rights groups. Malaysia, facing an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment, says the program is strictly…

image.caption: Buses transported people to a naval base in the northwestern Perak state in Malaysia on TuesdayImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Buses accompanied by security vehicles, carrying migrants to a boat to be repatriated to Myanmar, arrived at a stadium near Malaysia's Lumut naval base on Tuesday.
Malaysia is starting the first phase a process agreed with Mynamar's military regime to send as many as 5,000 people back to the wartorn country.

Malaysia say the process is strictly voluntary, but the UN refugee agency and civil society organizations have voiced concerns about the security of those returning, saying they could face either military recruitment, persecution or detention amid the ongoing civil war.

blocks.caption: Ships were docked at the naval base, seemingly ready to transport the people to MyanmarImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What happened as Malaysia began the repatriation process?
The buses full of people arrived at the Lumuk naval base on Myanmar's northwest coast on Tuesday.
Two naval vessels and a hospital ship were docked on site seemingly ready for a naval transport.

Malaysia's Home Ministry had said in late August that the first phase of the repatriation would start in September. It said that the repatriation involved 1,476 Myanmar citizens identified by the Myanmar government.
Malaysia has tightened immigration enforcement in recent years amid rising local hostility against refugees, particularly ethnic Rohingya ⁠Muslims ​from Myanmar.

Myanmar's state media this month also cited the Foreign Ministry as saying it was working with countries to facilitate the voluntary return of verified displaced people in a safe and dignified manner.

blocks.caption: The identites of the people returning were not clear, though Malaysia had previously said that phase one of the returns scheme would involve almost 1,500 people in totalImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the security situation in Myanmar?
Myanmar has been in more pronounced turmoil since a 2021 coup triggered a civil war, with the military now fighting armed groups across multiple frontlines.

However, allegations of persecution and even ethnic cleansing of the country's Rohingya Muslim minority were prevalent long before the full-scale civil war broke out. To the same token, some of the country's regional conflicts and uprisings have been ongoing for decades.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) says the current conditions "do not suppor the safe and sustainable return of refugees from Myanmar." It also said it had not been involved in agreements like the one struck with Malaysia.
UNHCR data suggests that roughly 193,000 refugees from Myanmar are in Malaysia, around two-thirds of them Rohingya.
Activist James Bawi Thang Bik said that based on accounts of refugees who had previously been deported, they could risk detention or forced conscription.
"We fear that they may be forced to fight on the frontlines of the conflict. For many it is akin to sending them to a death sentence in their own home," he said.
A wave of online agitation this year had amplified harassment and scrutiny of Rohingya in Malaysia.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said this month that he would invite Myanmar's military chief turned president, Min Aung Hlaing, for an official visit in return for accepting the Rohingya returns.

Myanmar's largely ostracized government, trying to portray itself as more politically legitimate five years after ousting former President Aung San Suu Kyi, is seeking greater acceptance among the international community.
New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees

articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions – US politics live
articles.summary: President uses social media post to deny reports that he was willing to ease sanctions in return for ‘concrete’ steps over its nuclear program

blocks.text: Key events

items: 4m agoTrump to speak at America's 'golden age' event
17m agoTrump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions

blocks.text: Trump to speak at America's 'golden age' event
Donald Trump will give a speech as part of an event celebrating America’s ‘golden age’ at 10am EDT.
The president is set to discuss a new tool, America.gov, which is aimed at improving citizens’ access to federal government services.

Other participants are expected to include SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, US secretary of state Marco Rubio, energy secretary Chris Wright, Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
The event takes place on the same day that Trump meets at the White House with House speaker Mike Johnson and artificial intelligence leaders.
Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting media ⁠reports that cited US officials saying ⁠he was willing to ​ease sanctions and release frozen funds for “concrete” steps regarding Iran’s nuclear program.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to ⁠give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed “concrete progress” on the nuclear issue.
It comes as Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Trump was ⁠a “big liar”, citing the ⁠president’s statements ​on ‌nuclear ‌weapons and other ‌issues.

“The ​enemy (US) knows that Iran ‌is not after ‌nuclear weapons,” spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said. “Their issue with Iran is ‌not its nuclear programme but rather its vastness, which they want to destroy.“

Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, ⁠along with ending its ability to attack its neighbours and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership. Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants ​to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic ‌nuclear energy capacity.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, in an ‌interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or ‌coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday as part of a renewed effort to end the seven-month war, according to officials of both countries.
In other developments:

items: Anthropic will caution investors that artificial intelligence could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” in its IPO prospectus. As Anthropic prepares for an IPO listing, which could value the AI company at a monumental $2tn, it dedicated almost a third of its prospectus to discussing concerns around AI safety. The news comes as OpenAI has halted the release of its next AI model over safety concerns, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Trump will be on the campaign trail this week – hosting rallies in Durant, Oklahoma, on Thursday, Mobile, Alabama, on Friday and Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday. The first two states are GOP strongholds, and Trump has pushed voters to turn out to the polls and pretend the president was at the top of the ballot this midterm cycle.

Pete Hegseth ordered the defense department to “protect and uphold the reliability of America’s voting mechanisms against external manipulation and disruption from foreign actors” in a 22 September memo. Hegseth’s order comes as concerns about artificial intelligence are on the rise, but also as the Trump administration has spread misinformation about voter fraud. In July, Trump accused China of interfering in the 2020 election, which he lost.

Andrew Bailey said he is stepping down as one of the FBI’s two deputy directors after just over a year in the role – a short tenure that unfolded as he helped oversee several of Trump’s election‑related investigations. Bailey was appointed in August 2025 to serve alongside Dan Bongino at a moment of sharp tension between the FBI and justice department leadership over the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Pope Leo addressed concerns about artificial intelligence and the war in Ukraine during a press conference onboard the papal plane today. Saying that concerns about AI are not “fake news”, the first US pope appeared to criticize Trump, who called concerns about AI a “hoax” during a UN address last week.
