articles.title: AI: Concern as Germany plans to double data center capacity
articles.summary: Germany is rewriting the rules to attract data center investment from AI companies. But local communities are becoming increasingly skeptical.

image.caption: A Google hyperscale data center is being built in Dietzenbach as part of a €5.5 billion ($6.2 billion) investment announced last yearImage: DW

blocks.text: The digital future is here, and it is unfolding in the town of Dietzenbach.
Google, EdgeConnex, and Maincubes, two US tech companies and one German, have each reserved a spotfor a data center in the small town near Frankfurt am Main.
Dietzenbach is a logistics hub near Frankfurt's airport, and home to 35,000 people.

The Frankfurt region, the center of Germany's financial industry, is one of the most attractive locations for digital cloud operators worldwide, and as demand for computing capacity continues to grow, more centers are planned for the region.
Locals worry about electricity and water usage

However, the news of plans for a fourth mega data center has been met with resistance by locals. The stacks of tens of thousands of computers in a data center need a high supply of energy to run around the clock. They radiate large amounts of heat and need cooling, which requires huge quantities of water.
The people of Dietzenbach DW met were worried about their water and electricity bills rising, as well as a higher temperature in their town.

"We want to know two things: What are the benefits for the local community here in Dietzenbach? And what are the environmental impacts?" said Dietzenbach resident Wilhelm Sauer, pointing at the four imposing chimneys rising from the EdgeConnex data center.
He and the other local activists believe that the toll the data centers will take on regional resources may not be offset by the limited number of new jobs announced.

Dietzenbach's mayor, Dieter Lang of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, is optimistic. He predicted that around 100 "high-value jobs" would come to his town through the Google data center.
He also expects it will benefit his city's coffers: "We expect a substantial tax contribution," Lang told DW.

But Tara Merk, researcher on Community Data Centers at the Weizenbaum Institute, is skeptical: She believes Germany can probably expect little revenue from data centers operated by US companies, "because the profits may be taxed elsewhere."
"Especially thinking about big tech companies — they're not going to be doing their taxes in Dietzenbach," she told DW.
Where will the next AI data centers go?
Data centers and lack of information
In August 2026, the German government launched a data centers registry listing energy consumption, water consumption, and energy efficiency measures for the data centers that are already operating.
But the list includes only around 300 data centers, far fewer than the estimated 2,000 data centers the government says are running across the country.
"Some companies report their smaller projects but not the big ones," Werner Neumann, board member of the environmental group BUND, told DW.

There is no official overview of how many data centers are being built or where. The civil society project Heisse Luft (Hot Air) has decided to fill these information gap, and has developed an online map of the planned data centers across Germany. The map is updated every day with information based on crowdsourcing from local communities.

"Theoretically, we should have access to this information," Tiziana von Witzleben, co-founder of the Heisse Luft initiative, told DW. "Maybe the German government doesn't have the capacity to [collect this information] and share it. But I believe it is on purpose, particularly [on the part of] big players like Google and Amazon. [They] are known to be very secretive about what they do. Because they know that if they tell people, they will get a lot of protest."
Unlike in the US, where a nationwide movement mobilized protests all over the country, protests against data centers in Germany remain a local community phenomenon.

In February, the local council of Groß-Gerau in the Frankfurt region voted against a €2.5-billion ($2.8 billion) data center proposed by a US operator, at least partly as a result of massive protests from the residents wary of heat waste, the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported.

In Maintal, another town in the region, an EdgeConnex mega data center faced intense protest against its plans to build its own gas-fired power plant. The €1-billion project is now searching for power alternatives in a region which is already hitting its grid limits.

blocks.caption: Many Dietzenbach residents view the construction of massive data centers in their neighborhood with concernImage: DW

blocks.text: The race for computational power

Germany is the largest data center market in Europe, both by capacity and number of sites, and the Frankfurt/Rhine-Main region, which includes Dietzenbach, holds over a third of the country's total data center capacity.
Its proximity to the Commercial Internet Exchange (DE-CIX) infrastructure in Frankfurt makes the region attractive for digital cloud operators.

To achieve its strategic goal of doubling data center capacity by 2030, the federal government, a coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the SPD, has proposed amending the Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) that regulates energy consumption and climate protection.

The environmentalist Green Party questions whether the targets are based on real demand. The socialist Left Party, on the other hand, is skeptical of the expansion as a whole. Both parties oppose the government's plans to relax the rules to attract more data centers.

On the opposite end of the political spectrum, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) supports the expansion of data centers but criticizes the law promoting the use of renewable energy to power them.
Europe's quest for digital independence
Why are energy efficiency amendments controversial?
The proposed amendment would push back the deadline for operators to achieve renewable energy targets, and would relax requirements for the reuse of heat waste.
Despite this plan, Tara Merk still considers the push for energy-efficient data centers in Germany to be a progressive example in the global context.
But she is critical of the parts of the law that would give companies the right to declare that the data on the amount of water and electricity they use are trade secrets.

"This proposed amendment shifts the regulatory landscape very much in favor of operators," she told DW. "Having good data is needed to regulate, intervene, and build trust and acceptance within local communities."

"I think [lack of transparency] is ultimately going to foster more antagonism between data centers and local communities, making it harder for operators to expand or even keep their existing sites running the way they are," Merk warned.

Algorithm Watch, an AI watchdog, argued in a public statement that the legal changes the government is proposing are not about cutting bureaucracy, but more about appeasing US tech giants Microsoft, Google, and Vantage.
"German and European operators mostly have no problem with the current rules," Algorithm Watch said. "The amendments run counter to the government's own aim of strengthening German/European firms,"
This summer, the watchdog launched a campaign and collected 150,000 signatures against the amendments to the law, calling for the public reporting obligations of data centers to be retained.
The amendments were presented to the Bundestag in September. If the new law passes, the government hopes it will take effect in January.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Spain grows fruit and vegetables for Europe — but it's running out of water
articles.summary: Spain's southern coast produces up to 25% of Europe's fruit and vegetables. But amid intensive farming, climate change and illegal wells, the water it takes to grow them is drying up.

image.caption: Spain's southern coast grows one-quarter of Europe's fruit and vegetablesImage: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Donana National Park in southwestern Spain — one of Europe's most important wetlands, home to millions of migratory birds and threatened species like the Iberian lynx — is running dry. But rising temperatures and drought caused by climate change are only part of the problem.

The UNESCO-protected region on the Atlantic coast relies on an underground aquifer that's been tapped by hundreds of illegal wells. The reason: Europe's fruit and vegetable supply. Spain provides one-quarter of Europe's fresh produce, supplying colder parts of the continent with fruit and vegetables year-round.

The scale of water extraction in Spain is staggering: In 2016, WWF Spain estimated that the Donana wetland was home to over 1,000 illegal wells and more than 1,700 ponds illegally irrigating an area as big as 4,200 football fields.

blocks.caption: The 'sea of plastic' in Almeria is a massive expanse of plastic-covered greenhouses key to Spain's agricultural productionImage: Viajar24h/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "It's gotten hotter every year. And the water dries up so quickly," one local resident in the town of El Rocio, just north of the wetlands, told DW.

"For me, day to day, the main issue is my animals," said another, hitching his horse up to a tourist carriage. "I have to draw water for them, but the well doesn't have enough water to provide it all at once."
Strawberries are lucrative — but come with a cost

The Donana area used to be royal hunting grounds, consisting of marshes and ponds. In the early 20th century, parts began to be used for dryland farming, agriculture in arid regions that relies heavily on rainwater.

But in 1971, Spain — still under the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco — declared the region's irrigation to be of national interest. The Almonte-Marismas Plan, named after the aquifer it tapped into, was part of a massive, state-sponsored effort to increase food production.

Authorities decided to bet on strawberries, which they called "red gold." According to calculations based on FAO data, strawberries can yield up to €150,000 (about $170,000) in gross revenue per hectare per year, compared to roughly €20,000 for potatoes or €15,000 for grapes.

But growing strawberries at scale also meant using a lot more water. Authorities handed out generous quotas and allotments, seemingly without considering how much extraction the aquifer could handle. Even those legal quotas weren't enough for the ever-expanding fields.

blocks.caption: Strawberries are one of Spain's most lucrative crops, earning up to €150,000 in gross revenue per hectare per yearImage: Adri Salido/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Farmers turned to illegal wells and reservoirs to make up the difference. They built them to stockpile water, draining supplies from local residents and the UNESCO World Heritage Site next door.

"There was extreme drought and lack of attention from the administration," said Pedro Banez, of the Condado Water Users' Association. "And we found ourselves with a number of farms — or parts of farms — that fell outside the land classified as irrigable agricultural land."
Police, NGOs track down water thieves

The turning point came in 2019 when, following numerous reports of unlawful wells, a 2-year-old fell into deep, reportedly illegal borehole on farmland near Malaga and died. In the aftermath, Spain's Civil Guard police force created dedicated units focused on water theft.
Two years after that, in 2021, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Spain had failed to protect the Donana aquifer, finding the country in violation of EU law.

Today, police and NGOs like WWF Spain track illegal extraction — near Donana, and other overtaxed agricultural regions across the country — using a mix of old and new tools. They start with satellite images of the region, comparing them against land rights maps to flag areas that appear greener than their legal status allows. Drones follow, giving investigators a closer look at where the water is actually coming from.
With Spain in drought, farmers drill illegal wells
Some wells are completely illegal. Others are legal but extract more than they're allowed, which requires closer, on-site inspection to prove.

Investigators check the flow meters that measure how much water a well is pulling. Tampering is common, often using a powerful magnet which disrupts the internal mechanism of the flow meter, allowing water to pass through unrecorded.
Farmers caught extracting illegally can be charged with crimes against the environment and fraud. Most face fines, but sentences can run up to five years in prison.
Spain's government, farmers tackle water misuse

In a bid to undo decades of overuse, local and national authorities have negotiated a €1.4 billion joint plan. The government has continued shutting down illegal wells, sealing almost 300 in the Donana region alone.
Officials have also started buying up farmland, rewilding it and turning it into protected areas, while setting up funds to create jobs in other sectors like tourism and renewable energy.
Spain's invisible war for water
Farmers, meanwhile, have had to change how they water their crops.

Many have switched to drip irrigation systems, where each plant gets its own individual dripper, paired with moisture sensors that report exactly how much water a plant needs. That cuts down on the overuse of both water and fertilizer.
Farmers have also begun planting less water-intensive crops and shifting their growing season to colder months.
Sustainable solutions to secure water
Spain isn't alone in confronting this problem. As economies mature, fruit and vegetable production starts being outsourced to places with cheaper labor, fewer restrictions and more sun.

Mexico, Brazil and Colombia grow food for parts of the US, while countries in southeast Asia export a lot of produce to China or Japan. Some countries in northern Africa, including Morocco and Egypt, also supply fresh fruits and vegetables to their European neighbors to the north. But, as in Spain, intensive agriculture has strained local water supplies.
Saving Europe's largest wetlands

Morocco has tried to turn the tide by using satellite comparisons to monitor irrigation and offering subsidies for farmers who switch to drip irrigation. In India, the government is trying to move farmers toward less water-intensive crops.
And in California, the US state has paid farmers to halt certain types of irrigation and introduced legislation to monitor and allocate water more sustainably.

Securing water, no longer seen as an unlimited resource, will increasingly be a challenge as the effects of climate change intensify. Addressing overextraction will take a coordinated effort from governments, farmers and the industries that depend on their water.
Additional research by Nicole Ris. Edited by: Martin Kuebler, Sarah Steffen

articles.title: Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
articles.summary: A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.

image.caption: Milei spoke at the UN General Assembly in New York days before threatening international legal action against the UK (FILE: 23/09/2026)Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance

blocks.text: Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.
The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.
What has Argentina threatened to do?
Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.

"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.
"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.
Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

blocks.caption: Port Stanley is the capital of the British-controlled Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas (FILE: 07/10/2019)Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.
His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.
Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.
What is the Sea Lion oil project?
Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.
The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.
Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.
The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.

blocks.caption: Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falkland Islands in 1982 after Argentine forces invaded the British-controlled territory [FILE: 1982]Image: PA/empics/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.
Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?
The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.
Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.
The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.
The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.
Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.

articles.title: UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
articles.summary: The US government sees "the hand of a foreign actor" in the security scare at RAF Fairford, a hub for US heavy bombers in Europe. Donald Trump criticized the suspects being released on bail amid…

image.caption: Police sealed off the area near the air base amid Sunday's operation Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US government has described the security alert over the weekend at the RAF Fairford base in southern England as a "very serious situation," thanking UK authorities for their cooperation.
But President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also both questioned the move to grant the five suspects bail under strict conditions as investigations against them continue.

RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

blocks.caption: Long-range US bombers have operated out of Fairford since it was set up near the end of World War IIImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Rubio and Trump say about the case?

Marco Rubio said in an interview with Fox News that while there was much he could not say on air for now, the security scare during which five young men were detained constituted a very serious situation.

"It's one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won't get into great detail about that yet," he said, without mentioning Iran until a later point in the interview in a more hypothetical context.

"I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," Rubio said.
The Iranian Embassy in London, meanwhile, said that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" of Iranian involvement.
Rubio also echoed President Donald Trump in saying that "a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have released on bail."
Trump had mentioned the issue in comments to reporters in the White House earlier on Monday.
"I will tell you, I would have said, 'Don't let them have bail.' I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that," he said.
UK releases air base plot suspects
What have British investigators said about the case?

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday in the vicinity of the air base, which is in a rural area roughly two hours' drive west of the capital. They were wearing face coverings.
Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.

Locals were able to return home on Monday, and preliminary reports from the British Press Association and others suggestd the materials in the vehicles were not viable explosives, but counterterrorism and explosives experts continued to examine the scene.

The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged the "significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident," and said investigators were considering "every possible angle."
One of these angles, he said, was the possibility "that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Taylor said that the men had been released under stringent conditions, and that granting them bail did not in any signify an end to investigations against them.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said that decisions like granting bail were operational matters for police and prosecutors, not politicians.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a security meeting known as Cobra, after the secure Cabinet Office Briefing Room A that hosts such sessions, on Monday evening.

blocks.caption: Even prior to Sunday's deployment, security was already tighter than usual at sensitive UK facilities like RAF FairfordImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is RAF Fairford?
RAF Fairford is a large military airbase not far north of Swindon in Gloucestershire, west of London.

It's a base for US heavy bombers in Europe and has been used as a launch point for operations involving long-range B-52s in a series of conflicts in recent decades including both Iraq wars, the NATO bombing of the former Yugoslavia, and most recently in a limited capacity in Iran this year.
Residents in the Cotswolds region had noted an increased security presence and activity at the base amid the conflict, as is often observable around such bases during such periods.

Because of the longstanding close military ties — and very often infrastructure set up during World War II when Nazi Germany occupied much of Europe — southern England is home to a string of airbases also used by the US military.

articles.title: 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide are caused by infections, study finds

image.caption: A health worker shows vials of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine during a campaign aiming to protect girls from cervical cancer, in Karachi, Pakistan, in 2025. The virus causes 100 per cent of cases of cervical cancer. (Fareed Khan/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: For many people, sun exposure, smoking and family history are the first thoughts that come to mind regarding cancer risk factors. While infections are rarely high on the list, new research shows one in eight cancers worldwide are actually caused by them.

These viruses, bacteria and other microbes are the focus of a new paper published Monday in The Lancet Oncology that linked an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 — 12 per cent of all new cases — to these infectious agents.

A team of researchers at The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), an arm of the World Health Organization, conducted the study. They found the largest number of cancer cases attributed to infections globally were caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which can increase the risk of stomach cancer and accounted for 760,000 cases, predominantly in eastern Asia.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed close behind. HPV, which causes 100 per cent of cervical cancer cases and also anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers, accounted for nearly 750,000 new cases globally, with high rates in sub-Saharan Africa. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) were also linked to a significant number of liver cancer cases.
For the first time, researchers linked even more cancers to infections, expanding their list to include 16 additional ones.
Gary Clifford, a cancer epidemiologist and study co-author based in Lyon, France, said the science has advanced significantly.

"There's been new infectious agents identified in this time as being cancer-causing, and even the infectious agents that we knew about in the past, the evidence has increased about the number of different cancers that they can cause," he said.
Some of those new infectious agents included HIV and its link to cervical cancer, and a very rare virus called Merkel cell polyomavirus that can lead to an aggressive form of skin cancer.

To come up with numbers, researchers first examined which infections cause cancer, then calculated what fraction of these cancers can be linked to specific infections and applied those calculations to global databases of new cancer cases.

Another significant shift is the recognition of the role of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV was linked to about 260,000 cases globally in 2024, and can lead to nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers and Hodgkin's lymphoma.
"That's quite a big burden of cancer caused by Epstein-Barr virus that was not counted in the past, but is now recognized," Clifford said.

Epstein-Barr virus is also a key risk factor in developing multiple sclerosis, and unlike some of the other infections that have vaccines or antibiotic treatments, there are no available tools to fight against it.

items: New findings 'strongly suggest' Epstein-Barr virus may help trigger multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: "The fact that we're seeing Epstein-Barr has caused all these chronic diseases — it's increasingly becoming a target that people need to focus on for prevention," he said.

The global report highlights vast regional differences, mostly driven by historical disparities, researchers said. High-income countries that established cancer screening and vaccination programs over the last few decades are doing much better compared to lower- and medium-resourced countries where access to prevention and treatment is limited.
"We really still have a lot of work to do implementing things that we know work and we've known for a long time but haven't really made it into all populations in the world," Clifford said.
In North America, the burden of cancer-causing infections is much lower, but H. pylori and HPV are the most common sources.
Infections causing cancer in Canada

In Canada, according to a 2019 study, the rate of cancers attributable to infections was estimated to be at four per cent. Karena Volesky, an epidemiologist in Montreal, led the Canadian research team while at McGill University.
"It tells us how important each of the 12 infections are," Volesky said of the new global numbers.
While there is a lower prevalence of these forms of infections in Canada, her study estimated these infections lead to more than 7,000 cancer diagnoses each year.
Doctors urge Canadians to get HPV vaccine to prevent cervical cancer
"HPV is certainly an infection that we're keeping an eye on in Canada," said Elizabeth Holmes, the director of health policy at the Canadian Cancer Society.
Holmes said cervical cancer rates had been steadily declining in Canada due to robust childhood vaccination programs, but plateaued last year.
"That's certainly a concern — that we might not meet our goal of elimination of cervical cancer by 2040 unless those rates start to decline again," she said.

items: Cervical cancer rates show a 'concerning plateau,' according to new Canadian Cancer Society data

blocks.text: Human papillomavirus is transmitted through sexual contact, but the HPV vaccine protects against the most common forms of infection that can cause cancer.
Canada's cervical cancer elimination plan aims to increase vaccination rates to 90 per cent, increase screening rates to 90 per cent and ensure timely followup care after screening.
"Right now, only about five provinces are above 80 per cent, and I think at least one is as low as 66 per cent," Holmes said.
The stomach bacteria that can lead to cancer

The infection leading to the most cancer cases is Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium first discovered in the early 1980s that mainly leads to gastric cancers. While the research found the highest burden in eastern Asia in countries like Japan, South Korea and China, it's a problem here, too.
"It's a horrible disease to die from," said Dr. Paul Moayyedi, a leading researcher and gastroenterologist at McMaster University. About 2,000 Canadians die every year from stomach cancer.

Moayyedi wants to see a universal screening program for the bacterium, which can be detected through a blood or breath test, stool sample or endoscopy and treated with a combination of antibiotics over a two-week period.

Helicobacter pylori is associated with crowded living conditions and poor sanitation in childhood. While most people with it can live a long life without any issues, if left untreated, it can cause ulcers and stomach cancer for some.

Moayyedi said stomach cancers may not be seen as high priority compared to other types of cancers, but believes screening programs for those at high risk, such as people with a family history of stomach cancers or First Nations communities, would save lives.
"In consultation with the elders of local communities it would be important to at least offer those groups screening if they would want it," he said.

articles.title: How a rape rumour sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
articles.summary: Police are trying to verify whether a female student was raped at Lovely Professional University (LPU).

blocks.text: Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBC
Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday
ByZoya Mateen & Azadeh Moshiri
BBC News, Delhi
One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.

Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.

Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.
But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.

Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.

Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.
By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.

University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.
Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests

blocks.text: Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests
What happened?
The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.

The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.
BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.

Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.
Behind the gates, students described a night of fear.

"We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."
Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Punjabi
Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence
So why have police lodged a case?
Because that was among the protesters' central demands.

"The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.
Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.
Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room.
"As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.
But they are continuing to examine the footage.

"The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday

blocks.text: Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday
Why did the protests grow so large?
It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.

There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university.
"We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."

Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.
Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.
On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.

The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.

Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.

blocks.caption: Image caption, There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest

blocks.text: Image source, ANI
There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest
What is happening now?
For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.
Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.
The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.
The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?

Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest.
"I feel students can't do this," she said.
Additional reporting by Harmandeep Singh, BBC Punjabi

articles.title: Hurricane Polo makes landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
articles.summary: The storm moved ashore on the Baja California peninsula, which is a popular tourist destination.

blocks.text: Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and heavy rain that has already flooded some coastal areas.
Mexican officials said Polo moved ashore just south of the surfing and fishing village of Las Barrancas bringing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h).

Polo is moving northeast and on the forecast track, its core is predicted to continue passing over Baja California Sur before moving inland over the southern part of the Mexican state of Sonora later on Tuesday.
Residents in threatened areas have been encouraged to seek shelter.
Shopkeeper Maria Palomino, 57, spent the night at a high school which has been turned into a temporary shelter. "If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," she told AFP news agency.
A whale-watching and fishing guide who was boarding up the facade of his home told AFP the storm was "coming with full force".

The US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) said that while Polo was expected to weaken as it moved over the Baja California peninsula, it was forecast to still be at hurricane strength when it makes its second landfall in mainland Mexico.

Meteorologists said Polo could dump between 6 and 12 inches (150-300mm) of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, which they warned could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.

The NHC said a storm surge was also expected to produce significant coastal flooding in areas of onshore winds. "Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves," it said in an update.
Even before Polo made landfall, residents said there were power cuts in Baja California Sur.

US media reported some flooding in the fishing town of Puerto San Carlos and the Associated Press said waves crested sea barriers in the area, where many residents had been evacuated due to the threat.

articles.title: Grave of boy who vanished at residential school found decades later, First Nation looks for others like him
articles.summary: The family of 11-year-old Johnny Kiyawasew, who never came home from St. Francis Xavier residential school, spent decades searching for answers. Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of…

image.caption: Robert Kiyawasew's brother Johnny Kiyawasew was 11 years old in 1943 when he didn't return from St. Francis Xavier residential school in Calais, Alta. (Justin Pennell)

blocks.text: Indigenous

The family of 11-year-old Johnny Kiyawasew, who never came home from St. Francis Xavier residential school, spent decades searching for answers. Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of Alberta say they're doing extensive research to uncover the stories of other children like Johnny who went to residential school but never made it home.
'It's not right… the church should have told my dad that he had passed away,' says brother
Johnny Kiyawasew was 11 years old when he died in a small town hospital in northern Alberta in 1943, a world away from his Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation family.
Forced to enroll at Catholic-run St. Francis Xavier Residential School in Calais, Alta., Johnny never returned home, and it was decades before his brothers and sisters learned what happened to him.
"My parents, like my dad, was never told about nothing. They wrote a death certificate without his knowledge or nothing," said Robert Kiyawasew, Johnny's younger brother.
"It's not right… the church should have told my dad that he had passed away."
After years of unanswered questions, Robert Kiyawasew said his older sister Roseann, with the help of a private investigator, found Johnny's gravesite in 2013.
"That caretaker said, 'I know exactly where he's buried and I'll show you where,'" said Robert Kiyawasew.
According to provincial records, Johnny died of pulmonary tuberculosis in a hospital in High Prairie, where he is buried, over 75 kilometres away from the residential school.

Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of Alberta say they're undergoing extensive research to uncover the stories of children like Johnny, including many of his relatives, who went to residential school but never made it home.
'It is heartbreaking'
Sheldon Sunshine, chief of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, said research shows many children enrolled at St. Francis Xavier died from tuberculosis and malnutrition.
"It's not data, it's people," said Sunshine.

"When you see the names and, you know, it's saddening, what our people went through, having perished because of the results of the living conditions in that school, having perished because of the results of the living conditions in that school. It is heartbreaking."
Robert Kiyawasew said he's thankful his sister was able to track down Johnny's grave before she died.
"I visit every time I have a chance now," said Robert Kiyawasew.
"To see that lonely little grave, out there all alone."
Sturgeon Lake family's search for a brother lost at residential school
A day school survivor himself, Robert Kiyawasew said he experienced harms similar to his siblings who attended St. Francis Xavier, and was punished for speaking his language.
"To treat us Natives like we don't exist… no," said Robert Kiyawasew.
"We belong in our culture. Our heritage is our right to be like that."

items: After 50-year search, Inuk mother finds daughter's grave 2,000 km from home
Letitia John died at a residential school. Her identity was lost until now

blocks.text: According to the Sturgeon Lake residential school narrative at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (NCTR), a summary of the school's history prepared by the Government of Canada as part of its response to litigation, at least five children died at the school in 1943.

It quotes a 1943 document saying the school "is falling to ruin and has become a source of danger for the health of Indian children as well as a fire hazard," adding some student deaths "last winter" had been said to be due to "the lack of comfort" resulting from poor heating.
Difficulty obtaining records
Raymond Frogner, senior director of research and head of archives at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, said residential school records were disorganized, inconsistent and unreliable.
"It was managed by church groups, which are private, provincial governments, federal governments, and all of these organizations never talked to each other," said Frogner.
"It's like putting a jigsaw puzzle back together when the pieces are missing."
Frogner said many church records are not available, have incorrect or different dates from provincial or federal documents, and when they are tracked down they are often withheld.
Sunshine said several times Sturgeon Lake researchers have been told by church officials they will only release the documents of a student to someone with family ties.

items: Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation says 62 potential unmarked graves found on northern Alberta reserve

blocks.text: "How do you have family ties when a lot of them are passing away?" said Sunshine.
"That really shuts the door on finding that information…. It's going to limit us to finding all of our children."
Sunshine said the First Nation will continue to work to piece together the stories of children who were enrolled at St. Francis Xavier and never came home.
"If we don't know where these children are, how can we find closure for some of our families?" said Sunshine.
"Talking about intergenerational trauma? That's part of it."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Edzi'u Loverin is a graduate of CBC's Indigenous Pathways Program and has reported in Vancouver and Winnipeg since 2024. Edzi'u is a member of the Taku River Tlingit First Nation and a registered member of the Tahltan Nation, but is currently based in xʷməθkʷəy̓əm, Sḵwx̱wú7mesh, and səlilwətaɬ territories. articles.title: What no one told me about the land that would become my home
articles.summary: When Ashish Barua's daughter brought home Métis beadwork, it made him realize that as a newcomer, he'd been taught virtually nothing about Indigenous history and culture.

image.caption: After his 10-year-old brought home Métis beadwork, it sparked an interest in Ashish Barua to learn more about Indigenous history and culture. Here he visits a monument to Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG) in Prince Albert, Sask. (Lisa Risom/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·First Person
When Ashish Barua's daughter brought home Métis beadwork, it made him realize that as a newcomer, he'd been taught virtually nothing about Indigenous history and culture.
Learning Indigenous history was not on my to-do list as a newcomer to Canada until my daughter opened my eyes
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
This First Person column is the experience of Ashish Barua, who lives in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
My daughter came home from summer camp with a piece of art — six little flowers, dot-painted in red and yellow. She set it on the dining table like she'd been waiting all day to show us.
"It's Métis beadwork. Do you know there's a story behind it?" she asked, clearly proud of herself.

I was curious. She told me Métis hunters used to bead their gloves in patterns unique to their own family. During a hunt, a man might drop his glove beside an animal he'd killed as a gauntlet to prove it was his. Later, his family would spot the pattern and know it was theirs.
I wasn't sure she had it right. I looked it up that night, half expecting she'd mixed up some detail.
She hadn't.
My 10-year-old taught me that. I'd lived in Saskatchewan for a couple years after moving to Canada in 2024 — Saskatoon first, then Regina, now Prince Albert. But I'd never once heard this.
I was proud she'd learned about Indigenous history at school and at camp. But it also bothered me a little. Why hadn't anyone taught this history to us, the adults?

Before that evening, my knowledge of Indigenous Peoples in Canada was sparse, and not always kind. I'd absorbed local stereotypes the way you do when you're new somewhere — a comment here, a headline there, a passing remark nobody bothered to explain.

I never sat down and decided to believe any descriptions of Indigenous people in particular. Those viewpoints just settled in, quietly, the way secondhand furniture ends up in a house nobody remembers buying. I think a lot of newcomers arrive carrying some version of this reality. Nobody hands it to you on purpose. It just comes with the move.

Various settlement services we used had covered the basics of making a move: getting a health card, a lease, a driver's licence and teaching how to survive a winter that hits faster and harder than anything I'd ever known. But nobody mentioned I'd moved onto treaty land.
Nobody said this year marks 150 years since Treaty 6 was signed. Nobody told me Prince Albert is Métis homeland too, with its own history running under the one I could see.
So I looked into that history myself, signing up for a course called Advancing Reconciliation that was offered through the First Nations University of Canada.

I expected something dry, but it wasn't. I learned about the treaties, what the Crown promised, and what still hasn't been delivered to Indigenous Peoples. I learned how much of what I thought I knew about Indigenous people was wrong or missing context.

I come from Bangladesh, a country that was under British rule for nearly 200 years, and then under Pakistan's rule for around 24 years. I'd read that history my whole life without ever once piecing it together. My country had faced colonization, just as Indigenous People did, but I'd never actually connected those two things before.

None of this was ever hidden. This history was all just sitting there. What was missing wasn't the information. It was someone putting it in front of me early on and saying, "This matters. You should know it."
My daughter went to a powwow this year through her school. I didn't go. At the time, it barely registered, just another school thing, another event. I couldn't have told you why it mattered.

But a few weeks ago, I stood in front of Passage Home, the new bronze sculpture down by the Saskatchewan river in Prince Albert. It's shaped like a travois, the kind once pulled by dogs and horses across the plains, and it's meant to symbolize carrying home the Indigenous children who never made it back from residential schools. The city unveiled it in August to mark the 150th anniversary of Treaty 6.
A year ago, I might have walked past it.

Now I stood there longer than I meant to. Inside the sculpture, there are small shoes, standing in for the children who never made it home. I thought about a glove dropped beside a fallen animal, so a family could find their way to it. I thought about a course I'd almost skipped, a powwow I didn't go to.

Standing there, it struck me plainly. You can't really make a home somewhere until you understand the history behind it. And no one was going to hand me that understanding; I had to go find it myself.
I hope the next person who moves to Canada to learn that sooner than I did.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ashish Barua moved to Canada from Bangladesh in 2024. He lives in Prince Albert, Sask., with his wife and daughter. He enjoys exploring the province's parks and lakes, learning about the land's history and watching his daughter grow into her own love of sport and art.

articles.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
articles.summary: The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but it cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared with journalists.

image.caption: ShinyHunters told CBC News they achieved their goals with a massive FBI data breach and do not intend to release the information to the public. (Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but it cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared with journalists.
A representative added, however, that data they already shared is 'out of our control'
The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared.

ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI last Tuesday — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — and gave the law enforcement agency one week to rescind an ⁠unflattering statement about the group.

With the deadline approaching, a ShinyHunters representative sent CBC News a statement Monday saying they were never planning to release the sensitive data, adding that the media and the public have "made many false assumptions and wild speculations."

The group has been linked to dozens of cyberattacks targeting large companies and institutions. ShinyHunters typically demand ransom payments in exchange for not releasing sensitive data, but they have been adamant that was not their intention in this case.
Campaign to 'combat disinformation'
ShinyHunters denied asking the FBI for a ransom, but acknowledged "past operations" could leave them open to misinterpretation.

"The reason why we have stated multiple times that this is not extortion is because since the very beginning we had made our decision that we would never publish this data. We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to," the statement said in part.
The group told CBC News that their actions against the FBI were part of a campaign to "combat disinformation" about their tactics.

"If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would've never been this widespread. We'd have been ignored and disregarded. However, now everyone knows what the issue is and what we are doing."

ShinyHunters took issue with an FBI report from May that said, among other things, the group is known to threaten family members of its targets and threaten to release embarrassing or compromising images of its victims.

items: What drives ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for hacking the FBI?
Dutch police arrest security professional in ShinyHunters investigation

blocks.text: ShinyHunters denied ever using those tactics and released a statement following last Tuesday's data breach giving the FBI one week to remove or "correct" the report.
The group shared a 5,000-line spreadsheet of breached FBI data with some journalists, which it said represented only a small piece of its claimed two- to three-terabyte trove.
The sample included names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for what it claimed were thousands of FBI employees.

When CBC News asked ShinyHunters on Monday whether they have taken any steps to ensure the shared data isn't leaked by other sources, the representative said they "cannot guarantee" what will happen to those samples, "because that is out of our control and certain journalists violated our trust."
There's a data breach at Canadian schools. What do we know?
'Can't trust them,' researcher says
Ian Lin, an ethical hacker and head of research and development at Toronto-based cybersecurity company Packetlabs, says that's concerning.
He says he's seen "a number of researchers" claiming online to have obtained the data, in addition to journalists.
"There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," Lin told CBC News.

items: A cyberattack hit universities worldwide, including top Canadian schools. Here's what we know
Telus probes cybersecurity incident that 'ShinyHunters' group claims responsibility for

blocks.text: The hack, which one former FBI operative called a "foreign intelligence service goldmine," has raised concerns about the safety of the agency's employees.

The New York Times reported Monday that the FBI sent out a staff memo acknowledging employees had personal information stolen in a cybersecurity incident, and instructing them to remain vigilant at home and at work and report any unsolicited contacts or threats.

Lin says he does not have high hopes ShinyHunters will keep their word, saying it's common for criminal hacking groups to renege on their promises or to use the same set of data as leverage multiple times.

"Why they did this, I think was for attention. But you still can't trust them to keep safe your data. Because now this is leverage over the law enforcement and FBI. And at any moment they could choose to use this data for their own additional purposes," he said.
"The FBI and law enforcement should all still remain vigilant. There should be massive lessons learned from the FBI side."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Germany news: Bremerhaven port to receive defense boost
articles.summary: Bremerhaven's port and Bremen's airport will be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs in case of an attack on the alliance. It comes as European countries upgrade militarily amid Russia's war in…
articles.byline: Wesley Dockery, Richard Connor, Roshni Majumdar

image.caption: Bremerhaven is Germany's second-biggest cargo port after Hamburg Image: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 29, 2026
Bremerhaven's port to be upgraded for German, NATO defense needs
The North Sea port of Bremerhaven will be upgraded to better serve German and NATO defense needs, German officials said on Tuesday.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius signed a memorandum of understanding on Tuesday which will transform the port into a "Deployment Hub" in the case of an attack on the NATO bloc. The plan will cost some €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion).

blocks.caption: German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius (right) signed the memorandum of understanding with Bremen Mayor Andreas BovenschulteImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has caused European countries to draw up plans in case of an attack on a NATO member, such as Germany.
"Tens of thousands of soldiers will need accomodation and food. Machinery and equipment must be maintained and operated accordingly," Pistorius said.

Bridges, roads and railways will need to be boosted to facilitate the transportation of NATO equipment arriving at the Bremerhaven port. Bremen's airport will also be expanded with more logistics space as part of the plan.

articles.title: Burnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference – UK politics live
articles.summary: Union leader says getting rid of triple lock not ‘the right thing’ as the PM prepares to lay out his ‘hope comes from honesty’ vision in Liverpool this afternoon

blocks.text: LIVE Updated 4m ago
Key events

items: 4m agoLucy Powell says Labour committed to triple lock for this parliament - but won't say if it could go after election
21m agoBurnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

blocks.text: Burnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

Good morning. The day after Donald Trump won his first US presidential election in 2016, Ed Miliband (at that point just an ex Labour leader) went on the World at One and gave an astute assessment of the lessons to be learnt from Trump by progressives. Trump was offering “big solutions”, he said – a theory he later fleshed out in a book called “Go Big”. Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader at the time, and he certainly offered voters a “Go Big” vision – but for various reasons he could not persuade the electorate. But today a more mainstream Labour leader is also going to embrace “Go Big”.

According to the Labour party’s overnight briefing, Andy Burnham is going to use his first conference speech as leader to set out what he will describe as “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”.
Burnham will say:
double quotation markWe can’t carry on as we are. Politics-as-usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.

According to the Labour briefing, Burnham will say this will require “honest conversation” with the public and taking on the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long by Westminster, including social care, youth unemployment, and the need for greater public control of energy, water and housing. He will say:
double quotation markHope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.

As Kiran Stacey, Jessica Elgot and Pippa Crerar report in the Guardian splash, Burnham will take his first major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.

blocks.caption: Guardian splash Photograph: Guardian

blocks.text: But, for most of the media, it looks as if the story of the day will be another “Go Big” gamble by Burnham. On Sunday he revealed for the first time that he wants to fight the election on a colossal promise – a pledge to set up an NHS-style care service, with care free at the point of delivery. He did not say how this would be funded, but over the past 24 hours Downing Street has done nothing to quash speculation that part of the proposal will involve getting rid of the pension triple lock. This is one of the sacred cows of British politics, conventionally viewed as untouchable (even though in private many politicians from all parties agree with the view of almost all reputable economists, which is that in the long run its costs are unsustainable.)

blocks.caption: Times splash Photograph: The Times/Times
Telegraph splash Photograph: Daily Telegraph/Telegraph
i splash Photograph: The i
Express splash Photograph: Daily Express

blocks.text: Burnham does not seem likely to say he will definitely fight the next election on a proposal to get rid of the triple lock. (Labour promised in its manifesto to keep it for this parliament, and Burnham is sticking to that.) “Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether,” we report today in our splash. So it looks as if Burnham will launch a pre-election debate, in the hope that he can persuade the public that axing an expensive and badly-targeted perk for pensioners is a price worth paying for transformative reform to adult social care. In his LBC phone-in yesterday, Burnham accepted there was a chance voters might just say no.
One of the voters saying no is Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite, one of the most powerful unions in the Labour party. Asked about getting rid of the triple lock, she told the Times:

double quotation markI think it would be almost electoral suicide. Morally, I just don’t think it’s the right thing. We’re the lowest in the G7 in terms of how much we spend on pensions. I think that’s an embarrassment, quite frankly, because we’re one of the six richest economies in the world. I think it would be an absolute disaster, it would send completely the wrong message. I cannot understand why we keep going back to pensioners.
Here is the agenda for the day.
10am: The conference opens. The first speaker in a debate on power to communities is Chris Byrant, the Northern Ireland secretary. Claire Ward, the mayor of the East Midlands, is also speaking.

10am: Lucy Powell, the deputy leader, speaks at a “what can Labour learn from its members” fringe event. Other ministers speaking at fringe events this morning include Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, and Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister.
Around 11.40am: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, addresses the conference.
2pm: Andy Burnham gives his speech to the conference.
5pm: Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, and Alan Milburn, the former cabinet minister who has chaired a review on Neets, speak at a Tony Blair Institute fringe event.

Given that it will be a big day in British politics, we will have comments open later for a few hours. I do look at comments when they are open, but I can’t read them all and if you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

items: 4m agoLucy Powell says Labour committed to triple lock for this parliament - but won't say if it could go after election
21m agoBurnham is told axing pension triple lock would be ‘electoral suicide’ as he prepares to address Labour conference

blocks.text: Lucy Powell says Labour committed to triple lock for this parliament - but won't say if it could go after election

Lucy Powell, the deputy Labour leader, has been doing a media round this morning. In interviews, she stressed that Labour is committed to keeping the pensions triple lock for the duration of this parliament. But she did not deny reports that Andy Burnham might use his speech to suggest that it should go in the next parliament. (See 8.40am.)
She told Sky News:

double quotation markWe are committed to the triple lock. It’s in our manifesto. The triple lock has really delivered for pensioners, in this country, over the course of this parliament … I don’t know what Andy’s going to say about that today, but I know that what he’s talking about is this big conversation about solving these big problems, but being really honest with people that they come at a cost. You can’t just solve the social care crisis without having the big conversations about how you’re going to do this.

articles.title: From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on women
articles.summary:
As outrage grows over cases​ of sexual violence, activists are demanding a shift from controlling women to confronting men’s behaviour. Plus, Tony Klor’s ‘hella dope’ city vlogs

As an Indian…

blocks.text: As an Indian woman, I often feel myself oscillating between states of anxiety or anger. The anxiety is about doing the mental maths of how to stay safe – thinking about what I’m wearing, where I am going and how I’ll get there, and so on. The anger is at the sheer absurdity of this, and the stories of of sexual violence and harassment I read about every day. I am not the only one.

Last week, two particularly enraging incidents captured national attention. First, a video showing a group of men accused of harassing and molesting two teenagers at night in Bihar’s Jamui went viral. Then, a 17-year-old, out with a friend in Delhi, was allegedly gang-raped in a park by men posing as police. After, women in Bihar told Outlook how the incident in Jamui triggers greater controls and pressure on them. In Delhi, authorities curbed access to public parks and a premier women’s college, Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), briefly moved classes online.

I have noticed this pattern repeatedly: after incidents of sexual violence go viral on social media, the fallout further ensnares women. We are the ones who get told to avoid certain places, regulate our behaviour, dress modestly or be home earlier, thereby placing the burden of escaping this menace on us. Feminist activist Kavita Krishnan has described this phenomenon as “perhaps the most widespread form of gender-based violence in India”.

Instead of figuring out why sexual violence remains entrenched in our society, how patriarchal agency perpetuates such violence or what kind of social conditioning is needed for men, women are instead expected to take up less public space. (It is another matter that women might not be safe even inside their own homes.)

Regulating women is easy because “it does not require any institutional cost and, most of all, it sends the signal to concerned parents that the problem is being handled”, says Meena Kandasamy, a feminist author, whose latest novel, Fieldwork As a Sex Object, is about a woman’s life being upturned when a deepfake video using her face goes viral. “Their target audience is not the young women who feel unsafe but the rest of society.”

In my experience, this repression happens at three levels: first in the realm of family, then in broader society, and ultimately by the state. It begins at home, under the guise of protection, with arbitrary curfews or dress codes. It gets reinforced at a community level with institutions and social groups through moral policing, victim-blaming and the expectation that women should not put themselves in “unsafe” situations.

Then there is the response of the state. Restricting access to parks after sunset can surely reduce the number of people in those places, but it doesn’t address why women are unsafe there. Harassment and sexual violence are, unfortunately, not tied to timings or daylight. And further restricting women’s lives is not the solution to injustices foisted on them. All three, Kandasamy says, consider women as a “problem to be handled”.

“She’s not a citizen (for the state), a member (for the community), or an adult (for the family). She is treated like an inanimate but precious object – like a diamond that has to be locked up to prevent theft,” she said.
‘Moral policing’ of the wrong target

blocks.caption: Indian women commuters board a women-only train carriage. Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPA

blocks.text: Women, however, are pushing back against this approach. In recent days, students from Delhi University have come out on the streets demanding safer public spaces including more street lighting, usable public toilets, more housing and scholarships for female students. Vedayana, 20, a student at Lady Shri Ram College (LSR), says locking up parks is not the solution: “If you are not putting up safety measures to make it accessible to women, then it is as good as saying that the park is only for men.”

The scale of the issue is devastatingly clear. A recently published survey of more than 4,000 women in New Delhi and Bengaluru, found that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year.

Another 2024 study from India and Pakistan found that women’s overall mobility remains abysmally low, and what freedom they do have is almost entirely tied to education, employment or unpaid care work. Substantive mobility for leisure or pleasure is practically nonexistent.

Despite how widespread and urgent the problem is, the political response can further shake public confidence. A female minister from Bihar, commenting on the molestation video said: “Moral policing can be done in a more decent and elegant fashion.” Another minister from the state drew fire for describing it as an “isolated” incident”.

Minimising crimes against women reflects a political culture in which accountability becomes optional. Students such as Vedayana want this to change. Political parties, she tells me, should pledge to not give tickets or positions to anyone accused of sexual harassment. “We don’t want the leaders sitting at the top to perpetrate and preach rape culture,” she adds.

Parliament is not immune to accusations, either: the BJP politician Brij Bhushan Singh, who formerly headed the Wrestling Federation of India, was recently accused of sexual harassment by six female wrestlers – he denies the allegations, and was acquitted by a magistrate, in a case that is undergoing appeal. According to an analysis of 2024 parliamentarians by the Association for Democratic Reforms, 15 winning candidates declared cases related to crimes against women.

For Vedayana, changing the mentality has to begin early with families and the way boys are raised. “If you are in a position of authority, use it to influence people by speaking out against patriarchy and groom your sons first.”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: The Indian women’s cricket team triumphed at this year’s Asian games in Japan Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Smriti Mandhana’s smashing 79 off 45 deliveries helped India reach a formidable 216 in 20 overs. Deepti Sharma’s three-wicket haul helped India end Sri Lanka’s hopes with just 69 runs on board. Sri Lanka settled for silver, while Pakistan claimed the bronze after beating Bangladesh.

Moma | A solo exhibition by one of south Asia’s most distinguished artists, Nilima Sheikh, opened at New York’s Museum of Modern Art at the weekend. Fractured Skies, presented in collaboration with the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art in Delhi, will run until next June.

EC under fire | An explosive Indian Express investigation has revealed how two of the top three election officials objected at least 14 times over a period of 10 months to changes made by the Election Commission over its controversial exercise that has struck 130 million people from the voter rolls.
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: The Ram temple, Uttar Pradesh. Photograph: Press Information Bureau/EPA

blocks.text: An inquiry committee probing the theft of donations from Ayodhya’s Ram Temple has uncovered 105 instances of cash being removed or concealed. The thefts were caught on CCTV cameras.
According to a preliminary report, some of the accused allegedly hid the money on themselves during the process of counting donations and then walked out.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Tony Klor showing India, and the rest of the world, the beauty of Satara. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: Tony Klor’s city vlogs from Indian towns are “hella dope,” to use his own words. The 32-year-old American has visited about 200 cities around the country, taking his Instagram followers to places that rarely feature on a travel itinerary.

It’s a treat to watch him having the time of his life. He marched with Anganwadi workers in Nashik chanting “pay my didis”, ribbed with middle-aged uncles sweating it out in a park, whom he christened “Nizamaddies”. Wandering through the mining town of Ballari, which he describes as “highkey vibey”, he films its temple, church and mosque.

“A lot of people who watch my videos are Indians and they have no idea about these magnificent places in India,” the tech professional-turned-content creator says. “India is like the easiest place to make a friend in the world. People invite me to their weddings on the street that I met five minutes before that. Hospitality is so, so next-level.”
